exp40v2-tech.architecture:
Reading an architecture diagram

Monoliths, services, queues, and where a feature will actually touch.

1. Two meetings, five days apart

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Kinjal Joshipura stood in front of a diagram she had looked at perhaps two hundred times without reading it. She is senior product manager for fares at Kalrav Transit Network, which runs contactless fare collection for a metro and city bus system in western India: 38 stations, 1,250 buses, 9,30,000 taps on an average weekday, of which 6,20,000 are metro and 3,10,000 bus. Three weeks earlier the state transport authority had mandated a daily fare cap of ₹90 and a weekly cap of ₹450, live by 26 January 2027 — 112 days away. A rider who crosses the cap travels free for the rest of that day, on either mode.

The commercial arithmetic was settled. About 26,650 of the 4,10,000 riders who travel on a given day would cross the cap (6.5 per cent), forgoing an average of ₹14 each, or ₹3,73,100 a day — ₹1.12 crore a month against monthly fare revenue of ₹58.59 crore (9,30,000 taps a day at ₹21 is ₹1.953 crore a day, over 30 days). The authority's model expected a 1.5 per cent ridership lift, 13,950 extra taps a day at the blended fare of ₹21, worth ₹2,92,950. The policy therefore ran at a net ₹80,150 a day, ₹24.05 lakh a month. The question was whether it could be built by January.

Kinjal's instinct was that this was a fare-engine change. Lokesh Khaparde, Kalrav's principal engineer, asked one question instead: "When the bus is between two towers and the validator is offline, which box decides whether this rider has already spent ₹90 today?" Nothing on the diagram answered it. Ten days later, on Friday 16 October, the validator firmware had to be frozen for the quarterly over-the-air window of 15 November. The next window was 15 February 2027 — twenty days past the mandate.

Five days earlier, on Thursday 1 October 2026, Jayant Kelkar faced the opposite problem at Laabh Wealth Partners, which administers ₹26,400 crore for 11,40,000 accounts — 4,30,000 on its own app and 7,10,000 through three bank tenants reselling the platform under their own brands. Its diagram is mostly white space around one box: a nine-year-old monolith called Kendra, which contains almost everything that matters. Jayant wanted family accounts: one login seeing a spouse's, a parent's and a minor child's portfolios. Support had logged 2,310 such requests in the year to 30 September, and 1,07,160 accounts already share a mobile number or address with another. His engineers said "one box, one release, six weeks." They were wrong in a way the diagram could not show: the coupling they would break lived inside the box, not between boxes.

2. What a diagram is, and who disagrees about it

An architecture diagram is a projection: a deliberately lossy drawing of a system onto one chosen set of concerns. Perry and Wolf's 1992 formulation remains cleanest — architecture is elements, form and rationale — so a diagram showing elements and form but omitting rationale is half an artefact. The lineage runs from David Parnas's 1972 argument that modules should be drawn around decisions likely to change, through Melvin Conway's 1968 observation that a system's structure mirrors the organisation that built it, to Kruchten's 4+1 views (1995), Evans's context maps (2003), Brown's C4 model (2011), Nygard's decision records (2011) and Team Topologies (2019).

The problem it was invented to solve is coordination under ignorance: no individual holds the system in their head, so a shared, lossy picture lets several people reason about the same change. The question a product manager brings — "where will this feature touch?" — is not about code but about who must be asked, what they must agree, and when their release windows are. Five schools answer it differently, and it is worth being precise about what each would and would not sign.

The structural school (C4, UML, most enterprise-architecture practice) would sign: a hand-drawn diagram at one consistent level of abstraction, every container named and owned, is the primary instrument for planning a change. It would not sign that a picture generated from production traces can replace it, because traces show what the system does, not what it is permitted to do.

The socio-technical school (Conway, Team Topologies) would sign: an element with no owning team is a liability rather than an element, and the org chart predicts change cost better than the component graph. It would not sign that a diagram without ownership annotations can be used for estimation at all.

The data-first school (Evans's bounded contexts, Martin Kleppmann) would sign: the architecture is the set of data-ownership boundaries plus the consistency guarantee on each edge; the rest is decoration. It would emphatically not sign that two components sharing a database are two components — to this school they are one, badly drawn.

The runtime school, grown out of distributed tracing, would sign: every drawn diagram is a hypothesis, and the only evidence is a trace of a real request in production. It would not sign that a diagram is wrong merely because it is simplified; simplification is the point.

The decision-log school (Nygard, and Fowler's definition of architecture as the decisions expensive to reverse) would sign: the picture is a by-product; what matters is the ordered log of irreversible choices and their rationale. It would not sign that a diagram with no recorded rationale is useful six months later, citing how often teams re-litigate settled choices because nobody wrote down why.

The sentence that survives all five: every box is a team, a release window and a data owner; every line is a promise with a failure mode and a price.

3. Mechanics: deriving the touch set

Expert practice turns the vague question into four sets, the last two usually left implicit. D, the data owners: take every noun in the requirement — rider, day, fare, cap, tap, settlement — and ask which component is the system of record for it, because a feature touches every component owning data it reads or writes, not only the one where the user acts. B, the behaviour owners: every verb — cap, refund, reconcile, settle — maps to a component that must execute it. P, the presentation surfaces: every place the change becomes visible, including surfaces the company does not control, such as a tenant's own app. O, the observers: everything downstream reading the resulting events — reporting extracts, audit logs, support consoles, reconciliation jobs. The observer set is where most underestimates hide, because nothing in the user story mentions it.

Applied to the fare cap, D holds the rider ledger (spend so far today), the fare engine (the rule) and the validator (which must decide offline). B adds the reconciliation worker and the settlement service, because a cap earned on a bus leg reduces revenue the metro operator expected. P is the rider app and gate display; O is the authority reporting extract and the support console. The result is Figure 1: nine elements, not one.

At Kalrav's internal rate of ₹21,000 an engineer-day, 121 days is ₹25.41 lakh — trivial against ₹58.59 crore of monthly fare revenue. Effort was never the constraint; three second-order quantities were.

Coordination grows quadratically. Seven teams have 21 pairwise interfaces (7 × 6 ÷ 2). Two sit outside Kinjal's division and one outside the company, and the effort column prices none of those conversations.

Elapsed time is quantised by release windows, not effort. The firmware is 22 engineer-days across three engineers, about eight working days, but must clear the freeze on Friday 16 October — ten calendar days, and only eight working days, after the meeting. Miss it and the fleet update slips from 15 November to 15 February 2027, twenty days past the mandate. The binding deadline was never 112 days away; it was ten.

Non-functional budgets add and multiply. A tap must complete in 300 ms or the gate feels broken. The synchronous chain already consumes 285 ms; a cross-mode cap lookup measured at 55 ms would take it to 340 ms, 40 ms over. Availability compounds the other way: components at 99.95, 99.95 and 99.9 per cent give 99.80 per cent end to end, about 86 minutes of unavailability in a 30-day month, roughly 55,800 taps. Hence the validator holds a local copy of the rider's day-spend and completes offline — which puts firmware, not the fare engine, on the critical path.

4. The conditions, stated as testable claims

The "where will it touch" reading is reliable only when four claims hold, and each can be checked in an afternoon.

Claim one: each box is a separately deployable unit with its own release cadence. True at Kalrav — nine elements, six distinct cadences, one of them quarterly and physical. False at Laabh, where Kendra's fourteen internal modules ship together, so the diagram's single box conceals the only structure that matters.

Claim two: data ownership is exclusive. Broadly true at Kalrav; flatly false at Laabh, whose 2,100-table database is read by every module, so a change to one column's meaning propagates invisibly.

Claim three: the owner of every element is identifiable within one working day. At Kalrav the support console fails this — a vendor product with a six-week queue, which is why its five engineer-days are the longest-lead item after firmware. At Laabh the tax module has a single maintainer. Claim four: every edge has a declared contract and failure behaviour. Kalrav's tap stream does; its vendor console edge does not.

Two situations make the reading actively misleading. A tidy service diagram over a distributed monolith — services that must deploy together — flatters the reader into thinking coordination is cheap when it is dearest. And a diagram used as an estimate misleads both ways: Kinjal's nine boxes are not nine times the work of one, and Jayant's one box is not one-ninth.

5. Hard edges

Multi-product and platform. When products share a platform element, every feature pays a platform tax: the shared team's roadmap sets the date, and mature companies make that team publish a lead time, not a promise.

Two-sided systems. Kalrav's cap is owed to riders but paid for by two operators, so the same event needs two read models and two reconciliations. The settlement element is where the business model lives, and the box product managers omit most often.

Regulated. Audit and consent are first-class elements, not cross-cutting concerns, and external bodies are boxes you cannot roll back. Laabh's largest tenant requires 45 days' notice of a statement-format change: notified on 1 October, the earliest effective date is 15 November 2026 — a constraint with no technical content.

Hardware plus software. The installed fleet is a box with its own state, its own versions and no rollback. Kalrav has 3,032 validators (532 at metro gates, 2,500 on buses). An update on 15 November reaches about 2,790 of the 3,032 within 18 days, by 3 December (92 per cent); the remaining 242 need a depot visit. The feature must be correct on two firmware versions at once for weeks.

AI-native. A model is a box whose behaviour changes without your release and whose edges carry a unit price. The eval harness belongs on the diagram as a first-class element, because without it that edge has no contract at all.

At the seams, mature companies say they keep a canonical diagram. What they keep is a service catalogue with named owners, a generated dependency graph and a hand-drawn context diagram reconciled against it quarterly — plus two or three undrawn edges (a nightly file drop, a spreadsheet, a vendor webhook) that everyone knows and nobody owns.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

Zoom is rarely consistent. One box is a thousand lines of code, the next a platform with forty engineers. The tell: box sizes bear no relation to team sizes or release frequency. Reading boxes as comparable units produces estimates wrong by an order of magnitude both ways. The expert also hears "that isn't on the diagram" as a claim about the view, not the system.

Edges hide consistency, not just synchrony. Experts ask not only "does the caller wait?" but "how stale may this read be, and what if the same message arrives twice?" The tell: nobody can state the staleness bound. At Kalrav, 16,120 of the 3,10,000 bus taps a day are recorded offline (5.2 per cent), so the cap is computed on data hours old and the rule must be idempotent under replay.

The shared database is the undrawn edge; a monolith's modules are the undrawn boxes. The tell is an inversion in estimate error: service-shaped work overruns on coordination, monolith-shaped work on regression. Jayant's project is the second kind, and no Laabh diagram shows it.

Cadence, not count, sets the date. The tell is a plan whose milestones are all sprint numbers with no external window named. Kalrav's nine elements span weekly, fortnightly, monthly and quarterly cycles plus an app-store review; the quarterly one decided everything.

Fan-in measures risk better than depth. A deeply nested call chain is merely slow; a heavily depended-upon element is dangerous. The tell: the box everyone draws in the centre. Changing it costs a regression pass per consumer, so cost scales with consumers, not with the change.

Queued systems have memory you cannot see. Backlogs, retries and dead-letter queues hold state outliving any deployment. The tell: no one can answer "what happens to taps already queued when the fare rule changes at noon?" The obvious reading — asynchrony is safer — is half true; it converts failures from loud to silent.

The diagram's boundary is an organisational claim. Vendors, regulators and tenant banks appear as boxes, but they have notice periods instead of sprints and cannot be rolled back. The tell: the diagram stops neatly at the company's edge, and the longest lead time belongs to something just outside it.

Edges have prices. A synchronous hop costs latency, an asynchronous one reconciliation work, a model call rupees per invocation. The tell: a design review that debates correctness for an hour and never multiplies a per-unit cost by a volume.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the binding constraint is the critical path of one interaction: an extra synchronous hop is a measurable loss, and the question is "can this move off the request path?" In B2B and enterprise it is the integration edge: boxes you do not own have notice periods, certification cycles and their own customers, as Laabh's 45-day clause shows. In platform and marketplace products the distinguishing element is the settlement component where the two sides' money meets — the hardest box to change and the one most often missing from a product manager's first list.

In hardware the fleet is the architecture: version skew is permanent, rollback is a truck, and the freeze date dominates. In AI products the model box lacks a stable contract, so the eval harness and the fallback path are load-bearing structure rather than quality assurance.

By stage the difference is real but smaller than claimed. A twelve-person company's honest diagram has four boxes, and an hour with the engineer who wrote them beats any drawing; a large company's cannot be held by one person, so the ownership catalogue is the artefact that matters. What does not change is the derivation of D, B, P and O — only the cost of getting it wrong.

8. Three worked examples

Kalrav, succeeding by splitting scope. Kinjal split the feature along the firmware boundary. The validator change — carry and decrement a local day-spend counter, accept a cap flag — was cut to the 22 engineer-days that fit the eight working days before the 16 October freeze, and everything cloud-side kept its own cadence. Total effort was unchanged at 121 engineer-days and ₹25.41 lakh; what changed was that the only irreversible date was met.

Jwaala Energy Labs, failing. In February 2026 Janaki Lahiri, VP product at Jwaala, a rooftop solar and battery company, scoped a load-shifting schedule as three cloud elements and 46 engineer-days over six weeks. The diagram showed one box labelled "inverter". There were two: 68,000 of the 2,30,000 installed units (29.6 per cent) ran a first-generation controller that could not take the new schedule format over the air. Work began on 2 February 2026 and shipped on 13 July, 161 days — 23 weeks against six — at 212 engineer-days, 4.6 times the estimate and 166 days of overrun. The proposed remedy, a technician visit to each first-generation unit at ₹640, would have cost ₹4.35 crore. The recovery was architectural: a cloud-side scheduler commanding the older units through the existing daily telemetry channel, delivering 4 of the 9 promised behaviours to that cohort and none of the field visits. Jwaala's lesson was not "draw better diagrams" but "annotate every hardware box with its version distribution".

Lipi Vision Labs, pricing the edges. Lipi processes 4,20,000 insurance-claim pages a month at ₹1.90 of model cost per page, ₹7,98,000. Kabir Lohiya's question-answering feature added a retrieval step: 62,000 questions a month at three model calls each is 1,86,000 calls at ₹2.40, or ₹4,46,400 — a 56 per cent increase, taking the bill to ₹12.44 lakh. No box moved; one edge acquired a price. The conversation that mattered — caching, and which of the three calls could be dropped — began only once the edge carried a cost.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Counting only where the user actsOne team named; no cross-team datesFor each noun, which element is the system of record?Kalrav: the 15 Feb window, 20 days late
Ignoring the observer setNo mention of reports, audit or reconciliationWho reads the event after the user leaves?A wrong settlement file across ₹58.59 crore
Treating effort as elapsed timePlan dates equal the sum of estimatesWhich release window is furthest away?121 engineer-days across two quarters
Trusting a stale picture"That feeds the old job too," heard in week threeCan a new engineer trace a live request against it?Jwaala: 166 engineer-days of overrun

Leaving edges unpricedNo per-unit cost in the design reviewWhat does this edge cost per thousand calls?Lipi: ₹4.46 lakh a month, found after launch

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Drawn versus generated. The generated camp argues, with strong evidence, that hand-drawn diagrams are stale within a release and that an instrument of unknown error rate deserves distrust; traces are ground truth. The drawn camp replies that a generated graph of 400 nodes answers no human question, shows what happened rather than what is allowed, and cannot show an element that does not exist yet — exactly what planning needs. The question would settle against the generated camp if trace-derived graphs left mis-scoping unchanged, and against the drawn camp if audits found hand diagrams wrong on the edges features touch.

Whether the component diagram is the right artefact. The data-first position is that product managers should see a data-ownership map and nothing else, because components churn while ownership of the rider ledger does not. The counter is that release cadence and team boundaries — invisible on a data map — set the dates, as Kalrav's firmware freeze shows. Each side accepts the other's artefact as a supplement and rejects it as the primary.

Whether diagrams should be used for estimation. One camp holds the touch set is the most reliable schedule input a product manager has. The other holds that this is the abuse producing confident wrong dates, since boxes are not units of work, and that the diagram should yield only a list of people to consult. The evidence favours the second on effort and the first on elapsed time, which suggests splitting the practice rather than settling the question.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can name monoliths, services and queues and point at a diagram. Someone who has internalised it arrives with the noun list written, asks for the owner and next release window of every element before discussing design, and treats the first effort estimate as the least interesting number in the room. Staleness, duplicate messages and price per edge are reflex questions. They notice absences — no audit box, no settlement box, no eval harness — faster than they read what is present, and anchor dates to the furthest external window.

12. What each of them decided

Kinjal Joshipura committed on 7 October to a firmware change scoped to the 16 October freeze, and told the authority the cap would be enforced from 26 January with offline taps reconciling within 48 hours rather than instantly. She left the ₹24.05 lakh monthly net cost with the authority, and moved the support-console work forward six weeks to clear the vendor queue.

Jayant Kelkar withdrew "one box, six weeks". Having counted 148 read sites of the holder field across eight modules and 86 hours of regression, he chose the smaller seam: a new relationship table and a read-only family view for Laabh's own 4,30,000 app accounts — 31 engineer-days against 94, roughly a third — leaving the holder field untouched, the bank tenants unaffected and the 45-day notice unused. It serves the 1,640 of the 2,310 logged requests that asked only to view (71 per cent); the 670 wanting to transact wait for an authorisation model he has written down as a decision record rather than a diagram.

Holdings3820
