Three questions in the manner of a teaching note. First: Kinjal bought a date at the cost of a slower reconciliation promise to riders — under what conditions would that trade reverse? Second: Jayant's seam leaves the holder field unchanged, so Laabh will face the same 148 read sites again; is deferring an irreversible decision prudence or debt, and what evidence distinguishes them? Third: both diagrams omitted the element that mattered most — settlement at Kalrav, Kendra's module structure at Laabh. What would a diagram have to show for those omissions to be impossible?

13. Going deeper

APIs and integration basics — the edges in Figure 1 are contracts. Databases, storage and caching — where data lives decides the touch set. Integration patterns: sync, async, events, webhooks — makes the latency and availability arithmetic a design choice. Scalability and performance — why 285 ms survives today but not at ten times the volume. CI/CD, environments and deployment — cadence set Kalrav's real deadline. Feature flags and progressive delivery — shipping into two firmware versions at once. Having a system design conversation — the meeting skill this supports. Technical debt as a concept — prices what Jayant deferred. Multi-tenancy and enterprise configuration — the structure behind Laabh's tenants. Identity: auth, SSO, roles and permissions — the model family accounts needs. Data modelling for PMs — the holder field is a modelling decision. Cloud infrastructure basics — what the boxes run on. Security basics for PMs — every new edge is a surface. Internationalisation basics — a concern touching every presentation element. How web and mobile apps work — why the app store sits on the critical path.
case20v1-tech.architecture:
Hirakani Commerce: Where Will E-Invoicing Touch?

A decision case on reading an architecture diagram

1. Opening

At 8:40 a.m. on Monday 19 October 2026, Pankti Asher stood at a whiteboard in Hirakani Commerce's Surat office, holding a printout of the company's architecture diagram. By six that evening she had to tell Paresh Agarwal, the engineering manager in Bengaluru, which of three plans four of his engineers would start on the next morning. Code freeze for Diwali, which falls on Sunday 8 November, was Friday 30 October. Anything not in the app by then would wait until December.

The feature was easy to state: let a trader generate a GST e-invoice, with its government-issued reference number, the moment an order is confirmed. What nobody had yet agreed was how many boxes on the diagram that sentence touched.

2. Company background

Hirakani Commerce sells an order-taking and billing app to fabric wholesalers and agents in Surat's textile markets, from the Ring Road complexes to Sahara Darwaja. Two former cloth brokers founded it in 2019. Its 2,400 paying accounts generate ₹296.64 lakh a year (Exhibit 1). Traders keep their books in Tally Prime, so Hirakani exports each night's invoices to it. Payments run through Razorpay. Engineers in Bengaluru and Pune ship a release every fortnight, while Surat holds sales, support and product. The fortnight before Diwali is the busiest of the year, when traders restock for the festival and the wedding season that follows. Competition comes from two sides: Udaan pulls retailers into a marketplace, while Zoho Books and Tally itself pull traders toward accounting software that already issues e-invoices.

3. The situation

Since August 2023, any business with turnover above ₹5 crore must register each B2B invoice on the government's Invoice Registration Portal (IRP) and print the returned reference number on it. Hirakani's 640 larger accounts therefore re-key every invoice into Tally or the portal after confirming it in Hirakani. Pushpak Adhia, the customer-success lead in Singapore, had phoned 400 of the 640 in the past fortnight. A total of 148 of them, 37 per cent of those called, said they would move to a rival if Hirakani could not issue e-invoices by Diwali. The other 240 had not been called, and nobody knew what they would say. The 148 accounts carry ₹31.97 lakh of annual fees.

Pinal Antani, a data scientist in Toronto, had mined the order logs. In the busiest five minutes of last year's pre-Diwali week, 1,800 orders were confirmed, 738 of them from the larger accounts. The 640 larger accounts raised 33,280 invoices a month, an average of 52 each. Paresh's team had also tested the IRP sandbox: a call took 2.1 seconds at the median but 11 seconds or longer in its slowest tenth. To Pankti it was one extra button on the invoice screen. One long-standing Ring Road customer had told Pushpak that he copied the same numbers three times a day and would not do so after Diwali.

4. The people

Pankti Asher, product manager in Surat, owns the outcome and has no engineering background. She wants a plan she can explain to traders and defend to Paresh. Paresh Agarwal, engineering manager in Bengaluru, leads four engineers with nine working days, Tuesday 20 to Friday 30 October, before freeze: 36 engineer-days. He wants nothing that destabilises order confirmation in the festival fortnight. Pushpak Adhia, in Singapore and 2.5 hours ahead of Surat, wants a dated promise for the 148. Pinal Antani, in Toronto and 9.5 hours behind Surat until clocks change there on 1 November, wants the team to design for the peak. Her 8:30 a.m. is Surat's 6 p.m., so her morning view of the logs would reach Pankti exactly at the deadline.

5. Exhibits: reading the diagram

Exhibit 2 is the diagram Pankti printed. The apps talk through one API gateway to a single deployable unit, the Core, which holds orders, invoicing, inventory and ledger, and customer pricing. Core writes to one primary database. Three things hang off the Core and its database: a queue feeding a WhatsApp notifier, a payments service calling Razorpay, and a nightly job that reads the database and writes a file for Tally. The feature lands in Invoicing, the shaded box. Because Invoicing sits inside the Core, it shares the Core's 12 request threads with Orders and everything else.

The arrows carry meaning. Where the label says REST, the caller waits for an answer before it carries on. The queue arrow works differently: the sender publishes a message and moves on, and the consumer picks it up when it can. Pankti had thought of this distinction as plumbing. It turned out to be the whole of her decision.

Pinal's logs let Pankti test an idea, treating the sandbox's median and its tail as two scenarios. If Invoicing calls the IRP while the trader waits, each call holds one Core thread for its duration. Arrivals of eligible orders at peak are 738 in 300 seconds, or 2.46 a second. At the median 2.1 seconds, about 5.2 calls are in flight at once; in the slow tail, at 11 seconds, about 27 or more. Core has 12 threads. In the slow tail, the other 1,062 confirmations in that window, from traders who owe nobody an e-invoice, would queue behind the government's portal.

6. The options

Option A: Inline. Invoicing calls the IRP during order confirmation and saves the reference number in the database. It touches four boxes and takes 28 engineer-days (Exhibit 3), leaving eight spare. Traders see the number instantly. The cost is the thread exposure above: a slow portal slows every order in the festival fortnight.

Option B: Queue and worker. Confirmation publishes an event; a new e-invoice worker calls the IRP, retries on failure and writes the number back; the WhatsApp notifier sends it. The Core never waits on the portal. This touches seven boxes and takes 40 engineer-days, four more than the team has.

Option C: Partner link. A GST Suvidha Provider, an approved intermediary for the IRP, hosts the e-invoice screen. The trader taps through from the invoice, and the partner posts the number back to a new Core endpoint. It touches four boxes, takes 19 engineer-days and leaves 17 spare. The partner charges ₹2 an invoice, or ₹66,560 a month at today's volumes, and the trader sees a second screen.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, list every box each option touches. Which three boxes does every option share (counting the Core as one), and why does that matter?
  2. Pushpak's 148 is 37 per cent of 400 called. What can and cannot be said about the other 240, and how should that shape urgency?
  3. Test Option A with Pinal's numbers. At what portal response time do the 12 threads fill, and what happens to the 1,062 ordinary confirmations in that window?
  4. Which option would you take to Paresh by six o'clock, and what would you ask him to confirm first?

8. A note for the learner

An architecture diagram answers one question: where will this feature touch? Count the boxes and arrows each plan crosses, then ask which are shared and which arrows make the caller wait. B, with the most boxes, has the highest estimate, but the count alone does not set cost: A and C both touch four boxes yet cost 28 and 19 days. Risk tracks sharing. Invoicing lives in the Core, so a synchronous external call borrows threads that every trader's order needs.

One defensible path is Option C now and Option B after Diwali. C fits the 36 days with 17 to spare, adds no blocking call to the Core, and answers Pushpak's 148 with a dated promise that can be kept. B is the better long-term shape, since the queue is already in the diagram, but it overruns capacity by four days in the one fortnight when failure is costly. The partner fee is ₹66,560 a month, or ₹7.99 lakh a year, about 25 per cent of the ₹31.97 lakh a year at risk. It is charged on all 640 larger accounts, not only the 148.

The arithmetic on Question 3 settles Option A's risk: 12 threads divided by 2.46 arrivals a second fills at about 4.9 seconds, well below the 11-second slow tail, which would fill the threads more than twice over (about 27 calls against 12). Pankti should also ask Paresh to confirm that the return endpoint can be added to the Core without touching the order path, and should treat the 240 uncalled accounts as an unknown, not as safe. Option A is defensible only with a timeout short enough to protect the threads, and the case does not size one.
exp20v2-tech.architecture:
Reading an architecture diagram

1. A Monday in October

On Monday 12 October 2026, Ananya Rao, a product manager at Bhandar Order Exchange, opened a meeting with a one-line request. Bhandar runs a business-to-business marketplace on which about 1,400 Indian pharmacies and clinics buy consumables from regional distributors. It processes roughly 38,000 orders a month. Of these, 6.5 per cent are delivered only in part, because a distributor ships what it has in stock. That is 2,470 orders a month (38,000 × 0.065). Each one needs a corrected tax document, a credit note, so that the buyer pays and claims input tax credit only on what arrived.

Today the finance team prepares these by hand, at about 12 minutes each. The monthly cost is 29,640 minutes, or 494 hours. Ananya wanted the platform to issue the credit note automatically. The sales head had promised the feature to a hospital group by 1 December, 50 days away. Her draft plan read "small change, one sprint."

Bipin Kashyap, the engineering lead, did not argue. He walked to the whiteboard and drew eight boxes. "Tell me which of these you think this touches," he said. Ananya named two. Bipin circled six. If she took "one sprint" to the hospital group and Bipin was right, Bhandar would miss 1 December, and an auto-generated tax document with a wrong figure is worse than a manual one. The meeting turned on a skill she had never been taught: reading the diagram.

2. The idea

An architecture diagram is a drawing of a software system as boxes (units of code that run and own some responsibility) joined by lines (the ways those units talk to each other). Its purpose is to answer one question quickly: when something changes here, what else must change, and who must be asked? The practice grew from the structured-design work of the 1970s, when programs became too large for one person to hold in their head, and was popularised for networked systems by the "box and arrow" sketches of the 1990s and the C4 model that Simon Brown proposed around 2011.

Three terms recur. A monolith is one deployable program containing many functions. A service is a smaller program that owns one function and is reached over a network through an API (a published request-and-response contract). A queue is a holding area where one component leaves messages for another to collect later. The sentence Ananya could repeat in any meeting without sounding glib is this one:

"Every box is a team and a release; every line is a promise; show me which promises this feature changes."

3. How it actually works

Figure 1 is the diagram Bipin drew, tidied. A buyer's browser or app calls a gateway, the single front door that routes requests. Behind it sit four services: Orders, Catalogue, Payments and Billing. Orders and Billing each own a database; nobody else is meant to read those tables. Orders announces events ("order delivered in part") onto a queue, and a Notification worker and a data-warehouse loader collect them.

Reading it takes four steps, and practitioners usually leave the second and fourth implicit. First, find the box where the user's action starts. For the credit note, that is the Orders service, because a distributor marks a delivery partial there. Second, ask what the feature must know and store: a credit note needs the original invoice, which lives in the Billing database, and the delivered quantities, which live in the Orders database. A feature touches every box that owns data it reads or writes, not just the box where it starts. Third, follow each line out of that box and decide whether it is synchronous or asynchronous. A synchronous call makes the caller wait for the answer; an asynchronous message does not, so the sender cannot know whether the receiver succeeded. Fourth, count the people behind the boxes: who owns each, and when does each ship?

Applied to Figure 1, the walk runs as follows. Distributors mark a partial delivery in Orders. Billing must create the credit note, so the Orders-to-Billing line changes. Notifications must tell the buyer, so the queue message changes. Finance reports are fed by the warehouse loader, so the event shape changes there too. The mobile app shows invoices, so it needs a new screen state. Six boxes are touched, not two.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

Bipin asked each box's owner for an estimate in engineer-days. The first pass assumes Orders calls Billing directly and synchronously, as the solid line in Figure 1 shows.

Component touchedEngineer-daysWhy
Orders service4Record delivered quantity per line
Billing service6Credit-note rules, tax recalculation, numbering
Orders-to-Billing call contract2New request fields, error handling
Notification worker1.5New message template
Buyer mobile app3Credit-note screen
Warehouse extract2.5New fields for finance reports
Total194 + 6 + 2 + 1.5 + 3 + 2.5

At Bhandar's blended internal cost of ₹18,000 per engineer-day, 19 days is ₹3,42,000, or ₹3.42 lakh (19 × 18,000). That is cheap against the 494 hours of finance time per month. But it is effort, not elapsed time. Orders, Billing and mobile each ship on their own release schedule, so the earliest finish is set by the longest chain of waiting, not by the sum of the work. Ananya's "one sprint" had priced the effort of two boxes and ignored the coordination of six.

Now change one input: Orders announces the partial delivery as an event on the queue, instead of calling Billing. Billing and the warehouse loader both subscribe. The total effort is unchanged, but its shape moves.

ComponentSynchronous (days)Event-based (days)
Orders service44
Billing service66
Contract: call (sync) or event schema (async)23.5
Notification worker1.51.5
Buyer mobile app33
Warehouse extract2.51
Total1919

The event contract costs 1.5 days more (3.5 against 2) because it must survive duplicates and out-of-order delivery. The warehouse saves 1.5 days (2.5 against 1) because it already listens to the queue. Net change: +1.5 − 1.5 = 0. The diagram tells you where the cost will land and whom it will land on, and that the asynchronous version moves risk from the build into the failure cases.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A diagram is a claim, not a fact

Diagrams are drawn by people at a moment in time and age quickly. The one on the wall may omit the nightly script someone wrote in 2023. Always ask: when was this last verified, and by whom?

Boxes at different levels of zoom

One box may be a single function and another an entire company platform. Ask what each box contains before comparing them. The C4 model's discipline of labelling the level (context, container, component, code) exists to stop this blur.

Lines hide their type

An unlabelled arrow might be a real-time call, a nightly file, a shared database table or a queue. These behave differently under failure. Ask what travels along it, how often, and what happens when the other side is down.

Shared databases are invisible lines

If two boxes read the same table, a schema change in one breaks the other, yet no arrow shows it. Ask which boxes read which stores. This is the most common source of "we did not know it touched that."

Monolith is not an insult, and services are not a goal

A monolith has one release and one test run, so a feature that spans three modules ships together. Services buy independent releases and scaling at the price of coordination and network failure. Neither is better in the abstract; the diagram only tells you which price you are paying.

Synchronous versus asynchronous is a product decision

Whether the buyer sees "credit note issued" instantly, or "being prepared", is the visible face of that line. Figure 2 shows the difference. Ask what the user should see when the downstream box is slow.

What the diagram cannot tell you

It does not show how complicated a box is inside, how much data flows, how well-tested the code is, or whether the team that owns the box has capacity. Treat the diagram as a map of who to ask, then ask them.

Questions to ask before relying on it

What is missing? What is shared but not drawn? Which boxes ship on which cadence? Who is the single person who actually understands each box? If the answer to the last is "one person who is on leave in November," that is a finding.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and late

In a consumer product, the diagram's pressure point is scale and speed: a feature touches the boxes that sit on the critical path of a page load, and an extra synchronous call is a measurable drop in conversion. In a B2B product, it is the integration edge: customer systems, tax portals and the enterprise's own accounting software appear as boxes the company does not control, and any feature that changes a message those boxes receive can break a customer's workflow. In a marketplace such as Bhandar, there are two sets of users, buyers and distributors, so the same event often needs two views and two sets of permissions, and the diagram has a box per side.

The company's age matters as much. An early-stage company often has one monolith and one database, and the honest diagram has three boxes; "where will this touch" is answered by reading the code with a developer for an hour. A large company has hundreds of services and no one person holds the whole map, so product managers depend on a catalogue of services with named owners, and the diagram's main value is finding the dependency nobody mentioned.

7. Common mistakes

Counting only the starting box

Symptom: the estimate lists one team and the plan has no cross-team dates. Misunderstanding: a feature touches the boxes that own data it needs, not just where the click happens. Diagnostic: for every noun in the requirement (invoice, delivered quantity, buyer), ask which box stores it.

Treating all arrows alike

Symptom: a design review passes, then a launch fails when a downstream box is slow. Misunderstanding: sync and async lines fail differently. Diagnostic: for each changed line, ask "what does the user see if the other end is down for ten minutes?"

Trusting a stale picture

Symptom: an engineer says "oh, that also feeds the reconciliation script" late in the sprint. Misunderstanding: the diagram is current. Diagnostic: ask the newest engineer to trace one real request through the system and compare it with the drawing.

Confusing boxes with effort

Symptom: six boxes translate directly into six sprints, or one box into one day. Misunderstanding: a box count is a map of coordination, not a measure of work. Diagnostic: ask each owner for a range and for what they are waiting on from others.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Monday's meeting starts the same way but ends differently. Ananya brings the requirement as a list of nouns before she sees the diagram. She and Bipin mark each box with its owner and next release date. She asks the sync-or-async question aloud and chooses, with a reason, what the buyer will see. She leaves with a written list of touched boxes, an effort range for each, and the two people she must meet that week. Her date is a range tied to the longest dependency chain, and she has told the sales head what could move it.

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya withdrew "one sprint" the same afternoon. She went to the hospital group with a staged offer: credit notes for partial deliveries issued automatically by 1 December, with the mobile screen following one release later, since the web invoice view already showed the new document. She chose the event-based design because the warehouse and notification boxes were already listening to the queue, and because finance preferred a visible "being prepared" state to an order action that failed whenever Billing was slow. The 19 engineer-days of effort stayed, but the plan now had named owners and dates for six boxes rather than two.

To go further, read next about integration patterns (sync, async, events and webhooks), which expands Figure 2 into a decision tool, and about scalability and performance, which explains why a line that works at 38,000 orders a month may not at ten times that.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a feature you have asked for recently: which boxes did it touch that you would not have named, and how would you have found out? Second, if the diagram is only a map of who to ask, what is the cheapest way to keep that map true as the system changes?
case40v1-tech.architecture:
Delivery & Technology · Technical Fluency

Ilaaka Systems: The Diagram and the Code

Two engineering estimates for the same feature, one picture of the system, and a contractual date in November.

1. Sunday night, Baner

At twenty past nine on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Rajvi Bavishi had the architecture diagram printed at A3 and taped to a wall of her flat in Baner, Pune. Beside it, on ruled paper, were the two numbers that had ruined the weekend: fifty-eight and ninety-four.

Bavishi was Director of Product for Order and Payments at Ilaaka Systems Private Limited, a 243-person company selling a distributor-and-field-force platform to consumer-goods brands. At nine she owed the chief executive a two-page pre-read for the board meeting on 22 October; at three she would chair an architecture review with Bengaluru, Berlin, Toronto and Singapore.

The question fitted in a sentence and had consumed the four weeks since Bhojani's plan was circulated. Ijaara Mart Group, Ilaaka's largest customer, a Dubai distribution house moving Indian packaged goods across the Gulf, needed tax and credit decided when an order was taken rather than corrected afterwards, and the contract said that would be in production by 30 November. Bengaluru had costed the work at fifty-eight person-days and called it configuration; Pune had costed it at ninety-four and called it surgery on the monolith. Both had drawn their estimate off the same diagram. One of them had read the code.

2. The company, and a decision made in eleven days

Ilaaka was founded in Pune in 2017 by Rajesh Baheti and two colleagues from an IT services firm. The first version was one Django application against one Postgres database: an Android app for taking orders in a kirana store, a first crude pass at the discounts Indian fast-moving consumer goods runs on, and a nightly file exchange with whatever the distributor kept his books in.

The decision that shaped 2026 was taken in August 2021. A large consumer-durables group would sign before the festive season if order-time prices obeyed the group's own override rules. Baheti had eleven days. His engineers added a library inside the order application, schemes-lib, computing the override in process against the same database, and a table called scheme_events that a cron read five hundred rows every thirty seconds. The group signed; the shortcut stayed.

The Gulf business opened in June 2022 with an Ijaara Mart pilot, served from the same Mumbai-region cluster as every Indian customer. A ₹96 crore Series B in January 2023 paid for a platform team in Bengaluru under Ronit Bhojani, mandated to break the monolith into services. In March 2024 that team published the target architecture reproduced as Exhibit 1. In July 2024 it shipped schemes-svc, which settled claims after the order was placed; a second release in March 2025 let it price orders synchronously too, but only for tenants onboarded after that date. The older tenants were never migrated.

3. The industry

Ilaaka sold into a crowded category where Zoho and Freshworks had taught Indian mid-market buyers what software should cost. Its customers' worlds were rearranging faster than its roadmap: Reliance Retail and Flipkart buying direct, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart compressing the reorder cycle to hours, ONDC promising a portable catalogue, GST e-invoicing forcing an invoice reference number before goods moved. Collections had moved to UPI, and Ilaaka held Autopay mandates through a sponsor bank on NPCI's rails, which the Reserve Bank kept inside India.

The Gulf was the growth story and the complication. Ijaara Mart's auditors, after a Federal Tax Authority review of its returns, had told it that a price corrected after the fact was not an acceptable basis for a tax invoice. Ijaara sold into the UAE at five per cent, Saudi Arabia at fifteen and Oman at five, and shipped some orders from a designated zone where the treatment differed again; ZATCA clearance meant a Saudi invoice number had to exist before an order was confirmed. Ilaaka's counsel read the cross-border provisions of India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act conservatively, and Ijaara's group policy, written into the contract, required Emirati personal data processed in the UAE or the EU from 31 March 2027.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Ijaara Mart signed a three-year master services agreement in February 2026 worth ₹11.6 crore a year. The order-time requirement arrived in July. Bhojani's team read it, looked at the target architecture, and concluded that tax determination was a rule, that rules belonged to schemes-svc, and that the work was configuration with an Android release attached. Fifty-eight person-days, circulated on 14 September.

Bavishi asked for instrumentation before a decision. Counters went into the order path on 28 August, and the week of 1–7 September produced Exhibit 5. The figure that changed the conversation was that 8,42,100 of the 13,00,000 orders reaching the pricing step that week — 64.8 per cent — were priced in process, inside the monolith, by the library Baheti's team had written in 2021. Only 1,96,400, or 15.1 per cent, called schemes-svc over HTTP; 2,61,500, or 20.1 per cent, were priced on an offline handset.

Then the quarter closed. On Wednesday 30 September distributors loaded up against scheme targets and the scheme_events backlog reached 1,47,000 rows against a drain ceiling of 60,000 an hour: an event arriving at the peak had 1,47,000 rows ahead of it, about two hours twenty-seven minutes of waiting if nothing further arrived, and arrivals were what had built the backlog. Rajshree Bhimani's memo of 6 October, which produced Exhibit 6, set out edge by edge what the diagram asserted and what the system did. Rachita Bhanderi's lag analysis followed on 9 October and said the queue was fine. Both were measured honestly, under different loads.

5. The people

Rajvi Bavishi, Director of Product, Order and Payments, Pune, owns the 30 November date and told the board the requirement was understood — true of the requirement, not of the system. Unsaid: she approved Bhojani's plan in writing the day after it was circulated.

Rajesh Baheti, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune, defends the 2021 shortcut and wants a clean technical story for the Series C. Unsaid: how long he has known the diagram does not describe the order path.

Ronit Bhojani, Vice-President Engineering, Platform, Bengaluru, wants a service change, because extraction is what his team is measured on. Unsaid: his own catalogue assigns order-time pricing to schemes-svc, which is where the fifty-eight came from, and nobody has revised it since 2023.

Rajshree Bhimani, staff engineer, order and pricing, Pune, wrote schemes-lib as a junior engineer and wants order-time pricing extracted before anything is added to it. Unsaid: three weeks of unauthorised time already spent on a prototype.

Rachita Bhanderi, senior data scientist, Toronto, reports that queue lag is a non-issue, and her dashboards are what the board sees. Unsaid: her window closed three weeks before the quarter-end surge.

Reena Boricha, Director, Customer Success, APAC and Gulf, Singapore, has retention in her compensation and wants something in production in November. Unsaid: in August she told Ijaara's group IT director the change was "a configuration item on our side".

Rajvir Bothra, Head of Enterprise Sales, Americas, New Jersey, has two prospects worth ₹1.35 crore of pipeline needing SOC 2 Type II and single sign-on, twenty-two person-days from the same pod; the Gulf is one account, he argues, and North America a market. Unsaid: both have slipped a quarter already.

Reyansh Bagaria, product designer, Berlin, insists the price shown while the storekeeper watches cannot change on confirmation — which pushes the computation into the synchronous path, against what the target architecture wants. Unsaid: his sample was twelve salesmen in Surat and Coimbatore, none in the Gulf.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

Ronit Bhojani, design review, 14 September "The target architecture has schemes as a service. What Ijaara wants is a rule, and rules are configuration. Fifty-eight days, nineteen of them the Android app and the release. I am not reopening the monolith for a tax rate."

Rajshree Bhimani, engineering channel, 6 October "I wrote the thing all of you call a queue. It is a table, scheme_events in oms-db, and a cron reading five hundred rows every thirty seconds. On 30 September it was two hours twenty-seven minutes behind at worst, and it has never lost an event that I know of. Both are true. The diagram says neither."

Rachita Bhanderi, notebook comment, 9 October "Median lag nineteen seconds, ninety-ninth percentile two minutes eleven, and that tail is three ERP pushes that held the cron for about two minutes each, not queue depth. My window is 1 to 7 September, peak enqueue 22,000 an hour against a ceiling of 60,000. Rajshree's number is from a quarter-end. One system, two loads — and only one of us measured the load that matters in November."

Rajvir Bothra, email to the leadership list, 7 October "Let us be clear what is on the table. Ijaara is ₹11.6 crore of a ₹54.6 crore book, or 21.2 per cent. Nobody gets an architecture preference about that."

Reena Boricha, reply, 7 October "Rajvir, one correction and one date. Clause 9.3 lets Ijaara terminate the order-management module on its own, not the agreement: that module is ₹4.80 crore of the ₹11.6 crore, which is 8.8 per cent of ARR, not 21.2. And it needs ninety days' notice served from 30 November, so the revenue stops on 28 February 2027. What frightens me is February's service review, at which the whole ₹11.6 crore is repriced, and I cannot put a clause number on that."

Rimjhim Barot, Ijaara Mart Group, Dubai, 2 October "Our auditors will not accept a corrected price. The invoice has to be right when the storekeeper signs. Monolith or service is not my question. In August I was told it was configuration."

Reyansh Bagaria, chat to Bavishi, 9 October "It is 06:40 here and 10:10 in Pune, so forgive the brevity. Twelve salesmen in Surat and Coimbatore: every one read a price that moved after confirmation as the company cheating them. Decide tax after the order leaves the handset and the screen is lying."

Rajesh Baheti, voice note, 10 October "In 2021 I had eleven days and a signature to collect, and I would sign off schemes-lib again tomorrow. What I did not do was redraw the diagram, and then we hired forty people who learned the system from it."

8. The options as Bavishi now frames them

A. Treat it as configuration. Bhojani's fifty-eight days: change the Gulf rules in schemes-svc, ship the Android release. It fits the pod with room for Bothra's twenty-two days, and it addresses the path that carried 15.1 per cent of the measured week's orders.

B. Patch the monolith. Put country and zone tax determination into schemes-lib, where 64.8 per cent of orders are actually priced, accept Bhimani's ninety-four days, ship before 30 November. The feature lands where the traffic is; extraction gets harder, and the 2021 shortcut acquires a second customer depending on it.

C. Extract order-time pricing first. Bhimani's position: six to seven months, the pod full-time, a prototype three weeks old. The 30 November date goes, which means clause 9.3, and February's review arrives empty-handed.

D. Fork a Gulf instance. A separate deployment for Ijaara, allowed to diverge, which solves the residency clause too. Two codebases, and the single-platform story Bothra sells stops being true.

Two facts sit outside all four. In Exhibit 5, 2,61,500 orders were priced on offline handsets, and that path appears in no option and in neither estimate. And Barot's auditors are asking for an invoice that is right at signature: nobody has established which system allocates the invoice number, and it is not a box on the diagram.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The festive code freeze that the chief executive, Rubina Bodiwala, approved in August runs from Saturday 24 October to Monday 16 November. That leaves ten working days from Monday 12 October and nine from Tuesday 17 November: nineteen in all before the contractual date of 30 November, and that is before any public holiday is taken out, Dussehra falling on Tuesday 20 October. At five engineers it is ninety-five person-days, ninety if the holiday is observed. Option A plus Bothra's SOC 2 work needs eighty; option B plus the same work needs a hundred and sixteen. Two backend requisitions open since June would not clear onboarding before the freeze.

Money is not the binding constraint. At a loaded ₹18,000 per engineer-day, fifty-eight days is ₹10.44 lakh and ninety-four is ₹16.92 lakh, against a milestone payment of ₹1.80 crore that Ijaara may withhold on 30 November and ₹4.80 crore of module revenue that clause 9.3 can end on 28 February 2027. Regulation pulls both ways: the Reserve Bank requires UPI mandate data to stay in India, while clause 14.2 requires Emirati personal data processed in the UAE or the EU from 31 March 2027.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Working only from Exhibit 1, where would you say this feature touches? Write the list down, then say which entries Exhibit 6 changes.
  2. What does Exhibit 1 document — the system, an intention, or an org chart? What would it have to be generated from for the fifty-eight-day estimate to have been safe?
  3. Exhibits 5 and 6 come from two careful people who disagree. State the denominator and window behind each figure, and what a third measurement would cover.
  4. Bhojani's estimate records order-time pricing as zero days because a catalogue says another service owns it. What mechanism — not person — should have caught that?
  5. Bothra and Boricha disagree about what is at risk and both are right. Which figure belongs in the board pre-read, and what does that commit Ilaaka to?
  6. It is Monday, 12 October. What does Bavishi do before the three o'clock review, what two pages does she give Bodiwala, and what does she say on 22 October about a diagram the board has been shown before?

Bavishi turned the light off at a quarter past midnight. The A3 sheet was still on the wall, four edges circled in red and two boxes drawn in the margin that it did not have. The ruled paper still said fifty-eight and ninety-four. The pre-read was open on her laptop at a heading and one sentence, the sentence she had written on Friday and had not been able to finish.
exp20v2-tech.cicd:
CI/CD, Environments and Deployment

Delivery & Technology, Technical Fluency. How does code get to production, and how do we roll back?

1. Twenty-four days before the sale

On Tuesday 13 October 2026, Devika Ranganathan, vice-president of product at Dhanak Commerce Network, had one slide to prepare and one decision to make. Dhanak is a grocery and household-essentials app that delivers from dark stores (small warehouses closed to the public) in Pune, Hyderabad, Nagpur and Indore. Its festival sale began on Friday 6 November, twenty-four days away. In a peak sale hour the app expected 4,000 orders at an average basket of ₹640, or ₹25,60,000 an hour. In an ordinary hour it handled 1,500 orders, or ₹9,60,000.

Ejaz Qureshi, who led platform engineering from Pune, wanted to change how the company shipped software. Dhanak then held a release night roughly every two and a half weeks. Fifty-odd changes were bundled together, a quality team tested them by hand for two days, and a release manager, Dinesh Pandit, installed them on production by following a 41-step document. On Thursday 17 September the release carried 52 changes. The cart service began timing out. It took 45 minutes to notice and a further 90 to restore the previous version, because the database had to be put back by hand.

Qureshi proposed building an automated pipeline and moving to daily deployment, in the thirteen days before a code freeze planned for Monday 26 October. Pandit proposed keeping the release-night rhythm and freezing immediately. Ranganathan had to decide by Friday. The slow path left fifty changes exposed to one hard-to-reverse event; the fast path put unproven machinery in front of the biggest week of the year.

2. The idea

Continuous integration (CI) means that every developer merges small changes into one shared line of code several times a day, and each merge automatically triggers a build and a set of automated tests. Continuous delivery (CD) extends the idea: every change that passes is packaged and kept permanently ready to go live, so that releasing is a business choice, not a technical project. Continuous deployment, a stricter cousin, goes live automatically whenever the tests pass.

The problem it was invented to solve is the long gap between writing code and learning that it works. Grady Booch used the term continuous integration in 1991, and Kent Beck's Extreme Programming made daily integration a discipline in the late 1990s. Jez Humble and David Farley's 2010 book Continuous Delivery carried the logic through to production. In 2018 Nicole Forsgren, Humble and Gene Kim reported, from survey data, that teams who deployed often also failed less often and recovered faster.

The sentence Ranganathan could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: shipping small and often is safer than shipping large and rarely, provided the machinery to test, release and reverse each change is trustworthy. The proviso carries the weight.

3. How it actually works

An environment is a complete, separate copy of the system in which code runs. A developer’s laptop is one. A shared test environment is another. Staging imitates production as closely as cost allows. Production is the real system serving real customers. Code travels through them in order, being tested harder at each stage, and the pipeline automates the journey.

Walk a single change through it. A developer in Pune alters how the cart totals a discount and merges it. The pipeline builds it, compiling the code into an artifact, a single versioned package. The automated tests run: unit tests check small pieces in isolation, and integration tests check that the cart still talks properly to payments and inventory. If any fail, the change stops and its author is told within minutes. If they pass, the same artifact is installed in staging, where a few scripted journeys, such as placing an order and paying by UPI, confirm it behaves like the real thing.

Three steps are usually left implicit. First, the artifact is built once and promoted, never rebuilt per environment; what changes between environments is configuration, such as database addresses and payment keys, held outside the code. Second, database migrations, the scripted changes to the stored data’s structure, run as part of the deployment and are the hardest thing to reverse. Third, after going live someone or something must watch the numbers.

A rollback is the act of returning production to the last known good version. In the pipeline it is just another deployment, of the earlier artifact, which is why teams with a trustworthy pipeline restore in minutes while Dhanak’s manual process took ninety.

4. A worked example

Ranganathan asked Qureshi to price the two options over the 13-week quarter, using Dhanak’s own history. Both options ship the same 260 changes. Under the release-night process, five windows in the quarter, that means 5 releases of 52 changes. Under daily deployment on weekdays it means 65 deployments of 4. In the release-night process 2 of the 5 releases failed, a change failure rate (failed deployments divided by all deployments) of 2 ÷ 5 = 40 per cent. Qureshi estimated that 5 of 65 small deployments would fail, 5 ÷ 65 = 7.7 per cent.

Restoration time differs sharply. The manual process needed 45 minutes to detect and 90 to restore, 135 in all. The pipeline, with automatic health alarms, should detect in 6 minutes and redeploy in 4, 10 in all. During a failure, Dhanak assumed 30 per cent of orders were lost. At an ordinary 1,500 orders an hour and ₹640 a basket, ₹9,60,000 an hour, a minute of failure costs ₹9,60,000 ÷ 60 × 0.30 = ₹4,800.

Table 1. Cost of failed releases over one quarter (cost = minutes degraded × lost revenue per minute)
MeasureRelease-night manualDaily automated
Releases in the quarter565
Changes per release524
Failed releases25
Change failure rate40.0%7.7%
Minutes to restore, per failure13510
Minutes degraded, quarter27050
Cost at ₹4,800 a minute (ordinary hours)₹12,96,000₹2,40,000
Cost at ₹12,800 a minute (sale hours)₹34,56,000₹6,40,000

Read the ordinary-hours row line by line. The manual process loses 270 × ₹4,800 = ₹12,96,000, the automated one 50 × ₹4,800 = ₹2,40,000, a saving of ₹10,56,000. The automated process fails more often in absolute terms (five failures against two), yet costs less, because each failure is small and brief. That is the argument in arithmetic.

Now change one input: the hour. In a sale hour, ₹25,60,000 ÷ 60 × 0.30 = ₹12,800 a minute. The manual process then costs 270 × ₹12,800 = ₹34,56,000, the automated 50 × ₹12,800 = ₹6,40,000, and the gap widens to ₹28,16,000. Everything depends on the loss rate, 30 per cent, and Qureshi’s 10-minute restoration, which is a forecast, not a measurement.

5. Nuances worth knowing

Deployment is not release

Deploying puts code on production servers. Releasing makes a feature visible to customers. They can be separated with feature flags, switches that keep new code dormant until turned on.

Delivery is not deployment

Continuous delivery keeps a human decision at the last step; continuous deployment removes it. A regulated lender may rightly choose the former.

Rollback is one of two ways back

A roll-forward ships a fix on top instead of reverting. Where a change has altered stored data, such as reformatting every saved address, reverting the code may break against the new data. Rollback works cleanly only when changes are written to be reversible, typically by adding a database column first and removing the old one weeks later.

Green tests prove only what they test

A passing pipeline means the checked behaviours still work. It says nothing about behaviour nobody wrote a test for, nor whether customers want the change.

Staging is never quite production

Staging has less data, less traffic and different third-party connections. Bugs that appear only under sale-day load will pass staging. Hence the canary release: sending a change to a few per cent of users first.

The four measures

The research group DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) popularised four: deployment frequency, lead time from commit to production, change failure rate and time to restore. They are diagnostics, not targets.

A pipeline encodes a team’s trust

Each gate exists because something once broke. Before relying on one, ask what it does not check, how long a failure waits before someone sees it, and who may stop it.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

The mechanics are the same; the cost of a bad minute and the tolerance for change differ. A consumer app updates continuously on the server but depends on app-store review for the phone, so old versions linger in customers’ hands and rollback of the app itself is impossible; only server-side switches act quickly. A B2B product serves customers who plan around releases, so deployments may be frequent while visible change is scheduled. A marketplace can strand both a buyer’s payment and a seller’s payout, so money paths get the strictest gates.

Table 2. Where the deployment problem concentrates
Product typeHardest constraintTypical safeguard
Consumer appOld app versions cannot be recalledServer-side flags, staged rollout
B2B platformContracts and customer change windowsRelease notes, per-customer flags
MarketplaceMoney in flight between two partiesStrict gates on payment paths, reconciliation checks

Size changes things too. An early-stage company with eight engineers needs a simple pipeline and a fast rollback far more than it needs staging fidelity; a single production-like environment suffices. A large company’s difficulties become coordination, approvals and audit trails: who changed what, and with whose sign-off.

7. Common mistakes

Automating a broken process. The symptom: deployments are scripted, yet still need a Thursday-night war room. The misunderstanding: automation was treated as a speed-up, not a way to make steps repeatable. The cheapest diagnostic: ask a newcomer to deploy a trivial change unaided.

Confusing a fast pipeline with a safe one. The symptom: daily deployments and weekly incidents. The misunderstanding: frequency was adopted without tests, alarms or a rehearsed rollback. The diagnostic: roll back a harmless change on purpose in staging and time it.

Treating rollback as a promise. The symptom: “we can always roll back” from a team that has never done it after a data change. The misunderstanding: code is reversible and data often is not. The diagnostic: for the next migration, ask whether the previous code version could run against the migrated data.

Freezing as a substitute for confidence. The symptom: a long pre-sale freeze, then a large, nervous release the day it ends. The misunderstanding: risk was stored up, not removed. The diagnostic: compare the size of the first post-freeze release with a normal one.

8. What good looks like

Imagine the same decision handled well. Ranganathan does not ask whether to adopt CI/CD; she asks which parts of the journey the next 13 days can make trustworthy. A pipeline exists for the cart and checkout services first, because they earn the revenue. Every change passes automated tests before reaching staging. Each production deployment goes first to 5 per cent of traffic, with alarms on order success and response time. The previous artifact stays one command away, and a rollback has been rehearsed twice by someone other than its author.

Table 3. A target for 26 October
CapabilityEvidence that it exists
Tested changesNo merge reaches staging with a failing test
Fast restorationRehearsed rollback completed in 10 minutes or fewer
Early warningAlarm fires within 6 minutes of a seeded fault
Small changesNo deployment above 10 changes

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Ranganathan chose neither extreme. Dhanak would automate the pipeline for the cart and checkout services only, and move those to daily deployment from Monday 19 October. Everything else stayed on release nights until the sale was over. The freeze began on Monday 26 October as planned, but with the rollback rehearsed and Pandit, rather than a bystander, named its owner. Her reasoning: Table 1 favoured the pipeline, yet its 10-minute restoration was a forecast. Seven days of daily deployment on two services would turn forecast into evidence before the freeze, and the decision stayed reversible, since a failed experiment would cost a week and nothing more.

To go further, study feature flags and progressive delivery, which separate deployment from release and make a small blast radius deliberate. Then study logging, monitoring and observability, since every claim here about detecting a failure in six minutes depends on them. Revisit the architecture diagram too: deployment moves code into that picture.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Dhanak’s real restoration time turned out to be 60 minutes rather than 10, would the argument for the pipeline survive, and what would you want to know before answering? Second, what would a product manager gain, and risk, by being permitted to press the deploy button?
case20v1-tech.cicd:
Navkosh Pay: The Saturday-Night Release

A decision case on CI/CD, environments and rollback

1. Opening

On Monday 19 October 2026, Alpa Hemani, chief product officer of Navkosh Pay, sat in the glass meeting room at the company's Ahmedabad office with a printed release calendar and a cold cup of chai. Dhanteras fell on Friday 6 November, and Diwali on Sunday 8 November. The product team's festive feature, Dhanteras Khata, had to be live before the first of those dates. The chief executive wanted her recommendation on how to release it by Wednesday 21 October, because the company's change freeze would begin on Monday 2 November.

The engineering plan was the one Navkosh had always used: copy the new build to production by hand on a Saturday night. Alpa had just read the record of the last six such releases, and she was no longer sure the plan was safe.

2. Company background

Navkosh Pay, founded in 2017, sells a billing and UPI collection app to small merchants: kirana stores, sweet shops, jewellers and wholesale traders. About 4.2 lakh merchants pay a monthly subscription, and Navkosh takes a small fee on UPI collections. Annual revenue is about ₹110 crore. It competes with PhonePe for Business, Paytm for Business, Khatabook and Razorpay's point-of-sale products, all of which advertise heavily in the weeks before Diwali, when many merchants earn a large share of their year.

Thirty-eight engineers work in Pune and Bengaluru. Because Navkosh settles payments through banks connected to NPCI's UPI rails, a payment failure is visible within minutes: merchants cannot take money at the counter.

3. The situation

A release at Navkosh is a person copying files. An engineer builds the app on a laptop, tests it on a shared staging server, and at about ten on a Saturday night copies it to the production servers and runs the database changes by hand. The old version is overwritten, so going back means rebuilding it or restoring a backup. Staging is not a faithful copy of production: its payment-callback settings and some configuration files differ.

Exhibit 1 sets out the six releases from April to September 2026. Three of the six caused incidents, each with a different cause: a configuration file missing in production (9 May), a failed database change that needed a backup restore (11 July), and a payment-callback timeout that staging could not have shown (12 September). The mean deploy took about 119 minutes. The mean restore took about 212 minutes per incident, and the three incidents cost ₹21.0 lakh in total.

Continuous integration (CI) means every code change is merged, built and tested automatically. Continuous delivery (CD) means the tested build can then be released to each environment, from development through staging to production, by the same repeatable steps. Navkosh has neither: its release steps live in one engineer's checklist.

Anita Harsora, who leads customer success from Singapore, sees the consequences first. A 10 pm IST deploy is 12:30 am for her, and tickets from merchants begin to arrive after Pune has left for the night. Aniruddh Hirani, who sells to distributor chains from Edison, New Jersey, has a Dubai wholesaler in a renewal conversation and has been told, politely, that three outages in six months are one too many.

4. The people

Alpa Hemani (Ahmedabad) owns the decision. She wants the festive feature live, but not at the price of a Dhanteras outage.

Ashvin Haria, vice-president of engineering in Pune, wants to ship on 31 October as usual. His team knows the manual routine, and he worries that a new pipeline built in five working days will itself be untested.

Anita Harsora (Singapore) wants no more Saturday-night surprises and a release time at which she is awake.

Aniruddh Hirani (Edison) wants the feature, because distributors have asked for it, and above all wants to stop explaining outages to the Dubai client.

5. Exhibits and the options

Finance prices any payment-path outage from 28 October at ₹6 lakh an hour, or ₹0.1 lakh a minute, about three times the ₹0.033 lakh a minute implied by Exhibit 1 (₹21.0 lakh over 635 minutes), and, working with a data scientist in Toronto, expects Dhanteras Khata to earn ₹24.0 lakh in fees between 6 and 15 November if it is live by Dhanteras. Ashvin estimates that a basic pipeline, a production-like staging copy and a rehearsed rollback would cost ₹9 lakh and five working days from Wednesday 21 October, with the pipeline and staging copy ready by Friday 23 October, the rollback drill on Monday 26 October and Tuesday 27 October as buffer; a full rebuild would cost ₹30 lakh and finish after Diwali. Exhibit 2 prices the three courses; Exhibit 3 shows the calendar.

Option A: ship as always, Saturday 31 October. It costs nothing extra and meets the freeze. But if the past repeats, a failure costs the 212-minute mean, or ₹21.2 lakh, and the freeze would leave no time for a second attempt.

Option B: wait for the full rebuild. Releases become safe for good, but the feature misses the festive window entirely and the ₹30 lakh is spent first.

Option C: build the minimum safety net and ship on a weekday. Spend ₹9 lakh, keep the previous build running beside the new one, rehearse a rollback, and release on Wednesday 28 October at 11 am IST. If rollback takes 20 minutes, a failure costs ₹2.0 lakh. That figure is a target, not a measurement.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. In Exhibit 1, what do the three incidents have in common, and which of them would a production-like staging environment have caught?
  2. Why does the time to restore matter more than the incident rate when the festive week is priced at ₹0.1 lakh a minute?
  3. Which assumption in Exhibit 2 would most change the ranking of A and C, and how could Alpa test it before committing?
  4. What would you recommend on Wednesday 21 October, and what evidence on Monday 26 October would reverse it?

7. A note for the learner

Deployment is a product decision because it decides how much of a customer's day a mistake can consume. The lens has three parts. Environments should match production, so that a test result means something. A pipeline builds, tests and releases the same way each time, so that a person's memory is not a control. A rollback is the planned way back to the last good version, and it is quick only if the old build is still running and the database change can be undone.

A well-reasoned answer notices that Exhibit 2 is close between A and C on expected value (₹13.4 lakh against ₹14.0 lakh) but far apart in the worst case (−₹7.0 lakh against ₹9.0 lakh). It also notices that B gives up the whole festive window to avoid a risk C reduces more cheaply.

The numbers alone do not decide it. Option A bets that the next release resembles the three clean ones, with a Dubai renewal riding on it. Option B treats a problem that can be narrowed in a week as one that needs a quarter. Option C mainly changes the cost of being wrong, though a production-like staging copy should lower the odds too, which Exhibit 2 conservatively ignores.

One defensible path is Option C, with a gate. Ashvin's team builds the minimum net, makes the 28 October database change additive so that rolling back never needs a backup restore (the cause of the 310-minute incident), and rehearses a rollback on Monday 26 October. If the drill restores service in 25 minutes or less (expected net about ₹13.75 lakh), release on 28 October at 11 am IST, which is early afternoon in Singapore and 6:30 am in Berlin, after the clocks there change on 25 October. At a 30-minute rollback C's expected net is 24.0 − 9.0 − 0.5 × 3.0 = ₹13.5 lakh, level with A's ₹13.4 lakh; the break-even is about 32 minutes. So a 30-minute gate sits at the expected-value break-even, and C then wins only on the worst case. If the drill fails, fall back to a later release rather than to Option A. The 20-minute figure stays untested until the drill, and Alpa should say so to the CEO.
case40v1-tech.cicd:
Pathik Technologies: Eleven Minutes in Staging

Delivery & Technology · Technical Fluency · case for discussion

1. The night before

At ten past eleven on the night of Thursday, 15 October 2026, the garba drums behind Pathik Technologies' office on Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road were still going. Bhaswati Inani, vice-president of product, had the ninth floor to herself and three documents open: a proposal to rebuild the deployment pipeline, the 11 September incident review, and the service schedule of a contract signed in June with a Dubai money-exchange group.

Two meetings stood between her and the festive change freeze. At nine the next evening — 7.30 pm in Dubai — she would take the steering call with Panghat Exchange LLC, whose India-bound collections were due to go live on Pathik's rails on Tuesday, 1 December. On Monday at 9.30 am she would tell the board's technology sub-committee what Pathik intended to do about the way it shipped software. The freeze began on Dussehra, Tuesday 20 October, and ran to 10 November, so whatever she said on Monday could not be acted on until the freeze lifted, three weeks before the Dubai go-live.

She had asked for one number before the meeting: how often a Pathik release broke production. Three answers had come back, and they did not agree.

2. The company, and a decision from 2022

Pathik was founded in March 2019 by Bhupesh Italiya and two colleagues from a Mumbai payment gateway to do one unglamorous thing well: present recurring debit instructions for lenders, reconcile the returns, and tell the collections team who to call. By October 2026 it carried mandates for 37 non-banking financial companies and small-finance lenders, employed 198 people, and reported revenue of ₹96.40 crore for the year ended 31 March 2026, roughly seventy-two per cent of it transaction-linked.

In June 2022, facing a reconciliation dispute with its then largest client, the company made the decision that governs this case. Rather than shard mandates by lender, it put every lender's mandates, presentments and returns into a single PostgreSQL primary, on the argument that one ledger is one truth. Four years on, that primary holds 2,100 GB, every schema change touches every client at once, and no engineer has ever worked against a full copy of it.

A second commitment narrowed the room. On 1 April 2024, to satisfy a lender's auditors on data localisation, Pathik moved onto self-managed Kubernetes in a single Mumbai region under a three-year reserved-capacity agreement running to 31 March 2027. It covers ₹24.00 lakh of the ₹38.60 lakh production now costs each month (Exhibit 3) and is not transferable to a second region.

3. The industry

Recurring collections in India are regulated, thin-margin and high-volume. The Reserve Bank of India's e-mandate framework sets authentication and pre-debit notification requirements; UPI AutoPay mandates are presented through NPCI's rails on fixed windows; and the lenders Pathik serves are themselves inspected, so their auditors' questionnaires arrive as contractual obligations. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs what may be copied out of production. Razorpay, Cashfree and PhonePe compete for parts of the same wallet, and Indian boards have learned to ask why their engineering practice does not look like Zoho's or Freshworks' or Postman's.

Pathik's exposure runs outward. Panghat Exchange, a Dubai remittance and retail group, wanted instalments collected in India against loans it had made to Gulf-based Indian workers: an annual contract value of ₹18.60 crore, equal to 19.3 per cent of that FY2026 revenue, though none of it falls in that year. A North American pipeline had begun asking for release evidence Pathik did not produce.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Through the first half of 2026 the engineering story was good. Deploy volume rose from 44 production deploys in April to 57 in July (Exhibit 1) as the platform pod automated build and test. On Friday, 7 August, the pod ran its first rollback drill: it redeployed the previous container image to stage-1 and measured 11 minutes from decision to healthy. The number went into the board pack and into Panghat's security questionnaire as Pathik's recovery time. The drill carried no database migration, and stage-1 holds 4 GB of synthetic data, 0.19 per cent of the production volume in Exhibit 3.

On Friday, 11 September, release 2026.9.2 reached production at 9.05 pm, an hour into the evening presentment window. It carried migration 00412, which dropped the column mandate_ref_old at the end of what the team believed was a completed dual-write period. Debits began returning pending rather than failing, so the 5xx alarms stayed quiet; the first alert, on queue depth, fired at 9.34 pm and a Sev-1 was declared at 9.52 pm. At 10.40 pm the drilled rollback was attempted; the previous image still read the dropped column and would not start. The team built a forward fix by 11.18 pm and restored service at 12.14 am on Saturday, 12 September (Figure 1). Of the 1,84,000 instructions scheduled in that window, 61,000 failed the cycle and 1,23,000 cleared on retry by ten next morning (Exhibit 5). The outage ran 189 minutes from deploy, inside the 240-minute monthly maintenance allowance in every affected contract, so no service credit became payable. Ledger changes were then held for nine days.

Three beliefs have since failed. Recovery took 11 minutes only where no migration and no data existed; nothing in the pipeline makes a migration reversible, so rollback is a drill, not a capability. The dual-write period was believed complete because stage-1 showed no readers of the old column, when two lender-specific reconciliation jobs that run only in production were still reading it. And on 9 October Bishakha Ichhodia's reliability review and Italiya's dashboard went on one slide and did not agree (Exhibit 2). Proposal P-7, dated 2 October, prices a five-workstream rebuild at ₹168.0 lakh and 28 engineer-months (Exhibit 4); on 6 October the platform pod's only senior engineer resigned, last working day 31 October.

5. The people

Bhaswati Inani — vice-president, product (Bengaluru)
Owns the Panghat commitment and Monday's paper, and doubts Pathik can both hold the 1 December date and rebuild how it ships. Her bonus is tied to that milestone, which the pod does not know.
Bhupesh Italiya — co-founder and chief technology officer (Bengaluru)
Holds that the numbers are good and P-7 gold-plating: volume is up and the dashboard rate is 1.9 per cent. He wrote the migration runbook 00412 followed, and has said so in no review.
Bishakha Ichhodia — head of reliability, and of the nine-person platform pod (Pune)
Author of P-7; wants backward-compatible migrations and automated rollback before anything else. She is interviewing elsewhere and has told only her departing deputy.
Bhagirath Ilavia — chief financial officer (Bengaluru)
Notes that September cost Pathik ₹1.28 lakh of fees and no credits. He is preparing a January Series C data room, where deployment risk is a diligence item.
Bhavneet Ingadia — customer success lead (Singapore)
Carries Panghat day to day and insists the client needs an environment that behaves like production. On 29 September she told its team a dedicated pre-production environment "is being set up for you".
Binoy Ipcowala — head of sales, North America (New Jersey)
Wants release and rollback evidence for US buyers before the January conference season. His quota rests on one logo that has asked whether Pathik deploys blue-green.
Banhi Isardas — staff product designer (Berlin)
Opposes the feature-flag workstream as written: flags cache for 15 minutes, and the September forward fix left two versions of the collections screen live for a day, of which she keeps a private list.
Bhavtosh Ijatwala — data scientist, collections propensity (Toronto)
His retraining jobs ride the same deploy train and were blocked for the nine-day hold after 11 September. He wants ephemeral environments most; his model's lift has never been measured against a holdout.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

From the reliability review of 9 October:

"Our change-failure rate is 1.9 per cent. That is best-quartile for a payments platform, and I am not rebuilding a pipeline to improve a number that is already good." — Bhupesh Italiya

"That is 6 declared incidents over 310 production deploys, and 276 of those deploys never touched customer-facing code. Take the releases we actually shipped to clients: 8 of 34 failed. That is 23.5 per cent, and the contract measures us on the trailing quarter, where it is 5 of 18, or 27.8 per cent. We are not arguing about reliability. We are arguing about a denominator." — Bishakha Ichhodia

From the finance thread the same evening:

"I have read the incident note looking for the loss. Fees not earned, ₹1.28 lakh. Credits payable, nil. You want ₹168.0 lakh plus ₹9.40 lakh a month against that. Tell me what I write in the minute." — Bhagirath Ilavia

"Write that our lenders spent ₹51.85 lakh sending people to doors because we dropped a column, and that they cannot invoice us for it." — Bishakha Ichhodia

From a chat thread at 7.40 pm IST on 14 October:

"Panghat's CTO asked again when their environment will be ready. I said we are setting it up. I have been saying that since 29 September." — Bhavneet Ingadia, Singapore

"No client has been promised a dedicated environment. panghat-uat is the environment." — Bhupesh Italiya, eleven minutes later

"I do not need the rebuild. I need one page saying how you deploy, how you roll back and when you last tested it. The only page I have says eleven minutes." — Binoy Ipcowala, New Jersey

8. The options as Inani sees them

She had written four on the back of the P-7 cover sheet. Fund P-7 in full: ₹168.0 lakh and 28 engineer-months, leaving ₹42 lakh of the ₹210 lakh unallocated budget and no capacity for the Panghat feature scope. Freeze and run books: extend the freeze to 31 December, ship the Panghat integration behind the existing configuration flags and hire a replacement engineer — an estimated ₹22 lakh, printed in no exhibit — which concentrates ten weeks of frozen change into one January release. Buy the narrow fix: migration tooling and the blue-green rollback path alone, 11 engineer-months and ₹66.0 lakh, restoring the ability to undo a release without new environments. Give Panghat what Ingadia has implied: a dedicated production-parity environment, from panghat-uat's ₹6.40 lakh a month upward, answering one client and no others.

None of the four was what kept her at the desk. Three were denominated in engineering capacity she did not have and the fourth was a monthly bill, and the September release had run 29 minutes before any alarm fired. Two of the eight failed releases had turned on presentment behaviour that cannot be reproduced outside production, and the sandbox that might reproduce it belongs to a partner. The narrow fix, like the full programme, has a critical path ending on 25 January 2027 (Exhibit 4), nearly eight weeks after the go-live it is meant to protect, and she could not decide whether that was a reason to start it or a reason not to.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The sub-committee meets at 9.30 am on Monday, 19 October; the freeze runs from Dussehra on 20 October to 10 November. Panghat's go-live is 1 December, carrying a ₹310 lakh milestone, a delay penalty of ₹25 lakh a week capped at ₹200 lakh, and service credits capped at a tenth of the ₹465 lakh quarterly fee, or ₹46.50 lakh. Acceptance testing must run in panghat-uat: the DPDP Act and the MSA both bar production data leaving the Mumbai region. The largest lender's auditors expect a deployment and recovery evidence pack by 15 January 2027, and reserved capacity binds ₹24.00 lakh a month to one region until 31 March 2027. Approved headcount is four, two used, and the platform pod of nine loses its senior engineer on 31 October — against which 28 engineer-months inside the six weeks before go-live would need about twenty engineers doing nothing else.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. On the evidence in Exhibits 1 and 2, what is Pathik's change-failure rate? What would you need to know to choose among 1.9, 23.3, 23.5 and 27.8 per cent, and which belongs in the board pack?
  2. The drilled rollback was unavailable on 11 September. Which property of the system removed it, and which of the four options restores that property rather than working around its absence?
  3. Exhibit 3 prices parity environment by environment. What is the smallest set of gaps that would have caught migration 00412, and what does that set cost against Exhibit 4?
  4. Exhibit 5 shows ₹1.28 lakh of fee not earned by Pathik and ₹51.85 lakh borne by its lenders, with no credit payable. Whose figure should govern the investment case, and what does that imply about how Pathik prices reliability?
  5. Ingadia has told the client something Italiya says was never promised. What should Inani say on Friday's call, and what does each version of that sentence commit Pathik to?
  6. What should Inani do on Monday morning, and what should she say to the sub-committee about a remediation whose critical path ends on 25 January 2027 for a 1 December go-live — and about a recovery time of eleven minutes the board has already seen in writing?

It was almost midnight. In Berlin it was half past eight and Isardas was still online; from Toronto, Ijatwala had sent a third message about retraining windows. Inani drew a line through "ephemeral environments" on the P-7 cover sheet, then stopped, because she could not say whether she was cutting the expensive thing or the necessary one. She had twenty-one hours until the Panghat call, three readings of one register that did not agree, and the drums behind the building had stopped.
exp40v2-tech.cicd:
CI/CD, Environments and Deployment

Delivery & Technology, Technical Fluency — near-expert treatment. How does code get to production, and how do we roll back?

1. Two boardrooms, one Friday

At 07:58 on Monday 2 March 2026 a routine deployment went out at Lakeer Transit Systems, a Bengaluru metro and bus ticketing company. Lakeer issues 7,20,000 tickets a day at an average fare of ₹28 — ₹2,01,60,000 of ticket value — and earns a 2.5 per cent convenience fee: ₹0.70 a ticket, ₹5,04,000 a day. A quarter of the day’s tickets sell in the two morning peak hours: 1,80,000 tickets, 1,500 a minute.

The change was eleven lines. It altered how the ticket service cached fare tables, and under peak concurrency returned a stale fare that the payment step rejected. From 08:00, three in five ticket attempts failed.

Table 1. Lakeer, 2 March 2026. Failed attempts accrue at 1,500 a minute × 60 per cent = 900 a minute while the faulty version serves everyone.
ClockStepMinutes elapsedFailed attempts, cumulative
08:00Faulty version serving all traffic00
08:01Error-rate alarm fires1900
08:05On-call engineer acknowledges54,500
08:09Rollback begins98,100
08:13Previous version serving all riders1311,700

Thirteen minutes, 11,700 failed attempts, ₹8,190 of fee at risk — small, because most riders simply tapped again. What Lakeer lost was a queue at eleven station gates and a clause charging ₹40,000 for peak degradation beyond ten minutes. Meghana Lahoti, vice-president of product, had to bring a policy to the review on Friday 20 March: her chief operating officer wanted deployments barred from 07:00 to 11:00 and 17:00 to 21:00, while Lokendra Mahale, head of platform engineering, wanted a 2 per cent ring instead.

That same Friday, Lipika Mahadevan faced the mirror image in Chennai. Marham Clinical Works sells a hospital information system to 142 hospitals: 131 on its multi-tenant cloud, 11 large groups in their own data centres. Revenue is ₹96 crore a year, about ₹67.6 lakh a hospital. On the night of Wednesday 14 January 2026 Marham upgraded Maitreyi Hospital Partners, a 900-bed group in Coimbatore, from version 9.0 to 9.2, rewriting 2.4 crore rows of medication-order records. At 03:05 ward staff reported discharge summaries printing yesterday’s drug list. There was no rollback: the 9.0 binary could not read the 9.2 schema. The hospital ran on paper until 07:40.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Continuous integration is merging every developer’s work into one shared line of code several times a day, each merge triggering an automatic build and test run. Continuous delivery keeps every change that passes permanently installable, so going live is a business decision. Continuous deployment removes the decision. An environment is a complete running copy of the system; a rollback is a deployment whose payload is the previous known-good package.

The problem it solves is the delay between writing code and learning whether it works. Booch named continuous integration in 1991; Beck’s Extreme Programming made daily integration a discipline; Humble and Farley’s Continuous Delivery (2010) carried it to production and insisted on the sharpest rule — build once, promote that identical package. In 2018 Forsgren, Humble and Kim published evidence that teams deploying more often failed less often and recovered faster.

Three schools disagree, and not about automation. The flow school holds that batch size is the master variable: it signs “a team deploying sixty times a month is safer than the same team deploying five times” and refuses “therefore remove the human from the last step in a clinical system”. The control school holds that the binding constraint is irreversibility; it signs “an irreversible change deserves a window and a witness” and refuses “windows make systems safe”. The resilience school holds that failure is certain, so investment belongs in recovery; it refuses “ship anything, you can always roll back” — the sentence behind Marham’s January night.

3. Mechanics, including the parts left implicit

A pipeline is a chain of gates through which one artifact passes. Artifact is load-bearing: a single, versioned, immutable package built exactly once. What differs between environments is configuration — database addresses, payment keys, flag defaults — injected at start-up.

Walk one change through. A developer merges to trunk; the build produces artifact 4.31.0; unit tests check pieces in isolation and integration tests check that the ticket service still speaks to the fare engine and the payment gateway. Lakeer’s suite takes 38 minutes — a capacity question. The team merges about 24 changes across a nine-hour day, 2.67 an hour. One lane serves 60 ÷ 38 = 1.58 an hour, so the queue grows without bound; four lanes serve 6.32 an hour, a utilisation of 42 per cent.

Three steps are usually left implicit, and all three are where failures live. Database migrations are deployments with no natural inverse. Configuration and flag changes are deployments too, which is why incident reports so often open with “no change had been made”.

The quantitative core is one expression: expected loss equals failure rate × traffic exposed × the share of exposed traffic that fails × minutes until the last user is affected.

Table 2. The same faulty change under four strategies, at the 2 March peak rate of 1,500 attempts a minute and a 60 per cent failure rate while exposed. Fee at risk is attempts × ₹0.70.
StrategyTraffic exposedMinutes to last affected riderFailed attemptsFee at risk
