The last two rows hold the second-order argument. The canary exposes 2 per cent of traffic against the rolling release’s 25 per cent, yet needs fourteen minutes rather than eight to clear. At 2 per cent exposure, 1,500 × 0.02 × 0.60 = 18 failures a minute, barely above a ticketing system’s noise floor, so a clear signal takes nine minutes rather than one. Blast radius and detection latency trade against each other, and their product is what matters.

Blue–green’s reputation for expense rests on a misreading. Lakeer’s production compute costs ₹38,00,000 a month, of which the ticketing tier is ₹22,00,000 (58 per cent). Duplicating that tier permanently would add ₹22,00,000 a month — but the second environment need exist only during a deployment. At 60 deployments a month of 20 minutes each, that is 1,200 minutes of a 43,200-minute month, 2.8 per cent, about ₹61,100.

4. When the standard answer applies, and when it misleads

Four claims make the practice testable. One: smaller batches cut expected loss only where a failure’s cost scales with duration, not content. True for Lakeer at ₹0.70 a ticket a minute; false for Marham, where a corrupted medication order costs the same either way. Two: rollback exists only if every redeployable version can read the data now in production. Lakeer passes; Marham failed here. Three: progressive exposure beats fidelity when production traffic cannot be imitated. Lakeer’s fault needed 1,500 tickets a minute, and staging holds 7.2 lakh rows against production’s 2.4 crore — 3 per cent. For Marham’s on-premise sites it inverts: with no traffic to split, fidelity is the only lever. Four: deployment frequency may exceed release frequency. Both pass — flags for Lakeer, contract windows for Marham.

The idea misleads when the artifact cannot be recalled: a mobile binary in a customer’s hand, firmware on a meter. It misleads again when an organisation reads the DORA correlations as instructions. Frequency is a symptom of a system that can absorb change; mandating the symptom produces sixty deployments a month of nothing in particular.

5. Hard edges: multi-product, two-sided, regulated, hardware, AI

Lakeer is already a multi-product company and has not noticed. Ticketing, wallet and parking belong to three teams but ship inside one mobile binary on a weekly train run from Lisbon by Mariana Lobo, so a wallet defect blocks a parking release. Mature firms either split the binary or move the release decision into server-side flags.

Two-sided products add a coupling the single-sided case never shows. At Mehvar Freight Exchange a shipper-side change to how loads are described must be live before the trucker app can read it, so reverting one side breaks the other. The discipline is to deploy the reader first and the writer second, and reverse in the opposite order.

Regulation changes who may press the button, not how often. Marham works under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act; its hospital customers run their own change-advisory boards. It requires an auditable record of what was deployed, with whose approval, and a demonstrated restore. Nothing forbids a daily deployment. Regulated firms often use compliance as cover for a weak pipeline; the diagnostic is blunt: has the approval step ever rejected a release?

Hardware is the genuine exception. A bricked Mapan Meter Industries water meter cannot receive its own rollback: the channel the fix would travel on is the thing that broke. The mature answer is a bootloader watchdog that reverts to the previous image if the new one fails to check in. Lakeer has a smaller version in 3,100 station validators.

AI-native products break the pipeline’s oldest assumption: that the artifact determines the behaviour. At Lipi Document Labs a prompt revision, an index rebuild and a model change are deployments with no diff anyone can review. What works is a fixed evaluation set — 1,200 documents with known answers — as the test gate, with the model version pinned so rollback is a configuration revert. One prompt change raised whole-set accuracy from 88.4 per cent to 91.2 per cent while dropping handwritten discharge notes from 79 per cent to 61 per cent.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

The deployable unit is the artifact, not the branch. The tell-tale sign is a pipeline that builds once for staging and again for production. The obvious reading — that building twice is wasteful — is wrong: the thing tested is not the thing shipped, so every green result describes a package that no longer exists.

Rollback is a property of the data layer. The sign is a team that says “we can always roll back” and cannot describe its last expand-and-contract migration. Marham’s January failure was not a tooling failure; the deployment worked. Nor is the lesson to test migrations harder: a well-tested irreversible migration is still irreversible. What was missing was a window in which both versions could read the same data.

Detection latency, not blast radius, is usually binding. The sign is a canary set at 1 per cent and held three minutes, which flatters the dashboard and sees nothing. Experts compute the signal: 18 failures a minute at 2 per cent of Lakeer’s peak is detectable in nine minutes, while off peak the same ring yields 240 × 0.02 = 4.8 a minute, which is not detectable at all.

A freeze moves risk forward rather than removing it. The sign is a long pre-festival freeze followed by the year’s largest release the morning it lifts. Fifty changes deployed together are the same changes with fifty suspects. The defensible freeze is narrow: freeze what is unrecoverable, not the repository.

Configuration is a deployment, and flags are configuration. The sign is an incident timeline opening “no code was changed”. Flags, rate limits, pricing tables and model versions change production behaviour without a test gate, and change more often than code. Experts count a flag flip as a deployment.

Green tests measure the tests. The sign is a coverage percentage quoted with no record of a seeded-fault drill. The question is not how much code the suite executes but whether a deliberately broken behaviour turns it red. Lakeer’s 2 March fault would have survived: no test ran two concurrent fare lookups.

Forward-only recovery is a strategy, not a defeat. The sign is a team that insists on reverting every time, including after a migration, then argues while production stays broken. Where data has already moved, the fastest safe path is often a small fix deployed forward.

The owner of the button sets the real lead time. The sign is a release manager whose calendar is the critical path. Lakeer’s median lead time is 42 minutes, Marham’s cloud line 3.5 days, its on-premise line 68 days — and almost none of that difference is technical.

7. Product type and company stage

The mechanics are identical everywhere; what differs is which constraint binds.

Table 3. Where the deployment problem concentrates.

Enterprise, on-premise (Marham)Customer change windows and version spreadRestore from backup, unless migrations were reversible
Marketplace (Mehvar)Two sides must stay compatibleRevert in the reverse order of deployment
Hardware plus software (Mapan)The channel delivering the fix can itself breakA device-side watchdog, not a pipeline action
AI product (Lipi)Behaviour changes without a code changePin the previous model and prompt version

Stage matters more than most expect. A ten-engineer company should buy a fast pipeline and a rehearsed rollback, not staging fidelity. At Lakeer’s stage the next investment is detection, since every strategy in Table 2 is bounded below by how fast the alarm fires. At Marham’s it is cutting the versions in the field — an account-management problem in an engineering costume. Table 4 prices it: four releases alive in 11 data centres, 34 engineer-days a month of backporting at ₹9,600 a day.

8. Three worked examples

Lakeer’s canary pilot, 12 January to 20 February 2026. Mahale ran rings on the wallet service, which in those six working weeks took 84 deployments — 14 a week, against the ticketing line’s 720 a year, or 13.8. Six were faulty, a change failure rate of 7.1 per cent: five caught at the 2 per cent ring, one escaping to all riders. At Lakeer’s mix of one deployment in four in a peak hour, a ring-caught fault costs 0.25 × 252 + 0.75 × 67.2 = 113.4 failed attempts, so the five cost 567; the escape, exposed to everyone for the full thirteen minutes, cost 0.25 × 11,700 + 0.75 × 3,120 = 5,265. The pilot’s total was 5,832, against 6 × 5,265 = 31,590 had all six gone out at once — 25,758 attempts avoided. But the failure rate did not fall: rings change a fault’s consequence, not its frequency.

Marham’s reversible migration, 2 March to 20 April 2026. Mandeep Luthra rebuilt the January change as expand-and-contract. The nullable column was added on 2 March; a dual-writing version followed that week; the backfill of 2.4 crore rows ran in 480 batches of 50,000 at three a minute, 160 minutes over two nights; readers switched in week three; the old column was dropped on 20 April, seven weeks after the first step. Throughout, every version in the field could read the data — the definition of a rollback window. The cost was 11 engineer-days, ₹1,05,600 at ₹9,600 a day; January had cost ₹1,62,500 in service credits alone.

Where the approach failed: Mapan Meter Industries, August 2025. A firmware release went to a first ring of 20 per cent of the fleet, 1,880 of 9,400 meters. The image mishandled a power interruption during flashing and 1,842 of the 1,880 meters in the ring — 98.0 per cent — stopped responding. Because a bricked meter cannot receive an over-the-air rollback, recovery meant a technician at each site: ₹850 a visit, ₹15,65,700 in all, and at four crews doing 18 meters a day, 26 working days. The failure was not the ring but the assumption that exposure can be undone. A 2 per cent ring of 188 meters would have bricked about 184 at ₹1,56,400, saving ₹14,09,300.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Frequency without reversibility. Sign: frequency rising while time to restore goes unmeasured. Question: when did we last roll back on purpose, and how long did it take? Caught late, the cost is a Marham night.

Version spread in the field. Sign: a support rota that asks which version the customer runs before asking what broke. Question: how many versions are we patching, at what monthly cost in engineer-days? Caught late it compounds.

Alarms tuned to availability rather than the product. Sign: green dashboards during a customer-visible incident, because the service returned a stale fare with a success code. Question: which number would have moved within sixty seconds of the 2 March fault?

Gate proliferation. Sign: fourteen checks, three of which nobody can explain. Question: what did each gate last catch, and what does it cost in minutes times deployments? A 12-minute canary hold on 60 deployments a month costs 720 elapsed minutes and is nearly free, because the waiting is asynchronous; a sign-off costing four hours of attention is not.

Table 6. Expected failed attempts a quarter, from 12 faulty deployments in 180 (6.7 per cent), 3 in a peak hour and 9 off peak. At full exposure peak costs 900 failed attempts a minute, off peak 240.

Table 6 settles Lakeer’s argument more cleanly than either executive expected. The window ban alone cuts expected failed attempts from 63,180 to 37,440, a worthwhile 41 per cent. Canary rings alone cut them to 1,360.8. Adding the ban on top of the rings saves a further 554.4 attempts a quarter — ₹388.08 of fee. The chief operating officer’s policy is nearly worthless once the engineer’s is in place, and a ban also blocks fixes: a defect found at 08:15 affecting 4 per cent of attempts would live until 11:00 — 165 minutes at 1,500 attempts a minute, 2,47,500 attempts of which 9,900 fail, more damage than every faulty deployment of the quarter combined.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should the last step be automatic? The continuous-deployment position: approval at the end adds no information — the approver has not read the diff — only delay and a false sense of control. The control position: where a defect reaches a patient or a payout, approval is an accountability gate, and someone must be able to say who decided. The first is wrong if removing approval raises severe-incident rates; the second if the approvers never reject anything.

Trunk-based development or release branches? The trunk position rests on merge economics: integration cost rises with divergence. The release-branch position rests on Marham’s reality: when 11 customers run four versions in their own data centres, a supported branch per release is not debt, it is the product. What settles it is Table 4 — 34 engineer-days a month — against the revenue that insists on it.

Blue–green or canary? The blue–green camp values a reversal of one action and two minutes, with no partially upgraded state to reason about. The canary camp answers that blue–green exposes everybody meanwhile, and Table 2 shows the gap: 5,400 failed attempts against 252. The reply is that 252 assumes the signal was read correctly, and many organisations promote on a timer.

Are the four DORA measures diagnostics or targets? For targets: what is not a target is not managed, and frequency is the one number that forces the underlying investments. Against: the four are correlates of a healthy system, and a team measured on frequency will split changes to inflate the count while lead time and change failure rate worsen.

Two readings of Table 7 are available. One says the on-premise line is four years behind and should be migrated to the cloud. The other says it serves customers paying ₹67.6 lakh a year each, whose chief information officers answer for their own data centres, and a practice that cannot serve them is incomplete rather than superior.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks whether the company does CI/CD. Someone who has internalised it asks four questions: what is the smallest change this team can get to production unaided; how long until a fault is visible; how long until it is gone; and which changes cannot be undone at all. They read the migration plan before the release plan.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Friday 20 March, Lahoti proposed and the review accepted a policy in three parts. The blanket peak window is abolished for ticketing and wallet, replaced by a peak gate: in those hours a change goes out only through a 2 per cent ring held twelve minutes, promotion blocked unless ticket-success and response time stay in band. Validator firmware stays on depot-only overnight windows, because 3,100 devices are not recallable. The quarter’s one engineering commitment is detection: the 2 March alarm fired by itself at minute one, but acknowledgement took four minutes more and the rollback did not begin until minute nine, so eight of the thirteen minutes — acknowledgement plus decision — were human latency. Her reasoning was Table 6: the ban would have bought ₹388.08 a quarter and cost the ability to fix a peak defect during peak.

Mahadevan went the other way on cadence and the same way on substance. The cloud line moves to weekly releases; the on-premise line to six weeks rather than monthly, because the binding constraint is the hospitals’ own change boards. Every change touching stored data must pass through expand-and-contract and carry a rollback window of at least one release. Table 4 is the commercial target: from five supported releases and 34 engineer-days a month to two and nine, saving 25 engineer-days, ₹2,40,000 a month and ₹28,80,000 a year.

For discussion. First: the peak gate assumes the canary signal is read correctly under pressure at 08:00 — what evidence would you want first? Second: Marham’s refusal to move the on-premise line to monthly is defensible on customer grounds and convenient for a group that would struggle — which motive operates? Third: halve detection time, or make every migration reversible — which, and what in the numbers justifies it?

13. Going deeper

Reading an architecture diagram — which boxes share a database, and so cannot be reverted apart. Feature flags and progressive delivery — the sequel: separating deployment from release. Logging, monitoring and observability — every claim about thirteen minutes rests on detection. How web and mobile apps work — why a mobile binary cannot be recalled. APIs and integration basics — versioning lets Mehvar’s two sides deploy apart. Data modelling for PMs — the schema decides whether expand-and-contract is cheap. Databases, storage and caching — Lakeer’s fault was a cache-coherence bug. Cloud infrastructure basics — what an environment costs. Scalability and performance — the concurrency only production reproduces.
exp40v2-tech.build.log:
The build log

Delivery & Technology › Technical Fluency · near-expert treatment. The question: have I recorded the trade-offs I made while building?

1. Two decisions, five days apart

On Thursday, 9 July 2026, Prachi Rangnekar, vice-president of product at Pavitra Water Industries in Nashik, held two documents that disagreed. Pavitra makes connected reverse-osmosis purifiers — 71,400 of them in Indian homes — sold with an app subscription. The first was a Bureau of Indian Standards query, raised during re-certification, asking the rationale behind a safety-relevant default: the total-dissolved-solids threshold at which a device declares its filter exhausted. The second was a growth proposal to raise that threshold, extending a cartridge’s apparent life by five weeks.

The constant was frozen into firmware on 2 March 2023 by Siddhesh Phansalkar, who left fourteen months later. A log entry existed, reading in full: “TDS cut-off set to the value agreed with the lab; see test sheet.” No rejected alternative, no cost, no condition for revisiting it. One thousand two hundred and twenty-five days later, Prachi had to tell a standards body which was right, and nobody knew why the number was the number.

On 14 July, Shreya Pathak faced a sharper version at Sankhya Risk Systems in Bengaluru, whose underwriting assistant reads bank statements for lenders. On 18 November 2025 Ritika Patwardhan, its machine-learning lead, chose to send every statement to a hosted large language model rather than build parsers for the eleven commonest formats, shipping the pilot in nine days instead of nine weeks. Two hundred and thirty-eight days later, Sampratti Finance Group had moved to production at a contracted ₹58 per application against compute of ₹64.80 — and the model version the system was tuned against would go on 30 September 2026, seventy-eight days away.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A build log is a dated, append-only record of the decisions taken while a product is built: the context and numbers available at the time, two or more options with their costs, the choice, the property given up, and the measurable condition under which it should be reopened. It records not what the system does — code carries that — but what the team weighed.

The invention is old and repeatedly re-invented. Ships’ logs and laboratory notebooks were contemporaneous because that was the point: a dated, unalterable page settled priority disputes and later patent claims. In 1985 Peter Naur proposed that a program is a theory held in its builders’ heads — which reads as an argument against documentation but is the strongest case for recording reasoning, since theories leave with people. In 1986 Parnas and Clements argued that real design is never rational but should be documented as though it were. Ward Cunningham’s 1992 debt metaphor supplied the accounting language, Michael Nygard’s 2011 decision record the format. Five positions are held.

The decision-record school holds that a decision is not made until written, in the repository beside the code. It would sign: an unwritten architectural choice is a rumour. It would not sign: the record should carry prices or forecasts, which rot faster.

The working-software school, from the Agile Manifesto, holds that a separate narrative of intent decays into a lie, and that tests and small reversible changes are the honest record. It would sign: a stale document is worse than none. It would not sign: keep a register of rejected options.

The regulated-record school — ISO 13485, DO-178C, the files a certifying body may call for — holds that the record is part of the product. It would sign: every decision in scope is recorded, whether or not anyone expects to re-read it. It would not sign: record selectively.

The learning-from-incidents school, after Sidney Dekker and John Allspaw, holds that what matters is local rationality — why the decision made sense in the room — recovered by interviewing, not a form. It would sign: a template collects what is easy to write. It would not sign: an entry beats a good reconstruction.

The option-pricing school, where most product managers end up, holds that every shortcut is a dated option with a strike price. It would sign: an entry without a price and an expiry condition is decoration. It would not sign: the log is an engineering artefact.

3. Mechanics, including the step left implicit

Expert practice has five visible steps: notice the fork; write the context with the numbers then available; state the options; state the choice and its cost; file it where the team looks. The invisible step, which separates a log that pays from one that accumulates, is pricing the rejected option and attaching an expiry condition in a published metric. A price without a trigger produces regret; a trigger without a price, an unactionable alarm.

The value of a log is the reconstruction cost it avoids: forks of each class, times the probability each is reopened, times the hours to re-establish the reasoning, times the probability the entry is found, times the fraction of work it removes — less the writing cost. Over calendar 2024 Pavitra classified every fork it could identify and, to June 2026, timesheeted the reconstruction hours at ₹2,100 each.

Table 1. Pavitra: forks taken in calendar 2024 and reconstruction effort incurred when reopened, observed to 30 June 2026.
Class of decisionForksReopenedHours per reopeningHours spent reconstructing
Firmware / on-device341126286
Cloud service & API61239207

Vendor / bill of materials12520100
Interface & copy1409327
Total2655613.1 (avg)732

Of the 265 forks, 56 were reopened, a rate of 21.1 per cent — low enough that logging everything is wasteful. But cost is concentrated: interface and copy decisions are over half the forks and under four per cent of the hours, firmware an eighth of the forks and more than a third. Those 732 hours cost ₹15,37,200.

Now price the discipline. Pavitra’s rule is that a fork earns an entry if re-establishing its reasoning later would take more than one engineer-day — eight hours, since a day costs ₹16,800 at ₹2,100 an hour. On the 2024 figures that is every class whose hours per reopening exceed eight: firmware at 26, cloud and API at 9, data schema at 14 and vendor at 20, but not interface and copy at 3. Those four classes are 125 forks, 47 reopenings and 705 reconstruction hours. An entry takes about eighteen minutes, or 0.3 of an hour, so 125 entries cost 37.5 hours, ₹78,750. Pavitra measured retrieval at 81 per cent once the log was selective; round that to 0.80, and assume a found entry removes 70 per cent of the reconstruction work. The saving is 0.80 × 0.70 × 705 hours, or 394.8 hours, worth ₹8,29,080 — 10.5 times the writing cost. The break-even persuades more: writing 37.5 of the 705 hours at stake means the log need only eliminate 5.3 per cent of that work to pay for itself.

The second-order effect is less comfortable. Knowing a trade-off must be written changes which trade-off gets made: teams that log well take fewer undocumented shortcuts, as intended, but also drift toward choices easy to justify in writing, which is not. Experts keep the entry cheap — five fields, no reviewer — to limit that drift.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as claims a team can test on itself. One: the decision is costly to reverse. Pavitra’s constant passes emphatically — it is in firmware in 71,400 devices and cited in a certification file. Sankhya’s passes differently: reversing it is cheap in code and dear in commitments, since a contract is priced on its cost base.

Two: the reasoning is held by fewer people than the artefact will outlive. Both pass: Phansalkar left, Patwardhan is one memory, and Sankhya has grown from nine engineers to thirty-one in a year.

Three: an observable condition exists that would change the answer. Pavitra’s constant fails this — a lab-validated safety threshold has no volume trigger — and that is where the idea misleads. Inventing a trigger for a decision that should not expire invites a future team to treat a safety constant as tunable. The right entry records the evidence and the regulatory basis, and says the trigger is a change in the standard. Four: the entry costs little relative to the exposure. Both pass.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. In exploratory work — a two-week spike, a prompt tuned forty times a day — logging each fork taxes thinking; the right unit is one entry recording what the exploration concluded. Where the log has been quoted in a performance review, entries turn defensive and the record is worse than silence. And where a decision is contested, an entry freezes one side’s version.

5. Hard edges

Multi-product and shared platform. When a payments service is shared by three products, a trade-off made for one is inherited by the rest. Mature companies attach entries to the service, not the team: teams are reorganised and services are not.

Two-sided marketplaces. At a produce marketplace such as Rangoli Produce Exchange the consequential forks are distributional: a ranking change favouring large suppliers over smallholders, a fee waived to seed one side. The entry must record whom it favours and what ends the subsidy.

Regulated products. Here the log becomes evidence and candour has a legal cost. Counsel will resist an entry reading “we knew this was risky and shipped anyway”. The response is not to stop writing but to change register: facts, alternatives, measurements, conditions.

Hardware plus software. Lead times convert thresholds into dates. A bill-of-materials decision with a fourteen-week lead time cannot carry a trigger reading “revisit at 50,000 units” if ordering must start three months earlier; it needs a date computed from the threshold and the growth rate. Pavitra’s vendor entries carry two triggers, one physical and one calendar.

AI-native products. Three things break. The decision surface moves into configuration and data — prompts, retrieval settings, evaluation thresholds — where version control records the change but not the intent. Behaviour drifts without anyone deciding anything, so a successor needs a recorded evaluation score. And the clock belongs to someone else: Sankhya’s model goes on 30 September whether or not it is ready.

Mature companies say they keep a decision record in every repository. In fact they keep thirty to fifty entries that matter, a graveyard of templated files nobody opens, and much reasoning inside incident reviews. The forcing functions are not policies but diligence, certification, a service changing owner, a departure.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

The entry records a priced option, not a choice. The tell is an entry with no number in it. The obvious reading — that the log captures what was decided — is wrong, because that is visible in the code. What is invisible is the cost of the alternative, which lets a successor tell prudence from laziness.

A trigger must name a metric that already exists. The tell is a trigger phrased in a quantity nobody publishes — “revisit if parse latency becomes a problem”. Experts check it against the telemetry catalogue first: a trigger in an unmeasured quantity cannot fire, and one that cannot fire is worthless.

Contemporaneity is most of the value, and backfill must be labelled. The tell is entry dates clustered in one week, usually the week before diligence. Reconstructed reasoning is a different artefact: it shows what the team now believes it believed. Experts mark backfilled entries reconstructed, preserving what makes a log evidence, not advocacy.

The binding constraint is retrieval, not capture. The tell is a team that logs diligently and still asks the same question every quarter. The obvious fix, logging more, makes it worse: as volume rises the chance of finding the right entry falls, and the log acquires the economics of a drawer.

The log records belief, not truth, and must stay blameless. The tell is entries turning vaguer after one is first quoted against someone. A log is the only artefact that shows a decision was reasonable given what was known, separately from how it turned out — which is why using it for blame destroys it.

Authorship is split, and single-author logs fail predictably. The tell is a log with no money in it, meaning engineers wrote it alone, or one that misstates the mechanism, meaning the product manager did. The engineer owns why the alternative is expensive; the manager owns why speed was worth paying for.

The dangerous decisions are the ones nobody noticed making. The tell is the sentence “we never decided that, it just ended up that way” — a library default, a retry count, a constant copied from a test sheet. Pavitra’s threshold is one. Experts log non-decisions, recording that a value was inherited and never validated.

The log is an asset and a liability at once. The tell is the first time counsel or an acquirer asks to read it. Entries are quotable, discoverable, and read by people whose interests differ from the author’s. The conclusion is not to write less but factually.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

The five fields do not change. What changes is which class of decision dominates and how triggers are expressed. In consumer products the highest-value entries concern measurement — which metric defined success, which cohort was excluded — because a redefinition invalidates every comparison across it. In B2B and enterprise, entries cluster around integrations and contractual promises, and triggers are contractual: a price step, a renewal date, a volume tier. In platforms and marketplaces part of the log is external, since a deprecation notice is a trade-off published to third parties. In hardware, triggers become dates. In AI products, the entry pins a model version, a prompt revision and the score that justified shipping.

Where the difference is not real it should be said plainly: the discipline is identical in a two-person start-up and a two-thousand-person firm, and the claim that small teams are too fast to log is usually a claim that they are too fast to price their shortcuts. Stage changes the failure mode, not the practice. Below roughly fifteen engineers founder memory substitutes, and the threshold is the second departure. In growth it is the handover cliff; at scale, reorganisation.

8. Three worked examples

Where it worked: Pavitra’s over-the-air channel

On 20 January 2025, with 18,600 devices in the field, Pavitra shipped without a secure over-the-air update channel to hold a festive-season launch date. Rohan Sabnis wrote the entry properly: the rejected option costed at 54 engineer-days, ₹9,07,200 at ₹16,800 a day; the trade-off stated as ₹620 a device for a service visit; the trigger, revisit before the field population reaches 50,000. Population grew at 3,300 devices a month, so the threshold arrived in the first week of November 2025, the entry surfaced in planning, and the channel shipped on 19 December 2025. On 20 May 2026, with 71,400 devices in the field, a defect was found in a batch of 12 per cent of them, or 8,568 devices.

Table 2. Pavitra: cost of fixing the May 2026 firmware defect, by route. Engineer time at ₹16,800 a day; the update went to the whole field population at ₹0.90 a device.
Cost lineManual service route (₹)Over-the-air route (₹)

The avoided cost was ₹50,96,700. Even charging the whole ₹9,07,200 build against this one incident, the net benefit was ₹41,89,500. What did the work was not the entry but its trigger, a number on a dashboard.

Where it failed: Sankhya’s triggers that could not fire

Sankhya had a log: after an earlier incident it adopted entries diligently, and by 30 June 2026 held 212. Shreya Pathak audited it and found the discipline performed, not practised. 133 stated no trigger; of the 79 that did, 31 named a metric retired in a February 2026 telemetry migration — 39.2 per cent of those that had one. Only 48 of the 212 entries, or 22.6 per cent, carried a trigger measurable and owned.

Table 3. Sankhya: trigger audit of the same 212 entries, before and after a quarter of remediation.

The recovery was procedural: a quarterly review in which every entry must name a catalogued metric with an owning team, be rewritten, or be closed as superseded. Forty-two described decisions that no longer existed.

Table 4. Sankhya: monthly economics of the Sampratti contract at 36,000 applications, priced at ₹58 each. Compute is ₹64.80 per application on the hosted model. On the parser route parsers cover 78 per cent of volume and the remaining 7,920 applications fall back to the model at that same ₹64.80 each — ₹14.256 blended across all 36,000.
