Exhibit 5. Thirty-day months; MB are decimal (106 bytes). Fleet GB = 59,200 × MB per device ÷ 1,000; the panel row is 2,560 × 7.776 + 56,640 × 0.9216 = 72,105.98 MB. The money column is GB × 1,000 × ₹2.80 to two decimals, so aggregating saves ₹11.36 lakh a month and the panel adds ₹0.49 lakh back.

Aggregation cuts volume to 11.85 per cent of full, and the panel restores fidelity where the model is trained for 15.7 per cent of Qadir's bill — the general answer.

In AI-native products events are also the labels the next model trains on. Qudrat's model learns from the join between telemetry and what the technician found, so every gap in recording is a gap in the training set, and biased capture becomes biased learning — a more durable error than a wrong chart, because it ships. At the seams the plan is owned by whoever owns the metric, enforced by whoever owns the pipeline, reviewed by whoever owns the legal basis. Where those are one person it is fast and fragile; where three committees, slow and still fragile.

6. Eight distinctions that mark an expert

Loss inside a plane is free; loss across a boundary is not

The competent practitioner raises capture rates everywhere; the expert asks first which steps cross the client/server boundary, because only those are biased. The tell is a conversion at or above 100 per cent, or two segments whose interior steps agree while the boundary step differs by a stable ratio.

Differential capture, not average capture, destroys decisions

A uniform 20 per cent loss costs precision; 25 per cent on one platform against 12.5 on another costs a quarter of engineering aimed at a phantom. The sign is a segment gap correlated with device, operating system or app version rather than anything the product did. The expert monitors capture rate by platform.

Identity stitching rewrites the past

When an anonymous visitor signs in, a good pipeline merges the identities, changing counts for days already reported, so a cohort chart re-run next month will not match the board pack — and nothing is broken. The sign is a historical figure drifting with no code change; the expert publishes which numbers are provisional.

Three timestamps, two property-times, one settlement curve

Device, collector and business time differ, and a phone with a wrong clock emits events preceding the signup that caused them. A property may be read at event time or at query time: break a funnel by plan and the answer depends on whether "plan" means the plan held then or now. Late arrival compounds both, as Exhibit 6 shows.

Exhibit 6. Of a day's events 62.0% arrive that day, then 24.0, 7.0, 3.5, 1.8, 1.0, 0.5 and 0.2 per cent after seven days — 100.0 in all, so cumulative capture runs 62.0, 86.0, 93.0, 96.5, 98.3, 99.3, 99.8. On a flat true 9,000 a day the seven bars sum to 57,141 against 63,000, or 90.70 per cent, and today reads 27.9 per cent below yesterday though nothing changed.

The past is mutable, by law

Consent withdrawal and erasure remove records already counted, and a consent-gated SDK leaves structurally missing data for a non-random slice of users. The sign is last quarter's total shrinking between readings; keep the deletion log and accept that a lawful record is not immutable.

Instrument the absence

A plan written from a design mock records successes: tapped, selected, confirmed. The expensive questions concern what did not happen — timeouts, validation failures, empty states, the bank that returned an error. The sign is a funnel with no error branch and a support queue analytics cannot see.

Measurement-readiness includes the ability to change

A product is not ready because it emits the right events today, but when an event can be renamed or retired without breaking a dashboard a renewal depends on. The sign is an event everyone knows is wrong that nobody will touch. Mature teams version events, run old and new in parallel, and keep a deprecation register.

The plan shapes what the team can propose

Instrumentation changes organisations more reliably than users. A team with nine events generates ideas those nine can evaluate, and stops proposing work it cannot measure; the sign is a quarter of initiatives mapping onto existing charts. Exhibit 4's ₹4,98,150 monthly gap follows the same logic: it is the price of optionality, and belongs to whoever decides roadmaps.

7. By product type and stage

In consumer products volume makes sampling, consent and identity dominant, and client capture rates the lowest anywhere. In B2B and enterprise software the account, not the user, is the unit of commercial truth, so the question is whether usage can be summarised per account per week in a form a renewal conversation survives — Qist's predicament. Platforms and marketplaces need both sides of a transaction on one event. For hardware, bandwidth, battery and firmware cadence set the ceiling: a change to what a device records may take a quarter to reach the fleet. In AI products the instrumentation is the training pipeline, and the forgotten events are which suggestion was shown, accepted, edited, and what happened next.

By stage the technology barely differs and the governance differs completely. A fifteen-person company needs a shared document and one person who verifies events before release. A company with forty teams needs a named owner, automated rejection of unregistered names and a review gate in the pipeline, because the number of pairs of people who must agree on the meaning of "active" grows faster than headcount.

8. Three worked examples

A success. Trained on representative data, Qudrat's model flagged 6,400 devices a month for a pre-emptive visit at a precision of 0.72: 4,608 would genuinely have failed within the window, 1,792 would not. A planned visit costs ₹480, an emergency visit ₹1,650. The gain is 4,608 × ₹1,170 = ₹53,91,360, less 1,792 × ₹480 = ₹8,60,160 of wasted visits: a net ₹45,31,200 a month, or ₹5.44 crore a year.

A mixed result. Qist's account-level instrumentation told the renewal truth and cost money. The old report counted 1,042 monthly active users against 1,180 licensed seats, 88.31 per cent, by counting an API service account and a shared kiosk login. After stitching, 712 distinct human agents were weekly-active, 60.34 per cent, and only 494 — 41.86 per cent of licensed seats — had used Resolve. Procurement read the same dashboard and cut 240 seats, taking the contract from ₹5.52 crore to 940 × ₹3,900 × 12 = ₹4.40 crore, a loss of ₹1.12 crore a year — which Zaveri judged a fair price for a verifiable renewal.

A failure, and the recovery. Qudrat's first filter model, in late 2025, relied on the householder's app to record filter changes. Of 22,400 changes that quarter only 13,216 — 59.00 per cent — produced an app event; the other 9,184 were done by a technician with the app closed, skewing rural and offline. Trained on that slice the model reached a precision of 0.58 and sent technicians to the wrong homes. The repair ran from Monday, 2 February 2026 to Monday, 6 April 2026, nine weeks, joining the service CRM's technician records to telemetry and adding a server-side event for ticket closure. Two data engineers for nine weeks at ₹85,000 a week cost ₹15.30 lakh, and precision rose to 0.72. The real cost was the delay: three months at ₹45.31 lakh is ₹1.36 crore forgone, 8.9 times the repair bill.

9. Failure modes and early warning signs

Exhibit 7 sets the first four weeks of Qist Resolve against the tenant's payment ledger; weekly reconciliation is the cheapest diagnostic.

WeekLedgerEventsVarianceVariance %
28 June33,26433,26400.00%
5 July35,11034,902(208)−0.59%
12 July36,48033,108(3,372)−9.24%
19 July37,12033,690(3,430)−9.24%
Total1,41,9741,34,964(7,010)−4.94%

Exhibit 7. Weeks end on the Sunday shown. The total variance, −4.94%, is computed on the totals (−7,010 ÷ 1,41,974), not as the mean of the four weekly rates, which would be −4.77%. A deployment on Wednesday, 8 July renamed a property on the confirmation event for one payment channel; the registry rejected it, and nobody was watching the dead-letter count.

Five failure modes, each with its sign and the catching question. Instrumentation deferred to the next sprint: a chart whose series begins after the launch date; ask which event proves the launch worked and when it last fired in a test build. Caught late the cost is unrecoverable: the launch window cannot be re-run. A silent schema break: a rising dead-letter count; ask what the system of record says for the same period. Client-only measurement of commercial facts: a conversion at or above 100 per cent; ask which plane emits each event. Autocapture used as a plan: 340 event names and no answer to the board's question; ask for this quarter's three decisions and the events that settle them. Capture bias in a model: field performance below validation; ask which users could not have produced a training record. At Qudrat that cost ₹1.36 crore.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Curated plan against broad capture. The plan school's strongest evidence is interpretability: audits of large catalogues find most names unused and contradictory definitions of one action, and a team that cannot say what an event means cannot defend a decision built on it. For that to be wrong, naming would have to be cheaply deferrable — exactly the autocapture claim, whose evidence is the question that arrives after the fact. Qudrat's missing technician events argue for breadth, Qist's catalogue for discipline.

Vendor tool against warehouse-native. The vendor case rests on who asks the questions: a manager who can build a funnel unaided asks ten times as many as one who files a ticket, and value is realised in questions asked. The warehouse case rests on governance and locality: one definition of "active", in reviewed SQL, in a jurisdiction compliance will sign. For the first to fail, warehouse self-service would have to become as fast; for the second, duplicated definitions would have to stop causing disputes.

Server-only purity against client richness. One camp holds that anything touching money must be server-emitted, and that client events should never enter a reported metric. The other replies that the experience — what was seen, what was abandoned, where the thumb hesitated — exists only on the client, so server-only discipline produces a firm that knows its revenue and nothing about its product. The algebra above says which steps are safe, not how much a firm should accept not knowing.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied instrumentation writes a tracking plan. Someone who has internalised it starts from the decisions, names the three questions the next review must answer, works backwards to events, and can say for each which plane emits it, what its capture rate is, which identifier attributes it, and what happens when a user withdraws consent. They monitor capture rate as a metric in its own right, reconcile against a system of record on a schedule rather than after a surprise, and distrust a perfect rate more than an ugly one.

12. The decisions

Zaveri split the problem rather than choosing a school. Borrower events, which carried the regulatory risk, went to Qist's own collector and a tenant-partitioned warehouse inside India; agent events, carrying no borrower identifier, stayed in the vendor tool so product managers kept self-service. Both validated against one registry, and the dead-letter count became a line on the launch dashboard. The compliance head signed.

Zaman took the panel. Shuddh 2 shipped on 6 July with fifteen-minute aggregates for the fleet and full one-minute telemetry for 8,000 panel devices, 2,560 on SIM, at ₹2.02 lakh a month against Qadir's ₹12.89 lakh. She also insisted on the event learned the hard way: a server-side record written when a technician closes a ticket, app opened or not.

For discussion. First: better measurement cost Qist ₹1.12 crore at its first renewal — when would you advise a product leader not to instrument what she could? Second: Qudrat's panel is representative today; what keeps it so in two years, and who owns that? Third: Exhibit 3 shows a step conversion of exactly 100.00 per cent — what in your own dashboards is that number in disguise?

13. Going deeper

  • Deploying a web product — you instrument only what is live; cadence sets how fast a tracking mistake is fixed.
  • Designing an event taxonomy — naming rules that survive forty teams.
  • Building a metrics dashboard — the consumer of all this; it exposes unagreed definitions.
  • Building a golden set from real usage — depends on unbiased capture, as Qudrat found.
  • How web and mobile apps work — why a WebView loses events a browser keeps.
  • APIs and integration basics — an event is an interface; versioning it is an API problem.
  • Data modelling for PMs — where raw events become entities a metric sits on.
  • Databases, storage and caching — why a count over 300 million rows is cheap or ruinous.
  • Cloud infrastructure basics — the collector, queue and bill in Exhibit 4.
  • Reading an architecture diagram — to see which plane an event fires from.
exp20v2-tech.instrument:
Instrumentation with Product Analytics Tools

Delivery & Technology, Technical Fluency. The question: is the product measurement-ready from day one?

1. The Monday that was not

On Tuesday, 24 February 2026, Vandana Warrier, head of product at Vitaan Bazaar Network, a Pune-based app that takes grocery orders for some 2,400 neighbourhood stores, opened the launch checklist for "Weekly Basket", a subscription in which a household approves a standing UPI Autopay mandate (a recurring-payment permission, issued through the National Payments Corporation of India's rails) and receives its staples every Saturday. Launch was fixed for Monday, 9 March. The board would meet on Thursday, 30 April, and the chief executive had promised it a recommendation on whether to fund a further ₹1.8 crore of subscription work.

The checklist was green except for one line. Vikrant Waghmare, the engineering lead, wanted to ship. Analytics, he proposed, could follow in the first sprint after launch: the app already used a product analytics tool, and "we can add events once we see what people do". Wojciech Wrona, a data engineer in Warsaw, replied in the ticket: "Whatever we do not record on day one, we do not get back."

The decision was therefore concrete. Shipping on 9 March meant a feature nobody could properly evaluate. Holding two days, to Wednesday, 11 March, meant a visible slip and an awkward message to the chief executive. If Warrier chose speed, the first six weeks of the only evidence the board would see would be partial, and no later effort could reconstruct it. The idea at its centre, instrumentation, is easy to describe and easy to get quietly wrong.

2. The idea

Instrumentation is the deliberate placing of recording points in a product, so that specified user and system actions are captured as structured records, sent to a collection pipeline and made available to an analytics tool. The records are called events. An event has a name ("mandate_approved"), a timestamp, an identity (who did it) and properties, the descriptive facts attached to it (plan type, basket value, payment app used). A product analytics tool is software that stores such events and lets non-engineers count, filter and sequence them without writing database queries.

A product cannot be observed the way a shop can. A shopkeeper sees who walks in and who leaves; software shows its makers nothing unless someone first decides what to record. Server logs record that requests occurred, not that a person hesitated at a price. Event-based analytics emerged in the late 2000s: Mixpanel, founded in 2009, popularised the idea that the unit of analysis should be the user action, and in the early 2010s Segment popularised a single collection layer, so that an event is defined once and forwarded to many tools.

The sentence Warrier could repeat in a meeting: "We are not adding analytics to the launch; we are deciding now which questions the launch must be able to answer, because a question we did not instrument is an answer we cannot have."

3. How it works, step by step

Exhibit 1 shows the path an event travels. A user taps a button in the Vitaan app. A small piece of code, the SDK (software development kit, a library supplied by the analytics vendor), assembles the event and stores it briefly on the phone, because the user may be in a lift with no signal. It then batches events and sends them over the network to a collector, a server that validates and timestamps them. From there they are written to a warehouse, the company's long-term data store, and to the analytics tool's own index, which is what the product manager queries.

Exhibit 1. The path of an event. Events can originate in the app (left) or on Vitaan's own servers (right); both converge on the same stores.

Three steps are usually left implicit. First, someone must write a tracking plan: a document listing every event, when exactly it fires, its properties and who owns it. Second, identity must be settled. Before login a user is anonymous, known only by a device identifier; after login she has a user identifier, and the tool must stitch the two so that the browsing before login and the purchase after belong to one person. Third, someone must verify the events in a test build, by performing the action and checking the record arrives with the right properties, before release rather than after.

Warrier asked Wrona for the plan the same afternoon. It ran to six events (Exhibit 2); note the column recording where each fires.

EventFires whenFired fromKey properties
offer_viewedWeekly Basket card is on screen for one secondAppentry_point, basket_value
subscribe_tappedUser taps SubscribeAppplan, store_id
mandate_approvedBank confirms the Autopay mandateServerpayment_app, bank, mandate_amount
first_subscription_orderFirst Saturday order is placedServerorder_value, store_id
subscription_pausedUser pausesAppreason (picklist)
subscription_cancelledMandate revokedServerreason, weeks_active

Exhibit 2. Vitaan's tracking plan for launch. Names are lower-case, verb-in-past-tense, and written once.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

Suppose the first seven days, 11 to 17 March, produce the true behaviour in Exhibit 3. Of 2,40,000 users who view the offer, 20 per cent tap Subscribe, which is 48,000. Seventy per cent of those complete the bank mandate: 48,000 × 0.70 = 33,600. Eighty per cent of those place a first order: 33,600 × 0.80 = 26,880. The end-to-end conversion is 26,880 ÷ 2,40,000 = 11.2 per cent, which also equals 0.20 × 0.70 × 0.80. A funnel is exactly this: an ordered series of events, with the share of users who survive each step.

Exhibit 3. Funnel bar lengths are proportional to counts (2,40,000 = 600 units wide). Percentages are step conversions from the previous bar.

Now change one input. Exhibit 2 fires "mandate approved" from the server; suppose instead a hasty build had recorded it in the app. When approving, the customer is thrown to her UPI app and returns to Vitaan; on some phones the operating system has closed Vitaan in the meantime, and the return event is never sent. Say 15 per cent are lost. The recorded count becomes 33,600 × 0.85 = 28,560. The step from tapped to approved now reads 28,560 ÷ 48,000 = 59.5 per cent instead of 70, and the step to first order reads 26,880 ÷ 28,560 = 94.1 per cent instead of 80. The end-to-end figure of 11.2 per cent has not moved, because the first-order event was recorded on the server.

A team reading Pass 2 would see 40.5 per cent lost at the mandate (the truth is 30) and only 5.9 per cent lost afterwards (the truth is 20). It would pour effort into the approval screen and wave through the post-approval stage, where one customer in five drops out. One invisible recording choice has pointed the team at the wrong screen. This is why Exhibit 2 records where each event fires, and why Wrona put money-moving events on the server.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Client events versus server events

Client events fire from the phone or browser and are cheap and rich in context (screen, device, scroll), but they are lossy: apps are killed, networks fail, blockers and consent choices suppress them. Server events fire from the company's own back end and are close to complete, but know nothing about what the user saw. Use the client for behaviour, the server for commercial facts, and reconcile them: a gap between the two is a finding, not noise.

Identity is the quiet failure

If anonymous and logged-in identities are not stitched, one shopper appears as two people, inflating user counts and breaking funnels that straddle login. Before trusting any user count, ask which identifier it counts and when that identifier changes.

Autocapture versus a curated plan

Autocapture records every tap and screen automatically. It is a useful safety net, but it produces names like "button_click_47" that no colleague can interpret, and it is priced by volume. Suppose 6,00,000 sessions a month, 120 autocaptured events per session against 14 curated, at an illustrative ₹15 per thousand. Autocapture is 7,20,00,000 events, costing 72,000 blocks of a thousand × ₹15 = ₹10,80,000 a month; curated is 84,00,000 events, 8,400 blocks × ₹15 = ₹1,26,000, a difference of ₹9,54,000 monthly.

Events are not properties

A common blur is making "subscribe_tapped_monthly" and "subscribe_tapped_weekly" separate events when plan belongs as a property of one event. Properties let one funnel be split by plan in a click. The test: would you ever count these two together? If so, one event, one property.

Consent and personal data

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 treats an identifiable person's data as something collected for a stated purpose with consent. Instrumentation that sends names, phone numbers or full addresses as properties creates a liability that analysis does not require. Send identifiers, not identity, and ask legal counsel before the plan is final, not after.

Sampling and delay

Some tools sample at high volume, analysing a fraction of events. That is acceptable for a trend and dangerous for a small segment: a 1 per cent sample of 2,000 users is twenty people. Events also arrive late, since a phone offline for a day sends its batch the next morning; do not read the current day's number as final.

What instrumentation cannot tell you

Events say what happened, not why. They show that 20 per cent tap Subscribe, not whether the other 80 per cent were uninterested, confused or merely browsing. Nor do they reveal the customers who never arrived. Events locate the problem; interviews explain it.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products; early and large

In consumer products volume is high, so sampling, identity and consent dominate. In B2B software the purchaser is an account of many users, so every event needs an account identifier beside the user identifier; otherwise one cannot ask whether a customer's usage is rising, which is what renewals depend on. In a marketplace such as Vitaan, there are at least two populations, shoppers and stores, and a transaction connects them: events must carry both identifiers, and the same action is read differently from each side.

The early-stage and large-company difference is of governance more than of technology. A ten-person start-up can keep its plan in a shared spreadsheet. A company with forty teams needs an owner for the plan, a review step before events ship, automated checks that reject an unplanned event name, and a deprecation process.

7. Common mistakes

"We will add tracking after launch." Symptom: the first review meeting shows a chart starting on the date events were added, and the launch week is blank. Misunderstanding: instrumentation is treated as a reporting task rather than a property of the release. Cheapest diagnostic: make an event-by-event verification a line in the launch checklist, owned by a named person.

Trusting a funnel without reconciling it. Symptom: the tool reports 28,560 approvals while the payments ledger shows 33,600. Misunderstanding: the tool's count is taken as ground truth. Cheapest diagnostic: each week, compare order and payment counts with the system of record.

Inconsistent names. Symptom: "SubscribeTap" and "subscribe_tapped" both exist, and dashboards disagree. Misunderstanding: names are seen as cosmetic. Cheapest diagnostic: list distinct event names and count near-duplicates.

Tracking what is easy rather than what is needed. Symptom: 40 events against a plan of six, and no answer to the board's question. Misunderstanding: starting from the interface rather than the decision. Cheapest diagnostic: write the three questions the next review must answer, then check each can be computed from named events.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the same decision begins three weeks before launch, with the board's questions: what share subscribe, what share complete the mandate, how many remain after four weeks. Each maps to named events, in a plan of fewer than ten. The plan is reviewed by engineering, data and legal in a single meeting. Events are tested in a pre-release build. On launch morning a dashboard already exists, showing zeros, and a daily reconciliation of server events with the payment ledger runs.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Warrier held the launch for two days. She told the chief executive that Weekly Basket would go live on Wednesday, 11 March, giving six full weeks of complete data by 22 April, ahead of the 30 April board. Her reasoning was an asymmetry: a late launch costs two days of subscription revenue, which can be earned later, whereas missing launch data is unrecoverable.

Next, learn designing an event taxonomy, which extends the tracking plan into naming rules that survive growth; then building a metrics dashboard, which turns events into a view a team can act on; then building a golden set from real usage, which reuses recorded behaviour as test material and is only possible if the recording was good.

Two questions to sit with. First, which one number would your leadership quote with confidence, and from which system would you verify it? Second, if a launch were cancelled tomorrow, which question would you most regret not being able to answer, and which event would have answered it?
case40v1-tech.instrument:
Laghima Field Systems: Five Numbers for One Word

A case on instrumentation, measurement and what a contract can be made to mean. Mangaluru, October 2026.

1. Sunday night

Sunday, 18 October 2026, 22:40, Mangaluru. The rain had come back after a dry fortnight and was loud on the terrace. Vaanmathi Elanjickal, chief product officer of Laghima Field Systems Private Limited, had a board pack due at nine the next morning and one slide in it she could not finish. The slide was titled Active users, September 2026 and it carried five figures: 28,600, 24,900, 21,340, 19,460 and 11,580. Every one came out of a system Laghima owned and ran. Every one was defensible. Nobody in the company could say which of them the word meant.

Three things were waiting on that slide. Lujain General Trading LLC, the Dubai distributor that was Laghima's largest single customer at ₹3.60 crore a year, had returned its renewal draft on 29 September with the per-seat clause struck out and a per-active-user clause written in its place. The investors conducting diligence on a ₹180 crore Series C had asked on 9 October for a reconciliation of active users, and had not been answered. And Vikhyath Ennackal, who founded Laghima in 2017 and would chair Monday's call, had put a question to Vaanmathi three weeks earlier that she still could not answer: of the people we bill for, how many opened the app yesterday?

2. How Laghima got here

Laghima was founded in Mangaluru in 2017 by Ennackal and two classmates from NITK Surathkal, to replace the carbon-copy order book carried by salesmen who work the general trade. Its Android application, Laghima Beat, gives a salesman a day's beat plan, a stock position for each outlet and an order form that works with no network at all; its web product, Laghima Console, gives the distributor a view of the territory. In the year to 31 March 2026 the company earned ₹45.20 crore, ₹38.50 crore of it from seat subscriptions and ₹6.70 crore from implementation and ERP integration work. Seats have been added at about 375 a month since; annualised at September's 28,600 licensed seats across 184 tenants, a mean of 155 a tenant, and a blended ₹1,320 a seat a month, the subscription run-rate is ₹45.30 crore.

One decision from that period governs everything Vaanmathi could do in October 2026. In March 2023, competing for the Lujain tender against two better-funded rivals, Laghima promised an installed size under 15 MB. Engineering delivered 14.8 MB by stripping the application of both analytics SDKs it then carried, keeping only Google's Crashlytics for crash reports. The same tender produced clause 11.4 of the Lujain master agreement: no third-party SDK that transmits user-level data may be added to the application without Lujain's written approval, on 45 days' notice. Laghima signed it gladly. Beat has shipped without product analytics ever since. Console was instrumented in January 2025 with a self-hosted open-source tool and 46 named events, all of them on the web.

3. The market around the product

Laghima sells into the roughly 1.3 crore kirana outlets that still carry most of India's packaged-goods volume, through the distributors who serve them for brands such as Amul and Asian Paints. Its named competitors, Bizom and FieldAssist, ship with analytics built in and say so in every bake-off.

Two macro forces press on the product. Quick commerce, led by Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, and the ONDC pilots have given brands routes to the consumer that bypass the beat altogether, so distributors now ask what their field software is worth per head rather than per territory. GST e-invoicing has pushed order capture closer to the distributor's own billing system, which is where Laghima's ERP connectors sit. Regulation bears on measurement directly: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the rules notified under it require a stated purpose and a consent notice for what the application records about a salesman, who is a data principal employed by the tenant, not by Laghima; Laghima is a processor. In the Gulf, which contributed ₹7.30 crore of FY2026 revenue, the UAE's data-protection law and the Lujain agreement together confine the personal data of Lujain's users to India or the UAE. Lujain alone is ₹3.60 crore a year, about 8 per cent of the subscription run-rate.

4. What happened, and what was believed at each point

Until June the company believed it had a usage number. The API gateway in Bengaluru wrote one log row for every request, and the count of distinct user identifiers in those rows was quoted in board packs as monthly active users. On Friday 12 June 2026, as part of a ₹14 lakh a year saving on log storage, the gateway began sampling rows for its highest-volume endpoint, /sync/batch, at one in ten. The saving was approved; the consequence for the active-user series was not discussed, and the data team was not told.

On 1 September Vamika Erinjeri shipped a redesigned day-plan screen to 30 per cent of users. The redesign assumed salesmen set up the next day's beat in the evening, which is what the gateway's arrival-time chart had shown for two years.

From 14 to 27 September a debug build carrying eleven extra fields in the sync payload went to volunteers at nine tenants. It was the first time Laghima had seen a beat day as the handset saw it (Exhibit 4). Vibhuti read it as a morning rather than an evening, the queue and not the work arriving after dark (Exhibit 5).

Lujain's redline arrived on 29 September. On 6 October Vaishakh Ettumanoor presented a quarterly review to Lujain using his own spreadsheet figure of 2,200 active users, three days before the diligence team asked for a reconciliation that would have to explain why the gateway said 1,880 for the same month and the same accounts.

5. The people

Vikhyath Ennackal, co-founder and chief executive, Mangaluru. He wants a number that will not have to be restated once the Series C term sheet lands in mid-December, and would rather reprice the Lujain contract than instrument the application. He approved the June logging saving and has not connected it to the series he quotes.

Vidyut Edamana, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru, 38 people. He argues that everything needed can be derived from the gateway and the sync payload. He carries a 99.9 per cent availability commitment through the festive season. He has not told the data team how long the sampling has been running, and his team has a half-built event logger of its own.

Vibhuti Emmatty, data scientist, Toronto. She wants a written event taxonomy agreed before any tool is bought, on the ground that unnamed events cost her more than missing ones. She is the person asked to restate figures when they break. She has not said that the pilot she cites covers nine tenants and no Gulf account, or that one figure in the board pack is her extrapolation from it.

Vamika Erinjeri, principal designer, Berlin. She wants the vendor tool with session replay, this month. Her promotion case rests on the day-plan redesign now running with 30 per cent of users. She has not said that the redesign was reasoned from an arrival-time chart, or that a replay trial is already live on a staging build.

Vaishakh Ettumanoor, head of customer success, Singapore. He wants any usage figure he can take into a quarterly review this month. His renewal bonus is calculated on reported adoption. He knows that most tenant administrators send him licensed headcount, and has never written that down.

Vitthal Ezhuthachan, sales head for the Americas and EMEA, New Jersey. He wants the per-seat basis preserved in every contract. His commission is a function of contract value. He has already promised Lujain a usage dashboard in the January release, in writing, and priced none of it.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the series the board has seen for two years. Seats rose 5.5 per cent over the five months while gateway-active users fell 3.8 per cent, and Vaishakh reads the divergence as attrition inside accounts that keep paying for seats they no longer staff. Vibhuti reads it as an artefact. Exhibit 2 is the reconciliation the diligence team asked for.

The sampling matters arithmetically. A salesman whose only traffic is the sync endpoint, and who makes 22 such calls in a month, escapes the log altogether with probability 0.9 raised to the 22nd power, about one in ten; grossing up the 9,820 survivors in row 3 implies roughly 1,070 more who left no row at all, a step of about 5 per cent when sampling began. Exhibit 1 shows no such step. Vibhuti has written that she can explain neither the absence of the step nor the gradual slide. Exhibit 3 prices what can be done about it.

Route A cannot reach Lujain before February because clause 11.4 runs 45 days from written notice. Exhibit 4 is the only evidence Laghima has about the part of the day no server-side route can see.

Read by the handset clock, 48 per cent of check-ins fall between 10:00 and 14:00; read by arrival, 43 per cent land between 18:00 and 22:00. Exhibit 6 applies the counts in Exhibit 2 to the clause Lujain has proposed.

7. Voices

“Clause 11.4 is not an engineering ticket. Forty-five days from written notice, and the notice goes to a security committee that meets monthly. If we send it Monday the SDK is legal on 3 December. The renewal is signed on the 30th.”

Vidyut Edamana, product channel, 15 October 2026, 18:30 IST

“Attrition does not explain a number whose denominator moved the other way. Seats went up. But I also cannot find the step the sampling should have produced in July, and I will not put either story in the board pack.”

Vibhuti Emmatty, note to Vikhyath Ennackal, 12 October 2026

“Two-thirds of the beat day is invisible to us. I have been reviewing accounts for four years on a spreadsheet that tenant admins fill in by hand.”

Vaishakh Ettumanoor, review rehearsal, 5 October 2026

“Confirming our commitment: a usage dashboard for your supervisors in the January release, at no additional licence cost.”

Vitthal Ezhuthachan to Vrisha Eachara, category director, Lujain General Trading, 2 October 2026

“Our audit committee will not approve payment for 2,400 seats when your own review deck shows 2,200 people. We would rather pay for what is used. Whatever measures it must keep our people's data in the UAE or in India.”

Vrisha Eachara, reply, 7 October 2026

“I designed the evening planner because the chart said evening. Nobody told me the chart was the queue draining.”

Vamika Erinjeri, design review, 8 October 2026

8. The options as Vaanmathi sees them

A. Instrument the application properly. A written taxonomy, agreed with Vibhuti before code, then a client SDK that stamps events on the handset and queues them offline, with a consent notice. Nine weeks, ₹148 lakh in year one, and clause 11.4 puts it on a Lujain handset no earlier than February. No server-side route can see the draft step.

B. Server-side only. Switch the sampling off and read the device timestamps the sync payload already carries on every check-in and order. Three weeks, ₹32 lakh, inside the uncommitted budget, and nothing new on the handset. It sees orders and check-ins and nothing that happens on a screen.

C. Buy autocapture and replay. Two weeks, ₹131 lakh in year one, every tap recorded and named later. It is the route most exposed to the residency clause and to the consent question, since Laghima is the tenant's processor and not the salesman's employer.

D. Reprice on what is already captured. Offer Lujain a per-user price on users who submitted at least one order accepted by Lujain's own ERP in the month. ₹4 lakh, no engineering, available on Monday. Lujain's ERP, not Laghima's, decides which orders are accepted.

9. The deadline and the constraints

Vaanmathi presents at nine on Monday 19 October. Lujain's renewal is signed on 30 November; its quarterly release window closes on Friday 6 November, with a build cut on 30 October, and the next window opens on 1 February 2027. Indian tenants impose a festive freeze from 20 October to 15 November, Diwali falling on 8 November, so a build Lujain accepts in the November window is one Indian tenants will not take until the 16th. Written notice under clause 11.4 given on Monday matures on 3 December. The FY2027 product-engineering budget has ₹95 lakh uncommitted, which routes A and C both exceed, and headcount is frozen until the Series C closes; Vibhuti is the only person who can write the taxonomy and she is nine and a half hours behind. If the login basis Lujain has drafted spread to every contract, the 11,580 login-active users of September, priced at the blended ₹15,840 a seat-year, would yield ₹18.34 crore against the ₹45.30 crore subscription run-rate — ₹26.96 crore less, 59.5 per cent of that run-rate and not of total revenue.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the five counts in Exhibit 2 is the number of active users? What would you need to establish before choosing one?
  2. Seats rose while gateway users fell (Exhibit 1). Which explanations are consistent with both columns, and what single test would separate them?
  3. Exhibits 4 and 5 disagree about when a beat day happens. Which would you design from, and what does the footnote on clock skew do to that answer?
  4. Price the renewal on each basis in Exhibit 6. Which definition would you take into the negotiation, and what does Laghima owe Lujain if the cheaper definition is also the less true one?
  5. Suppose Laghima buys nothing. What could it know by 30 November from the five paths in Figure 1 alone, what would it still be unable to say, and what would it have to stop claiming?
  6. What does Vaanmathi do on Monday morning, and what does she say to the board — in particular about the active-user figure already sitting in the data room?

The rain had thinned by half past one. Vaanmathi had the five figures on one sheet, Exhibit 5 on another, and the renewal draft open with clause 11.4 highlighted in yellow. She had written one line of the slide and deleted it twice. The call was in seven and a half hours.
case40v1-tech.cloud:
Vatayan Live Technologies: What the Streams Cost

An ambiguous case on cloud infrastructure, regions and the cost model

1. Ahmedabad, the night of Thursday 15 October 2026

The office off Sindhu Bhavan Road was empty except for the far corner, where Grishma Munot had two monitors pushed together, the September bill on one and her own spreadsheet on the other. It was a quarter past eleven. The leadership call was at seven the next evening, Friday 16 October, an hour chosen so that Berlin, Toronto, New Jersey and Singapore could all be awake for it.

Vatayan Live Technologies had spent ₹342.0 lakh on cloud infrastructure in September 2026 against net revenue of ₹980 lakh — 34.9 per cent. In June the board had asked for 22 per cent by March 2027. Sixteen days from tonight, on Saturday 31 October, the discount the company's cloud provider had put on the table would lapse, and what followed it was smaller. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, the festive peak. Grishma had three memos open, each by someone she trusted, each with a different number for the same decision.

2. The company, 2019 to 2026

Vatayan was founded in Ahmedabad in 2019 by Grishma Munot and two classmates who had watched Surat saree wholesalers sell over video calls. A seller goes live from a phone, shows stock and takes payment through a UPI link; buyers watch in Gujarati, Hindi, Marathi or Tamil. By September 2026 Vatayan carried ₹118 crore of gross merchandise value a month, earning ₹980 lakh of net revenue on it, a take rate of 8.3 per cent.

One decision from 2024 shapes tonight. In March 2024, short of cash, Vatayan signed a three-year enterprise agreement with a single global cloud provider: 12 per cent off all services if at least 90 per cent of its cloud spend stayed with that provider, repriced retrospectively if the condition broke. It runs to Wednesday 31 March 2027, and every bill here is net of that 12 per cent. The engineering followed: managed services wherever the provider sold one, a single Mumbai region, and a replay library never pruned, now 1,400 terabytes of recorded streams.

3. The industry

Live commerce in India is contested from above and below. Meesho and Flipkart have pushed video formats at national scale; Nykaa and Lenskart run live shopping inside their own apps and need no marketplace. Payments ride on UPI through NPCI, with Razorpay and PhonePe as the rails Vatayan's sellers trust, and the commission attracts GST. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act governs what Vatayan does with viewer and seller data, which matters because the safety stack sends every live second to a moderation model, and that output is personal data about identifiable sellers.

The exposure is not only Indian. Vaslat Group DMCC, a Dubai jewellery and textile group streaming daily to Gulf buyers, was ₹115.6 lakh of September net revenue, 11.8 per cent of the total, and renews on Sunday 31 January 2027. Its procurement team wrote on 29 September asking that Vaslat's streams and buyers' data sit in a United Arab Emirates region. Two United States retail groups in late-stage talks have each asked where the data would live.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In January 2026 Vatayan shipped Live 3.0. Two choices in it drive the bill: every live stream is transcoded into a four-rung ladder — 360p, 480p, 720p and 1080p — and moderation runs continuously rather than on a sample. Both were defended on one argument: watch-time would grow faster than infrastructure cost.

Watch-hours did grow: from 240 lakh in May 2026 to 524 lakh in September, with the bill rising from ₹182 lakh to ₹342 lakh (Exhibit 4). On 24 August, Gehna Mavani circulated the cost per thousand delivered watch-hours for May to July, down from ₹758 to ₹693. The meeting read that as efficiency improving and turned to monetisation.

What has since turned out to be wrong is the denominator. A rising share of delivered hours is replay — recorded streams watched later, served from cache, carrying no commerce. Replay was 54 lakh of May's 240 lakh hours and 171 lakh of September's 524 lakh, 32.6 per cent. Against live hours only, where almost all the transcode and moderation cost sits, the cost per thousand hours went from ₹978 in May (₹182 lakh over 186 lakh live hours) to ₹969 in September (₹342 lakh over 353 lakh live hours) — a fall of 1.0 per cent, not the 13.9 per cent the delivered-hours series shows. A second finding landed more quietly: of September's 353 lakh live hours, 252 lakh (71.4 per cent) were delivered at 480p and 7 lakh (2.0 per cent) at 1080p, with 73 lakh at 360p and 21 lakh at 720p. Vatayan transcodes four rungs for every live second and pays for all four.

On Tuesday 15 September the provider offered committed-use pricing, open until 31 October; on Monday 12 October, Ganika Marfatia circulated a ten-week re-architecture plan. The October bill stood at ₹168 lakh on the fourteenth — ₹12.00 lakh a day against September's ₹11.40 lakh, 5.3 per cent higher. Figure 1 has the dates.

Scale: 3 pixels per day, 1 September 2026 at the left end of the axis. The ten-week bar begins on Monday 16 November, the first working day after the freeze, and ends on Monday 25 January 2027. Nothing in it has started.

5. The people

Grishma Munot, Ahmedabad, co-founder and chief executive, came from product and has owned the infrastructure budget since April 2025. She told the board 22 per cent is reachable; she has not said she no longer thinks the bill is an engineering problem.

Gunvanti Majmudar, Ahmedabad, chief financial officer, is building a Series C deck and wants the commitment signed before 31 October. She has not said that a signature lets her show a lower cost line whatever follows.

Girjesh Maheshwari, Pune, vice-president of platform engineering, runs fourteen engineers and the Diwali rota, and will ship nothing structural in the festive fortnight. He has not said that six engineers Ganika needs are on that rota.

Ganika Marfatia, Bengaluru, principal engineer for infrastructure, wrote the ten-week plan and believes much of the transcode bill avoidable. She has not said that her surviving-floor estimate assumes a sampling change legal has not cleared.

Gehna Mavani, Toronto, staff data scientist, produced the August unit-cost series and September's correction to it. She has not said that her own March revenue projection, ₹1,040 lakh, is below the plan.

Gavish Modani, Berlin, design lead, built the brand on streams that look like television and argues the 1080p rung is why large sellers stay. He has not said that the usage figure reached him only on 12 October.

Gyanendra Munshi, Singapore, customer success lead, owns the Vaslat account and reads the UAE request as a renewal condition. He has not said that his variable pay this year rests on that one renewal.

Gitesh Motiwala, New Jersey, head of sales for international accounts, wants a United States region and treats Dubai as a precedent. He has not said that neither prospect has asked for a region in writing.

Local times are those when Ahmedabad is at 19:00 India Standard Time on Friday 16 October 2026, the hour of the leadership call, which Vaslat does not attend. Berlin is three and a half hours behind IST, Toronto and New Jersey nine and a half; all three shift when their summer time ends.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Seventy point nine lakh a month is sitting on the table and it expires on the thirty-first. I am not asking engineering to stop improving anything, only that we stop paying list price while they do.”

The floor number is ₹48.82 lakh. What that is worth after January is a different question.”

Girjesh Maheshwari, platform channel, 14 October 2026

“The floor I am being asked to commit to for twelve months is the floor I am being paid to demolish in ten weeks. Both cannot be my objective.”

Ganika Marfatia, design review, 12 October 2026

Gyanendra Munshi, Singapore, 13 October 2026

8. The options as Grishma sees them tonight

A. Sign the whole floor before 31 October. ₹86.18 lakh a month committed, ₹1,034.16 lakh — ₹10.34 crore — over twelve months, against a projected 31 October cash balance of ₹38.8 crore; twelve months of saving at Exhibit 3's floor row is ₹585.8 lakh. If Ganika's plan lands, the floor needed falls to ₹89.0 lakh of on-demand equivalent and ₹28.76 lakh a month of committed capacity goes unused — ₹43.0 lakh of compute at the committed 62 per cent of list, plus ₹3.0 lakh of database at 70 per cent — or ₹258.8 lakh over the nine months from 1 February to 31 October 2027.

B. Re-architect and commit nothing. The bill settles near ₹241.0 lakh, 21.0 per cent of planned March revenue; the 38 and 30 per cent rates are gone and a later commitment is priced at 26 and 20.

C. Commit only the floor that survives, and re-architect. ₹57.42 lakh a month committed, ₹689.04 lakh over the year, a bill of ₹209.42 lakh from late January — and a bet on an estimate made before the work is done.

D. Open the UAE region. Unpriced, and the only course that answers a customer rather than a budget.

All four are purchasing decisions, which is how the memos arrived. Nobody has priced the replay library as a product question, though it carries ₹38.0 lakh of storage a month and 171 lakh of September's watch-hours. Nobody has costed letting the March 2024 agreement lapse, though a twelve-month commitment signed on 31 October 2026 runs to 31 October 2027, seven months past that agreement's end, with the clawback cap of ₹274.1 lakh in between. Both regional asks, if answered, change the floor A and C would have fixed.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The early rates lapse on Saturday 31 October 2026 and fall to 26 and 20 per cent. The festive freeze runs from 1 to 15 November, with Diwali on Sunday 8 November, so nothing structural ships before Monday 16 November, and ten weeks from there is Monday 25 January 2027 — six days before the Vaslat renewal. Headcount is capped until the Series C closes, and the six engineers Ganika needs are six of Girjesh's fourteen, on the Diwali rota. The March 2024 agreement holds the 12 per cent discount and the 90 per cent condition to 31 March 2027, with the clawback capped at the discount received in the trailing twelve months: cloud spend over those months was ₹2,010 lakh net, which at 88 per cent of list implies ₹274.1 lakh received, and the seven months to April 2026 averaged ₹106.4 lakh. Cash at bank was ₹41.6 crore on 30 September 2026; the projected 31 October balance, which opens the five months from November to the board's March deadline, is ₹38.8 crore, and at September's net burn of ₹2.80 crore a month that is 13.9 months. The sampling change in Ganika's forecast is not cleared against the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and the 22 per cent is set against a March 2027 revenue two people forecast differently.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Vatayan buy when it buys cloud infrastructure, and which lines of Exhibit 1 follow from a product decision rather than an engineering one?
  2. Exhibit 4's last two columns move in opposite directions. Which denominator should govern the decision, and what would you measure to defend that choice?
  3. Exhibit 3 gives three correct answers to one question. What must be true for each base to be the right one?
  4. Exhibit 5 is incomplete in a way that favours one course. How would you settle the regional question without those cells?
  5. A commitment signed on 31 October 2026 outlives the agreement it is signed under by seven months. How should that change the term, the quantity or the decision?
  6. It is Monday 19 October. What does Grishma do that morning, in what order and with whom — and what does she tell the board about what the September bill was measuring?

At half past midnight she wrote one line at the top of the blank page: what are we selling that these hours are for? Then she deleted it, because Gunvanti's deck went to the lead investor on Monday and the question did not have a number in it. The Mumbai dashboard showed 11,400 streams live. In Berlin, Gavish had sent a mock of a 1080p stream with the quality selector removed. Grishma left it unread, closed the laptop, and did not decide.
case20v1-tech.cloud:
Tantu Retail Technologies: The Cloud Commitment

A decision case on cloud infrastructure and its cost model

1. Opening

On Monday 19 October 2026, Eshani Lakdawala opened her laptop in the Ahmedabad office at 7:15 in the morning and read the email she had been avoiding since Friday. Tantu Retail Technologies' cloud provider would give a one-year discount on committed capacity only if the company signed by midnight on Saturday 31 October. Diwali fell eight days later, on Sunday 8 November, and the company's servers would carry their heaviest load of the year.

Eshani, Tantu's co-founder and chief executive, had until Friday 30 October to tell her finance chief what to sign, if anything. The September bill was Rs 38.0 lakh, and her board had asked for cloud costs below 5 per cent of revenue by March. Her team across three countries would join a call at 7:30 that evening.

2. Company background

Tantu was founded in 2017 in Surat by Eshani and a college friend, after watching textile traders keep ledgers in notebooks. Its app, Tantu Khata, handles billing, inventory, GST e-invoicing and payment links, and runs on a phone or a browser. It sells to textile wholesalers, kirana owners and small distributors at about Rs 1,000 a month.

By September 2026 Tantu had 62,000 paying merchants, giving monthly revenue of Rs 620 lakh, or Rs 6.2 crore. Its rivals are well known: Tally on the desktop, Vyapar and Khatabook on the phone, Zoho Books at the more formal end. Tantu's edge is Gujarati-language invoices, and merchants judge it on whether the invoice screen opens while the customer stands at the counter. About 11 per cent of revenue comes from a Dubai trading group that runs Tantu across its Indian suppliers.

3. The situation

Tantu rents rather than owns its computers. Its servers run in the provider's Mumbai region, a cluster of data centres, which keeps merchants' records in India and responses quick. The bill has four main parts. Compute is the virtual servers that run the app. A managed database holds every ledger entry, and the provider handles its backups and patches in exchange for a premium. Storage holds the photographs and PDFs of invoices, and data transfer is the charge for bytes sent out to merchants' phones. Exhibit 1 shows where the September money went.

The same Toronto analysis found waste. Invoice images older than 90 days sat on the costliest storage tier though almost nobody opened them. Servers ran at peak size around the clock, and images went to phones at full resolution.

4. The people

Eshani Lakdawala, Ahmedabad, chief executive, wants the 5 per cent target met and no outage during Diwali.

Eeshwar Lalani, Ahmedabad, chief financial officer, wants to sign the full commitment now. He sees a Rs 1.92 lakh a month penalty, on the current floor, for waiting.

Elias Lathia, Pune, head of platform engineering, leads fourteen engineers. He would rather cut waste first, fears locking in capacity he is about to make unnecessary, and has told Eshani his team cannot ship risky changes in Diwali week.

Elesh Luhar, Singapore, leads customer success. He speaks daily to the Dubai group and says a slow screen costs more in renewals than any discount saves. On the call it will be 10:00 in the morning in Toronto for Edison and 10:00 at night in Singapore for Elesh.

5. The options

Exhibit 4 compares the three courses, each against today's bill.

Option A: Commit to the whole floor now. Tantu signs for Rs 12.00 lakh a month of compute and database, as in Exhibit 2, before 31 October. The bill falls to Rs 30.80 lakh a month, and Rs 144.00 lakh is committed. The cost is idle commitment if the floor later shrinks.

Option B: Optimise first, commit nothing. Engineers spend eight weeks from 2 November tiering old images to cold storage, scheduling servers down at night and compressing images, with the server scheduling held until after 8 November. Compute falls from Rs 15.2 lakh to Rs 12.4 lakh, storage from 5.8 to 3.4, and data transfer from 3.4 to 2.6. The bill drops by Rs 6.0 lakh to Rs 32.0 lakh a month. The work costs a one-time Rs 14.00 lakh. The 31 October offer lapses, and any later commitment will be at the lower discounts.

Option C: Commit only to the floor that survives optimisation, and optimise. Tantu signs now for the post-optimisation floor: Rs 8.00 lakh of compute floor (down from 9.60) and the whole database. At the early discounts this commits Rs 4.80 lakh plus Rs 6.24 lakh, or Rs 11.04 lakh a month. The optimisation in Option B follows, leaving compute at Rs 8.00 lakh of floor plus Rs 4.40 lakh of burst, or Rs 12.40 lakh. The bill settles at Rs 25.44 lakh a month, with Rs 132.48 lakh committed and the same Rs 14.00 lakh of engineering work.

Merchant volumes are held at September levels.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which two components make up most of the bill, and why is on-demand pricing dearer than committed pricing?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows a Rs 1.92 lakh monthly difference between signing by 31 October and signing later. What does Eeshwar's penalty cost over twelve months, and what would it have to be compared against?
  3. Option A has the biggest immediate discount, yet Option C costs less. Which assumption in Edison's analysis explains the gap, and how would you test it?
  4. Which of the three options would you take to the board, and what evidence would make you change that view before 30 October?

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Cloud turns a fixed cost into a variable one. Tantu pays a premium for the freedom to scale with a festival peak, and a commitment trades that freedom for a lower price on capacity it is sure to keep using. The product question is therefore not whether the discount is large. It is how large the floor is that Tantu will still need after it has stopped wasting.

One defensible path. Option C. Over twelve months it costs Rs 319.28 lakh, against Rs 369.60 lakh for A and Rs 398.00 lakh for B, and it takes the bill to 4.10 per cent of September revenue, inside the board's 5 per cent. A meets the target only just, at 4.97 per cent. It commits Rs 144.00 lakh against C's Rs 132.48 lakh, a gap of Rs 11.52 lakh. That is exactly what A would pay for idle compute if Elias's team then cut the floor from Rs 9.60 lakh to Rs 8.00 lakh of on-demand value: Rs 0.96 lakh a month, or Rs 11.52 lakh over twelve months. Option B forgoes commitment discounts altogether, which is why it costs the most of the three.

C also respects the people. It commits only a floor that already exists, and the server scheduling waits until after 8 November, so Diwali is safe, and Elesh's concern is met because the burst layer stays on demand.

What would change the answer. If merchant volumes fall, the committed Rs 132.48 lakh is still due, so Eshani should ask for the smallest floor she is sure of. If optimisation cuts the floor by less than planned, the committed Rs 8.00 lakh is still used; if it cuts more, Tantu pays for idle capacity. The numbers rest on September volumes and on Edison's split of floor and burst, and a careful student would ask to see both.
exp20v2-tech.cloud:
Cloud infrastructure basics: where the product runs and what it costs

1. The Tuesday meeting

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Hema Iyengar, Head of Product at Hamsafar Ticketing Network, a Pune company that sells intercity bus seats on behalf of about 1,400 operators, sat down with Harsh Inamdar, the chief technology officer, and Indira Hegde, the finance head. Hamsafar's August bill from its cloud provider had arrived: ₹30,67,000 for a month in which customers made 12,00,000 confirmed bookings. The festive season began in mid-October, and the product team expected bookings to rise to 30,00,000 in the peak month, which is 2.5 times August.

The provider had made an offer, open for 22 days, until 30 September: commit to a year of baseline capacity and receive a 38 per cent discount on it. Indira wanted to accept. Harsh wanted to build a second deployment in another region before the festival. Hema realised she could not defend either position, because she could not say what the money was buying.

The stakes were concrete. A commitment that is too large is paid for whether or not customers arrive. A commitment that is too small leaves the company paying the highest price for exactly the weeks when volume is greatest. A system that falls over on the busiest weekend of the year costs bookings that go to a competitor.

2. The idea

Cloud infrastructure means renting computing capacity by the hour, or by the gigabyte, from a provider's data centres instead of owning servers. The principal providers in India are Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, each running data centres in Mumbai and elsewhere. Before such rental existed, a company like Hamsafar would have bought servers sized for its busiest day, housed them, and paid for them through the other 364. Rental at scale began in the mid-2000s, when firms that had built large private capacity for their own peaks began selling the idle portion.

Four terms recur. Compute is processing power, sold as instances: virtual machines of a stated size, billed per hour while running. Storage is data at rest, billed per gigabyte per month. Network transfer is data leaving the provider's network, billed per gigabyte. A region is a geographic cluster of data centres, such as Mumbai; an availability zone is one separately powered data centre inside a region. A managed service is software the provider operates for you, such as a database, so that you pay more per hour and employ fewer people to look after it.

The sentence Hema could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "We rent capacity by the hour, so our bill is a product decision as much as an engineering one, because every feature changes what we rent and for how long."

3. How it actually works

Follow one booking. A customer in Nagpur taps "Book seat 14" at 9 pm. The request travels to Hamsafar's address, where a load balancer, a managed service that spreads requests across machines, hands it to one of the application instances. That instance checks seat availability in the cache, a fast memory store, and writes the booking to the managed database. It places a message on a queue, a waiting line for jobs, so that the e-ticket and the SMS are produced a moment later without making the customer wait. The ticket PDF is saved to object storage, and the customer downloads it, which is the data transfer the provider charges for.

Several steps are usually left implicit. First, every instance in the booking path is on a meter, and the meter runs whether the instance is busy or idle; a server doing nothing costs the same as one at full load. Second, the application instances do not remember anything between requests. They are interchangeable, which is why the provider can add or remove them automatically, a practice called autoscaling. Third, the database is the exception: it holds state, so it cannot be duplicated casually. Fourth, availability zones exist because a single data centre can fail. Hamsafar spreads its instances over two zones in Mumbai, so the loss of one building halves capacity instead of ending service.

The 60 plus 60 instances in Figure 2 give the 120 in the bill below. The standby database in Zone B is why the database line is two machines: insurance, billed every hour.

4. A worked example

Hema asked Indira to rebuild the August bill from its meters instead of reading the invoice total. The assumptions: a 30-day month of 720 hours, 120 instances running flat for the whole month (a simplification; real autoscaling varies), and the prices in Table 1, which are illustrative for this case. Each row multiplies quantity by hours by price.

Table 1. Hamsafar's August cloud bill, rebuilt from meters (₹)

The total matches the invoice. The ratio Hema cared about is cloud cost per booking, defined as the month's total bill divided by confirmed bookings in that month: ₹30,67,000 divided by 12,00,000 is ₹2.56 (rounded from 2.5558). Compute is 62.0 per cent of the bill, so any serious saving has to come from there.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose Hamsafar accepts the commitment, but only on the 80 instances that never switch off, not on all 120. The discounted rate is ₹22 × (1 − 0.38) = ₹13.64 per hour. The other 40 instances stay on demand at ₹22. Table 2 shows the effect.

The monthly saving is ₹30,67,000 minus ₹25,85,464, which is ₹4,81,536, and cost per booking falls from ₹2.56 to ₹2.15 (from 2.1545). Over twelve months the saving is ₹57,78,432. But the commitment itself is a fixed obligation of ₹7,85,664 a month, or ₹94,27,968 a year, owed whatever happens to traffic. The break-even is simple: the commitment beats on-demand only if at least 62 per cent of the 80 committed instances, that is 49.6 of them, would otherwise have been running. If Hamsafar's baseline fell below roughly 50 instances, the commitment would lose money. Harsh's team had never run fewer than 95 in two years, so the risk was small, and the exercise showed Hema why: she could now say what the commitment was a bet on.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Rented capacity is a variable cost only if you let it be

Cloud is often described as turning fixed cost into variable cost. That is true of on-demand instances and false of commitments, which bring back a fixed obligation in exchange for a lower price. The practical skill is deciding which fraction of the bill should be fixed.

Idle is not free

A forgotten test environment of ten instances costs 10 × 720 × ₹22 = ₹1,58,400 a month. Nobody notices, because no customer uses it.

Region is a decision about law, latency and price at once

Mumbai is close to Hamsafar's customers, which keeps response times short, and keeps payment-related data in India, which Indian regulators such as the Reserve Bank of India expect of payment firms. A second region doubles the baseline unless it runs smaller.

Availability zones are not regions

Spreading across zones protects against a building failing. It does not protect against a regional outage or a software error that corrupts data in every zone.

Managed services trade money for attention

The managed database costs ₹480 an hour a machine. Self-run databases cost less per hour but need engineers for backups and failover.

Data leaves expensively

Providers typically charge little to bring data in and more to take it out, so features that send large files to users are priced by egress. Hamsafar's transfer is only 5.7 per cent of the bill now.

Cloud is not the same as scalable

Adding instances helps only if the work can be split. The database and a single hot seat record resist scaling. The cloud rents capacity; it does not repair architecture.

What the bill cannot tell you

The bill says what was rented, not whether it was worth renting. Read it alongside usage and revenue, or it misleads.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

In consumer products, such as Hamsafar's app, demand is spiky and tied to the calendar, so the gap between baseline and peak is wide and autoscaling earns its keep. The cost question is cost per transaction.

In B2B products, load is steadier, but each enterprise customer may demand its own isolated environment or region. The cost question becomes cost per account, and a fixed-fee dedicated contract can cost more to serve than it earns.

In marketplaces, which Hamsafar is, there are two sides with different loads: buyers search constantly and book rarely, while sellers upload inventory in bursts. A buyer-side search that costs ₹0.04 and converts at 2 per cent costs ₹2 of search per booking before anything else is counted, so the search design is the cost design.

Scale changes the picture as well. An early-stage company should usually avoid long commitments, since its baseline is unknown and engineer time is scarce. A large company has a stable baseline, negotiates discounts firm-wide, and employs specialists to find idle resources.

7. Common mistakes

Reading the invoice total as the cost of the product

Symptom: finance and product quote different "cloud costs" in the same meeting. Misunderstanding: the invoice mixes production, testing and experiments. Diagnostic: ask engineering to tag every resource by product and environment, then reconcile the tags to the invoice.

Sizing the commitment to the peak

Symptom: a procurement win announced in the quarter, followed by utilisation below 60 per cent. Misunderstanding: committing to the busiest day instead of the quietest sustained month. Diagnostic: plot hourly instance counts for twelve months and commit to the floor that was never breached.

Treating multi-zone as disaster recovery

Symptom: an outage lasting hours despite "full redundancy". Misunderstanding: redundancy within one region and one codebase shares failures. Diagnostic: run a rehearsal that switches off a zone, and separately ask where the restore point of the database lives.

Ignoring transfer and storage growth

Symptom: a flat user count with a rising bill. Misunderstanding: storage accumulates, and nobody owns deletion. Diagnostic: sort the bill by line and compare month-on-month growth per line, not in total.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Hema's meeting would have opened with a one-page model, not an invoice: the layers in Figure 1, the meters in Table 1 and the festival demand forecast. The commitment would have been sized against a floor of 80 instances with a stated break-even of 62 per cent, and an owner would review utilisation monthly. The second region would have been priced, not argued.

9. What Hema decided

Hema backed Indira on the commitment, but only on 80 instances, using the break-even arithmetic above, and told Harsh that the second region would be a staged decision, not a festival-season project. She asked him for two things instead: a rehearsal that switched off one zone before 1 October, and autoscaling limits tested against the 2.5 times peak. A second region, she argued, solved a risk Hamsafar had not yet measured, while the commitment saved ₹4,81,536 a month on a risk it could size. She signed off on 28 September, two days before the offer lapsed.

To learn next, study infrastructure cost as a product variable: how to attach a rupee figure to a feature before building it. That step uses the meters in this page as input. Then revisit how web and mobile applications fit together.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Hamsafar's baseline halved after a competitor's launch, what would you want to have negotiated into the commitment before signing? Second, which feature in a product you know best would change the shape of the bill the most, and who in your organisation would learn of that only after the invoice?

All company names, people and prices in this case are fictional and illustrative.
exp40v2-tech.cloud:
Cloud infrastructure basics: what the product rents, and what the renting costs

1. Two meetings, six days apart

At 11 a.m. on Tuesday 6 October 2026, Shalaka Purandare, vice-president of product at Saptak Streaming Network, put September's infrastructure invoice on the table and asked which line a product decision could change. Saptak sells subscriptions to regional-language film catalogues: 11,40,000 paying subscribers in September at a blended ₹120 a month, so ₹13,68,00,000 of revenue. The invoice came to ₹99,00,096, which is 7.24 per cent of that.

Her provider's offer expired on 31 October, twenty-five days away: commit to a monthly volume of delivered bytes for a year and take 20 per cent off the published rate for that volume tier. Rustom Daruwala, the infrastructure lead, had been pressing since July to re-encode the catalogue in a newer video codec, cutting delivered bytes by 28 per cent on capable devices. Sharmila Deodhar, the finance director, wanted it signed; Shalaka suspected, correctly, that the larger discount would destroy the codec's business case.

Six days earlier, on Wednesday 30 September, Sudarshan Ranade met the same arithmetic in Hyderabad. Sanrachna Imaging Labs, where he is co-founder and head of product, sells AI triage to hospital chains: radiographs and CT series arrive from fourteen customer networks and models flag the urgent ones. September brought 6,20,000 studies at ₹46 each, ₹2,85,20,000 of revenue, against an infrastructure bill of ₹51,71,840 — 18.1 per cent of revenue, and rising. Reshma Vaidyanathan, his engineering vice-president, held a reservation offer expiring on 20 October: graphics capacity for a year at 42 per cent off. Sarita Nambisan, the chief financial officer, had noticed worse: three of the fourteen had been sold their own isolated deployment, and she could not tell whether they made money.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Cloud infrastructure is the rental of metered, programmable capacity — processing, storage, network transfer — together with managed services the provider operates for you, from data centres grouped into regions. A region, such as Mumbai or Hyderabad, is a geographic cluster; an availability zone is one independently powered facility inside it. The defining property is neither remoteness nor virtualisation: the meter runs on resource-time, so an instance is billed per hour while it exists, busy or idle. Usage-metered lines — gigabytes stored or delivered — behave differently, and that difference matters most.

The problem the model solved was capital pre-commitment. Before 2006 a company in Saptak's position bought servers sized for its busiest evening, waited twelve to twenty weeks for them, and paid for them through the 364 quieter days. Time-sharing bureaus had sold mainframe slices since the 1960s and virtualisation made slicing cheap; what Amazon Web Services showed in 2006, and Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud after it, was that slices could be sold by the hour to strangers. In India a second constraint came attached: the Reserve Bank of India's 2018 direction on payment-data storage, and later the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, made "which region" a legal question first.

Four schools disagree about what follows. The utility school signs: buy capacity by the hour, and let no design decision create capacity nobody uses; it will not sign that long commitments are prudent risk management. The forward-buying school, finance-led, signs: buy a predictable baseline forward as you would hedge copper; it will not sign that elasticity is worth a seventy per cent premium on stable load. The repatriation school — argued after Dropbox left rented storage, and by 37signals in 2023 — signs: beyond that baseline, owning hardware is markedly cheaper per unit of work; it will not sign that the rented operating model is itself a product advantage. The abstraction school signs: the scarce resource is engineer-months, so buy the managed database and redeploy the people; it will not sign that lock-in is worth pre-emptive optimisation.

The first two give opposite advice on Shalaka's deadline, the last two on Sanrachna's graphics processors; a manager who cannot name the school behind a recommendation cannot referee it.

3. Mechanics: the identity that governs the bill

Expert practice rests on one decomposition. For any unit of demand — a study, an hour of viewing —

cost per unit = rate × intensity ÷ utilisation

where rate is the price of a resource-hour, intensity the resource-time one unit of demand consumes, and utilisation useful resource-time over billed resource-time. It is trivial algebra and the whole discipline: it names three independent levers and ranks them.

Work it on Sanrachna. A study consumes 10.8 seconds of graphics-processor time on average, or 0.003 GPU-hours: that is intensity. The on-demand rate is ₹260 per GPU-hour, so the floor is ₹0.78 a study. September's graphics spend was ₹25,53,200 over 6,20,000 studies, or ₹4.12 — 5.3 times the floor. The identity says why: Sanrachna was billed 9,820 GPU-hours and the models spent 1,860 of them on billable studies, a utilisation of 18.9 per cent, and ₹0.78 divided by that ratio is ₹4.12.

Figure 1 shows why the floor is six and not two. Sanrachna promises that 95 per cent of studies are triaged within 90 seconds, and models take forty seconds to load into graphics memory, so capacity cannot be summoned on arrival. The idle 81.1 per cent is the price of a latency promise; the only honest ways to cut it are to renegotiate the promise, speed up loading, or pool more tenants.

The step usually left implicit is the denominator. Saptak's bill divides by subscribers (₹8.68 each) or by viewing hours (₹0.53 an hour); only the second tracks what drives the bill, because bytes follow watch time. The other is separating floor from peak with an hourly histogram over twelve months, then committing below the lowest trough.

Now Saptak's bill, rebuilt from meters. September had 720 hours; subscribers watched 1,88,10,000 hours, 16.5 each, at an average delivered bitrate of 1.4 megabits a second — 0.63 gigabytes an hour, so 1,18,50,300 gigabytes delivered.
