Two readings lead to different places. Finance reads top-down: delivery is 38.30 per cent, so negotiate it. An engineer reads by meter type: delivery and storage, 55.75 per cent together, are usage-metered, where utilisation is 100 per cent by construction and only rate and intensity move; compute, transcoding, database and inference, 37.45 per cent of the exact total, are resource-time-metered, where utilisation dominates; the rest is flat.

4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

Claim 1: if provisioned-to-useful utilisation is below forty per cent, the bill is governed by resource-time, not by work done. True of Sanrachna's graphics processors at 18.9 per cent, and of Saptak's fleet, which runs 95 instances for a peak between 9 and 11 p.m. False of Saptak's delivery line, where every billed gigabyte left the network. On usage-metered lines it actively misleads: a team told to improve utilisation there hunts idle capacity that does not exist.

Claim 2: elasticity is worth its premium when the share of hours you would otherwise idle exceeds the discount offered. Sanrachna's discount is 42 per cent, so reserved capacity costs 58 per cent of on-demand and the break-even utilisation of a reserved hour is exactly 58 per cent: of 8,640 floor GPU-hours a month, at least 5,011.2 must be hours it would have bought anyway.

Claim 3: a commitment is safe only when its floor is independent of decisions you are about to take. Saptak's delivered-byte floor depends on a codec project it controls; Sanrachna's graphics floor depends partly on three contracts, one renewing on 31 March 2027.

Claim 4: for regulated data, region choice is legal first, latency second, price third. Sanrachna keeps imaging in Mumbai because its customers' counsel requires it, so cheaper capacity elsewhere is unavailable at any price. Saptak's catalogue is unconstrained.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In a multi-product company platform lines are shared and allocation turns political. The honest method allocates direct costs directly and shared costs on a published driver; the dishonest one allocates by revenue, protecting the product that should die.

In a two-sided product the sides consume infrastructure inversely to the revenue they generate. A search costing four paise that converts at two per cent carries ₹2 of search cost per transaction, so search design is cost design.

In regulated products the expensive demand is rarely encryption; it is isolation. A hospital group insisting on its own deployment removes the one lever — pooling — that made the unit economics work.

In hardware-plus-software products the fleet sets the floor and client behaviour amplifies it: a firmware release retrying every thirty seconds instead of every five turns a quiet backend into a billed incident.

In AI-native products intensity is a model decision: a product manager can move the bill by a third with a model swap and no code change.

At the organisational seams the bill is owned by engineering, the margin by finance, and the feature that moved both by product. Mature companies run a monthly showback where every line carries an owner, and a quarterly review of obligations beyond six months. What they do not say is that most carry a tenth to a fifth of spend as untagged residue.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Idle capacity is usually the cost of a promise, not of sloppiness. The tell is a team that can recite its latency target but not the warm floor it implies; the obvious reading, that machines were left running, is wrong, because cold start is slower than the agreement allows.

The denominator is a product decision, not an accounting one. Two people quoting different costs per user are usually both right on different denominators. The expert fixes it to whatever drives the dominant meter and refuses to change it when the number embarrasses.

Attack intensity before rate. Intensity gains compound, survive a change of provider and shrink every future commitment; rate gains are one-off, bought by signing away flexibility. The tell is a procurement win announced before an efficiency roadmap exists.

A commitment is a short position on your own efficiency. Commit to volume, then reduce volume, and you have paid for bytes you no longer send: under Saptak's larger tier the codec's monthly saving collapses from ₹7,43,250.82 to ₹14,335.50. The tell is a payback that lengthens just after a procurement success.

Managed services move money between lines, not out of the company. A managed node at ₹410 an hour costs more per hour than a self-run one and less in attention. The tell is a claimed saving with unchanged headcount.

Egress prices features, not infrastructure. Providers charge little to admit data and more to release it, so downloads, higher bitrates and exports are pricing decisions in product costume. The tell is a download button shipped without a gigabyte estimate.

Zones multiply capacity; regions multiply organisation. A second zone protects against one building; a second region against one region, but only if writes work in both and somebody rehearses the switch. The tell is two regions and one on-call rota.

Storage is a ratchet. Compute falls when traffic falls; storage never falls, because deletion has no owner and no deadline. The tell is a flat user count, a rising storage line and no retention policy written down.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

For consumer products usage-metered lines dominate and the discipline is intensity: codecs, image sizes, cache hit rates. For enterprise products the question is pooling, because one concession on isolation can double cost per account. For marketplaces the cost falls on the side that does not pay. For hardware the fleet is the floor; for AI, intensity is a model choice entangled with hardware generations.

By stage: an early company tags everything and commits to nothing, because its floor is unknown and a twelve-month obligation can outlive its strategy. A growth-stage company builds the hourly histogram and commits only to the trough. A company at scale negotiates across all lines at once. What does not change is the identity in section 3: a claimed fourth lever is usually one of the three in costume.

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Saptak: the commitment that would have killed the codec

The codec cuts delivered bytes by 28 per cent, but only on devices that can decode it, which carried 70 per cent of September's viewing hours. The blended reduction is 0.28 × 0.70 = 19.6 per cent, so delivery falls from 1,18,50,300 gigabytes to 95,27,641.2. Each volume tier has a published list rate — ₹0.315 at 95,00,000 gigabytes a month and ₹0.285 at 1,18,00,000, against ₹0.32 for ad-hoc volume — and a twelve-month commitment takes 20 per cent off it: ₹0.252 and ₹0.228. Volume above a commitment is billed at ₹0.285, the list rate of the tier it reaches, and unused commitment is forfeited.

The re-encode costs ₹60,14,000, so payback is 8.1 months with no commitment, 9.1 under Tier A and 420 under Tier B.

Her team then found the line nobody had modelled. Both ladders must exist during the transition, because older app builds cannot play the new codec. The new ladder occupies 72 per cent of the old one's 9,60,000 gigabytes, so a naive five-month transition carries ₹12,44,160 a month of extra storage; pruning the old ladder to its three lowest renditions, 45 per cent of the original, cuts that to ₹2,93,760 a month.

8.3 Sahityapath: the second region that protected nothing

Sahityapath Learning Collective, a Pune seller of examination-preparation courses, is the counter-example. At ₹38,60,000 a month in April 2025, it began a second-region project on 15 May 2025 and declared it live on 18 December, a little over seven months later. Run-rate rose to ₹61,40,000 — ₹22,80,000 a month more, 59.1 per cent above the April baseline. Engineering cost seven people for seven months at ₹2,60,000 each, ₹1,27,40,000, and six full months of duplication from January to June 2026 added ₹1,36,80,000: ₹2,64,20,000 in all.

On 14 March 2026 Sahityapath was down for two hours and forty minutes. A schema migration corrupted an enrolment table, and because writes were accepted only in Mumbai, Hyderabad held a faithful replica of the corrupted rows and served reads of it. The second region had been built against the wrong failure: region loss is rare, bad changes are weekly.

By 30 June 2026 the team had collapsed back to one region with a warm standby and a quarterly restore rehearsal, settling at ₹41,80,000 a month — ₹3,20,000, or 8.29 per cent, above the April baseline. They spent ₹46,00,000 of the released budget on replaying migrations against a copy of production and splitting the hot enrolment counter.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Committing to the peak. Sign: a discount announced in a quarterly review, then utilisation below sixty per cent. Diagnostic: what was the lowest sustained month of the last twelve? Late cost: the rest of the term, paid in full.

Untagged spend. Sign: product and finance quote different costs for one product. Diagnostic: is every line above one lakh rupees attached to an owner? Late cost: a cost programme that cannot measure itself.

Isolation sold without a premium. Sign: an enterprise logo won on a promise of a dedicated environment, with no price change. Diagnostic: cost per unit inside the dedicated stack against the pooled one? Late cost: a renewal negotiated from ignorance.

Autoscaling with an untested ceiling. Sign: a scaling policy whose upper bound nobody can quote. Diagnostic: when was it last reached deliberately? Late cost: finding it in the busiest hour of the year.

Multi-region theatre. Sign: "fully redundant" used without a rehearsal date. Diagnostic: where are writes accepted, and when was a failover last performed under load? Late cost: Sahityapath's ₹2,64,20,000.

Reserving the wrong generation. Sign: a long reservation on accelerators whose successor is announced. Diagnostic: the next generation is 1.9 times faster at 1.35 times the price, so cost per unit of work falls 28.9 per cent — does the reservation let us move? Late cost: a year above the market rate.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Repatriation. The strongest form is not nostalgia for racks. It is that a firm with a stable base load pays a rental premium on that base forever, large enough to fund an operations team with change left over; 37signals published figures to that effect. For it to be wrong, either the base load is less stable than the firm believes, or the operational burden is larger than the published accounts admit — which is what cloud advocates claim, noting that those cases are run by unusually strong teams.

Commitments. The forward-buying case rests on trough load being stable, so refusing a 40 per cent discount on it is a real cash cost paid for an option rarely exercised. The utility case rests on commitments outliving the strategy that justified them. The dispute is whether a firm will re-examine an obligation it already announced as a win.

Managed services and serverless. The abstraction case is that the premium buys engineer-months in the one market where they cannot be bought: your own hiring pipeline. The counter-case is that the premium compounds with scale while the engineering saving does not, so the crossover arrives sooner than teams expect. What would settle it is a measurement nobody takes: headcount actually redeployed rather than notionally freed.

Isolation for enterprise customers. One camp holds that single tenancy is the price of regulated enterprise revenue and should be priced rather than refused. The other holds that conceding once makes it every later customer's default demand, and that logical isolation with strong auditing meets the real requirement — often a procurement habit, not a regulation.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this names compute, storage, regions and managed services, and reads an invoice. Someone who has internalised it quotes a cost per unit of demand before a total, and names the meter its denominator tracks; asks what a commitment will make the firm stop wanting to do, the question that caught Tier B; treats utilisation as a claim about a latency promise, and reads the promise; and, told a system is redundant, asks for the date of the last rehearsal, because the diagram has never failed.

12. What each decided

Shalaka Purandare took Tier A on 23 October 2026, eight days before the offer lapsed, having put the codec's probability of shipping by February at 0.7 — above the 0.5545 cross-over — and negotiated a right to step the volume down at six months. She funded the re-encode at ₹60,14,000 with the pruned transition, moved the dashboard to cost per viewing hour at ₹0.53, and declined Tier B on the record.

Sudarshan Ranade reserved only the pooled floor of 4,320 GPU-hours a month at ₹150.80, leaving the dedicated floors and the burst pool on demand. That cut graphics spend from ₹25,53,200 to ₹20,81,456, a saving of ₹4,71,744 a month or 18.5 per cent, against the ₹9,43,488 he would have saved by reserving everything. The difference is the price of not betting on Rudrapath's renewal — a conversation he opened six months early with ₹11.52 against ₹7.29 on one slide.

Discussion questions. First: Shalaka's cross-over treats the codec's ship date as exogenous, yet she controls the team building it — how should the decision change when the probability is partly a choice? Second: Sanrachna's utilisation is 18.9 per cent against billable work and 29.3 per cent against all work — which belongs in the board pack, and what does the other hide? Third: what would have caught Sahityapath's mismatch before ₹2,64,20,000 was committed?

13. Going deeper

How web and mobile apps work supplies the request path every meter sits on. Infrastructure cost as a product variable is the sequel: pricing a feature before it is built with the identity in section 3. APIs and integration basics explains why integration volume, not user count, often drives compute. Data modelling for PMs decides whether work can be split across instances. Databases, storage and caching treats the one stateful component autoscaling cannot fix. Reading an architecture diagram locates the zone and region boundaries, where redundancy claims are lost. Scalability and performance makes the latency promise behind every warm floor measurable. Security basics for PMs closes the loop on isolation, which destroys pooling economics.

All companies, people and prices here are fictional; real providers and regulators are market context only.
case20v1-tech.data.model:
Nukkad Ledger: One Customer, Many Rows

A teaching case on data modelling for product managers

1. Opening

At 8:40 on Monday morning, 19 October 2026, Aman Handa stood at a whiteboard in the Koramangala office of Nukkad Ledger Technologies in Bengaluru, looking at a diagram he had drawn three times that weekend. It had two boxes, Merchant and Customer, joined by one line. Everything the company knew about the 6.4 crore customer rows its shopkeepers kept sat inside the second box.

Handa, vice-president of product, had until Friday 30 October to tell the Product Council which of three plans should carry the January to March quarter. The reason was a term sheet. Sarthi Credit Partners, a non-banking lender, would set aside a ₹50 crore pilot pool for a "Bharosa Score", a repayment reputation for shop-ledger customers, but only if the score was live by 1 April 2027. The diagram on the whiteboard was why that was harder than it sounded.

2. Company background

Founded in Bengaluru in 2018, Nukkad sells a free ledger app, and a paid tier, to kirana owners who sell on credit. A shopkeeper records what each neighbour owes, sends a WhatsApp or SMS reminder, and collects through a UPI link. Nukkad has 18 lakh merchant accounts, 410 employees and FY2026 revenue of ₹94 crore, almost all from subscriptions.

The market is crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit offer near-identical ledgers; PhonePe and Paytm give shopkeepers a free business app bundled with UPI acceptance; ONDC is pulling small retailers towards open commerce networks. Nukkad's edge is the depth of its ledgers: the average merchant has about 36 customer rows. Lending is the obvious next product, and the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending rules and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 both insist that a borrower's data be used only for a purpose the person has agreed to.

3. The situation

Nukkad's database was designed in 2018 for one job: a shopkeeper's private notebook. A customer row belongs to one merchant and is keyed by merchant and phone number. If the same woman buys on credit from her grocer, her chemist and her milkman, Nukkad holds three unrelated rows. Nothing in the schema says she is one person.

Anmol Hora, a data scientist in Toronto, counted the damage. Exhibit 1 shows 640 lakh customer rows collapsing to 410 lakh distinct phone numbers, 1.56 rows per number. About 118 lakh numbers, 28.8 per cent, appear at two or more merchants. Those are the only people for whom a cross-merchant score means anything.

Hora then audited 2,000 phone-matched groups by hand with the Singapore customer-success team, who phoned merchants to ask whether two rows were the same person. Exhibit 2 shows the result: 14.0 per cent of the groups were not one person at all. Families share a phone, and recycled numbers pass to strangers. A Berlin designer, reviewing early screens, asked a simpler question: what would the shopkeeper see when the score declined someone? Nobody had an answer.

In Pune, the engineers had already felt the schema. In August a "merge duplicate customers" button, requested by merchants, took five weeks to build, because a merge had to rewrite balances, reminders and payment history held in separate tables.

Consent is the other gap. Each customer row exists because a shopkeeper typed it in. The customer never agreed to anything with Nukkad, and today no table could record that agreement.

4. The people

Aman Handa, vice-president of product, Bengaluru, owns the decision and must defend it to the founders and to Sarthi. He wants a plan he can explain in one sentence.

Amarjit Hundal, head of engineering, Pune, has spent years patching around the schema. He wants the data model rebuilt properly and argues that every shortcut adds to the debt.

Ajit Hanspal, head of sales, New Jersey, signed the Sarthi term sheet. His evenings are the Indian night, and he calls with the lender's patience in hand. He wants the date held; a missed window, he says, means no pilot until the lender's next cycle in October 2027.

Anmol Hora, data scientist, Toronto, wants no score shipped on records he has seen fail. His weekly review is at 8:00 pm IST, 10:30 am for him, moving to 9:30 am after North American clocks go back on 1 November.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: match by phone number. Leave the schema alone and have a nightly job group rows by phone, then score each group. Two engineers could finish by 31 January 2027. The upside is speed and no migration risk. The cost is Exhibit 2: extrapolated to 118 lakh groups, roughly 16.5 lakh would be scored as the wrong person, and no table would record consent.

Option B: rebuild around a Person. Introduce a Person entity and a Relationship between Person and Merchant, carrying the balance, and migrate all 640 lakh rows. This is the clean model; the score, reminders and any later product would sit on it. Six engineers need eight months, and the work lands on 30 June 2027, after the lender's date.

Option C: link only verified people. Add a Person table and a link table beside the old one. A customer joins it only when they confirm their number by OTP and consent to sharing, at the moment they pay a reminder link. Legacy rows stay untouched. Four engineers, four months, ready by 28 February 2027. Reach is smaller and grows only as people verify.

Exhibit 3 shows the trade. Option A is the cheapest at ₹15 lakh, yet it is the only plan whose error rate has been measured, and it fails the lender's 5 per cent test. Option B costs three times Option C and arrives after the deadline. Option C is on time and is built to avoid the shared-phone failure, because each person confirms their own number, but its reach is smaller and unproven.

Handa also knew the prize. Nukkad would earn a 1.2 per cent referral fee on disbursals, ₹60 lakh on a fully drawn ₹50 crore pool. Figure 1 sets each plan against the lender's date.

Figure 1: Build windows against the Sarthi go-live date
Scale: 70 px per month, month ticks at the first of each month. Bars run from 1 Nov 2026 to the first of the month after each ready date.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does a "customer" row in Nukkad's database actually represent, and which features does that definition make easy or impossible?
  2. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, how many people could Option A score reliably, and does the lender's tolerance change your answer?
  3. What does consent look like as data, and which option gives it a home?
  4. Weighing Exhibit 3 and Figure 1, which option should Handa put to the Product Council on 30 October, and what would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

Data modelling for a product manager is the discipline of asking what the things in the product are, and how they relate, before asking what features to build. Here the entity was misnamed from the start. "Customer" in Nukkad's schema means "a shopkeeper's relationship with a name and number", while the feature needs "a person", and the lender needs a person who has agreed. The gap between those nouns, not a shortage of engineers, is the constraint.

A well-reasoned answer separates three tests: does the model match the feature, does the plan meet the date, and can the risk be measured. Option A meets the date but fails the model: 14.0 per cent wrong merges against a 5 per cent tolerance. Option B fits the model but fails the date by three months, which costs the pilot until October 2027, and has no verified people at launch either.

One defensible path is Option C. It makes the right entity real, starts with people who have consented, meets the date with a month in hand, and costs ₹40 lakh against ₹60 lakh of fees on a fully drawn pool. The Person table is also the first step of Option B, so the work is not thrown away. The risk is reach: 30 lakh is an estimate against a 20 lakh floor, so Handa should ask Hora to track weekly OTP confirmations from the day the link table goes live on 28 February, against the 20 lakh floor on 1 April, and bring a fall-back to the Council. Had Sarthi's window been open until October 2027, or the audit error been 3 per cent, the answer would differ. The method, not the verdict, is the lesson.
exp40v2-tech.data.model:
Data Modelling for PMs

Grain, identity, cardinality and time: the four decisions that settle which features are cheap, which are expensive, and which can never be built on the data you have.

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On 14 April 2026 in Hyderabad, Kalyani Dharwadkar had been asked to launch a product by 1 June. Kavach Diagnostics Network ran six accredited laboratories and forty-two collection centres across three states; in eleven months it had recorded 9,20,000 lab orders and 38,00,000 test results. A manufacturing group had signed a wellness contract worth ₹1.9 crore a year on one promise: each employee would see a three-year trend of their own HbA1c and lipid markers.

Jaidev Phatak, the engineering lead, had established that the product as sold was not buildable. Kavach's database had no patient: its root record was the lab order, and the human attached to it was three typed fields — mobile number, name as spoken, age. A trend requires joining a person to themselves across time, and the only candidate key was a telephone number, shared by families and recycled by operators.

Jaidev asked Lukas Brenner, Kavach's data engineer in Lisbon, to audit it. Lukas drew a random 2,000 of the 6,40,000 mobile-and-name keys and had the centres telephone each.

Table 1. The audit of 10–13 April 2026. The sample is 2,000 of 6,40,000 keys, so the factor is 320 and the scaled order column sums to exactly the 9,20,000 orders on the platform.

A callback of 500 repeat patients found 86 of the 500 patients (17.2 per cent) filed under two or more numbers, so the error ran both ways. Kalyani's feature would have drawn a diabetic woman's rising HbA1c and her son's normal one as one line.

Eleven days later, on 25 April, Jigisha Marathe faced the mirror image in Chennai. Kaarya Workforce Group sold shift and statutory-compliance software to forty-one industrial customers covering 2,30,000 worker records. Its largest prospect, an auto-components maker, had one clause in its proposal request: a worker who passed through three staffing agencies must keep one continuous attendance and skill history, each agency must see only its own period, and statutory filings must stay per employer entity per month. Kaarya's schema made a person be their employment. Kunal Zarkar's match on Universal Account Number and date of birth found 27,650 of the 2,30,000 rows (12.0 per cent) were one human entered twice or more.

Neither decision was about screens. Both were about the shape of a table, and both had a date.

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

A data model is a theory of a business written as constraints on what may be recorded: the entities a product remembers, the attributes kept about each, the relationships between them with their cardinality — how many of one may attach to one of another — and the keys by which a record is identified. A schema declares not what a product knows but what it is capable of knowing: a feature needing a fact it cannot hold is not expensive, it is absent.

Before 1970 each program carried its own file layout, so a fact existed only inside the program that wrote it. Edgar Codd's relational model put data in tables whose relationships were stated by shared values rather than pointers, and his normal forms, refined with Raymond Boyce, tested whether a fact was stored exactly once. Peter Chen's 1976 entity-relationship diagram gave a notation for arguing about entities first. Four camps matter, each identifiable by the proposition it signs.

The normalisers, after Codd and Bill Inmon: every fact belongs in exactly one place, and a duplicated mutable fact will eventually contradict itself. They will not sign that read performance justifies copying it.

The dimensional school, after Ralph Kimball: declare the grain of a fact table before anything else, and keep analytical models separate from operational ones. They will not sign reports sitting on the transactional schema.

The domain-driven camp, after Eric Evans: there is no single correct model of a customer, and the useful artefact is a map between contexts. They will not sign one canonical record per entity.

The log-first camp — event sourcing, Dan Linstedt's Data Vault: state is a projection of history, so store the events and derive the current row. They will not sign a mutable current-state table as the system of record, because a destructive update discards evidence.

Kavach and Kaarya each held, without choosing it, the position nobody defends: current state only, one fact in several places, analytical and operational reads on the same tables, and a natural key doing identity work it could not do.

3. Mechanics: four questions, worked

Expert practice reduces to four questions in a fixed order: grain fixes what a row means, identity decides whether rows can be joined, cardinality sets how many tables are needed, time decides whether a past answer can be reproduced.

Grain. Complete the sentence "one row here is exactly one ___" with no conjunction in the answer. Kavach's old answer was "one lab order, which is also one sample, one analyser run and one billing document" — four things, so four features blocked at once. The tell is a numbered column such as test_2_value.

Identity. A key is either natural — a telephone number, a Universal Account Number — or surrogate, an identifier the system mints and never reuses. Natural keys are seductive because they already exist and fail for the same reason: they belong to the world, and the world changes them. The expert move is to mint a surrogate and treat every natural identifier as an attribute with a measured confidence.

Cardinality, including its cheap half. Practitioners remember one-to-many and many-to-many and forget optionality — whether zero is allowed. Kaarya needed person-to-employer many-to-many, which means a junction table where the economics live. May an employment have no end date, may two overlap, may attendance fall outside every window? Each yes is a feature; each unanswered one is a defect waiting.

Time. Two clocks run in any serious model: valid time, when a fact was true in the world, and transaction time, when the system came to believe it. A grade effective 16 May but entered on 2 June needs both. The warehouse name for the choice is a slowly changing dimension: type 1 overwrites, type 2 keeps a dated row.

Worker K-40118, May 2026, 24 days workedDaysDay rate (₹)Wage (₹)
1–15 May, grade B2 (dated row valid to 15 May)137429,646

Total, dated rates (type 2)24—18,512

Table 2. Wage = days × the rate valid on each day. The Total row sums only the two dated segments (9,646 + 8,866 = 18,512); the rows beneath are comparisons, not components. 19,344 − 18,512 = 832.

Kunal measured the exposure: grade, plant or agency changed mid-month for 7,130 of the 2,30,000 worker records (3.1 per cent), at a mean absolute error of ₹214 each — ₹15.26 lakh a month, ₹1.83 crore a year.

The second-order effect: a figure's meaning now depends on the grain it is summed at. Worker K-40118 logged 38, 22 and 31 overtime hours under three employers, 91 in the year. The ceiling in the applicable state rules is per employer, per quarter, at 50 hours — so at person grain the worker looks 41 hours over a cap, and at employment grain no employer is in breach.

4. When the question matters, and when asking it is waste

The conditions are claims testable in an afternoon. One: the feature needs a fact at a finer grain than any existing table — true at Kavach, per person and per method where the finest grain was per order, and at Kaarya, per employment-day. Two: the required cardinality is many-to-many where the schema has one-to-many — true for both, since one number holds several people.

Three: the measured error rate of the identity the feature depends on is worse than the tolerance the use implies. Kaarya's 12.0 per cent duplication is reviewed by a payroll officer who knows the worker's face, so a wrong merge is caught before money moves; Kavach's 23.7 per cent contamination is read by a patient with no reviewer at all. Tolerance belongs to the use, not the data. Four: a past answer must be reproducible. Five: the table has many independent readers; Kavach's had twenty-three.

The apparatus also misleads. A team whose entity list is still a hypothesis buys nothing from modelling ceremony. A genuinely derived store — indexes, embeddings, aggregates — is recomputed rather than migrated, so treating it as a system of record imports expense for no benefit. And a schema says what is recordable, never what is wanted.

5. Hard edges: regulation, two sides, hardware and AI

Regulated products. NABL accreditation requires a result be traceable to the instrument, reagent lot and calibration that produced it. Kavach's schema held one analyser_id on the order, which looks like traceability and is not, because a repeat run on another instrument overwrote it. When a reagent lot used on three analysers from 3 to 11 March 2026 — nine days inclusive — was recalled, the exposure was 3 × 9 × 420 = 11,340 analyte results across 2,610 orders. Without a sample-run entity the only defensible scope was 19,800 results: 74.6 per cent more recall letters than the facts justified.

Two-sided businesses. Lavani Produce Collective kept sellers and buyers in separate tables with separate keys. A match on mobile number and PAN found 1,160 of its 19,400 sellers (6.0 per cent) were also among its 7,800 buyers, holding ₹2.94 crore receivable and ₹1.17 crore payable — ₹1.77 crore net.

Hardware and software together. A device is a source of truth you do not control. Kavach's analysers wrote timestamps from their own drifting clocks, and an offline centre uploaded queued orders in a batch whose arrival order had nothing to do with events. Treat one timestamp as both "when it happened" and "when we learned it" and no operations head will believe the turnaround report.

AI-native products. Jigyasa Labs built a retrieval assistant over enterprise documents: 4,20,000 documents became 68,00,000 chunks, a mean of 16.19 per document. The system of record stayed the customer's document store; the chunk-and-embedding store was derived. Permission is then a modelling attribute of the derived row: 11.4 per cent of documents carried restricted access lists, and at a mean 23 chunks for those longer documents that is 11,01,240 chunks needing inherited permissions. Before the chunk row carried tenant and access-list keys, 600 test questions produced 14 of the 600 answers (2.33 per cent) citing content the asker could not open; afterwards, none. Reshaping a derived store is a compute bill, not a migration: halving chunk length doubled the count to 1,36,00,000 and cost ₹1.63 lakh at ₹0.012 a chunk.

At the organisational seams. Mature companies do not have one model; they have several, and what they maintain is the mapping: a hub of identifiers with a dated, reversible mapping to each context's key, owned by a named reconciliation function.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners do not

Grain is the only decision that cannot be patched

Attributes can be added, relationships introduced with a junction table, keys migrated. A table whose rows mean two things at once cannot be fixed without rewriting every reader. The tell is numbered columns, and the obvious reading — that they are a convenience — is wrong: they report a grain already violated and paid for in application code.

Identity is a process with an error rate, not a column

The tell is that nobody can quote the false-merge and false-split rates or name who measured them. Teams point to a customer_id as if its existence settled the matter, when the questions are who mints it, what happens when the identifier behind it changes, and how often two of them are one person.

NULL is three different questions

An empty cell may mean "not yet known", "not applicable" or "refused to say", and a product treating them alike will count a refusal as a zero. Kavach's sex field was blank on 4.1 per cent of orders, conflating three populations with three reference ranges.

A status column is an unlogged state machine

Current status answers "where is it now" and silently refuses "how long did it wait" and "who changed it". The tell is an escalation about last month that cannot be settled from the database. The deeper point is bi-temporal: a backdated correction needs both what was true and what was believed.

The same noun means different things in different contexts

The tell is a long meeting about the definition of "active patient" in which both sides are right. An expert writes down both definitions with the contexts they serve and builds the mapping. The obvious reading — that one must be wrong — licenses a canonical-model programme that cannot finish.

Permissions are a schema feature, not an API feature

The tell is an access-control requirement answered with "we will filter in the API layer". A row that does not carry the key by which access is decided cannot be filtered reliably, because every new reader must reimplement the rule. Jigyasa's chunk row had no tenant key.

Store the inputs, not only the output

A derived fact that cannot be recomputed cannot be restated or audited; the tell is a metric nobody can reproduce for a prior month. Kavach used one column for both the panel's catalogue price and the price charged. When the lipid-profile price moved from ₹650 to ₹720 on 1 February 2026 the script touched 48,200 rows and missed 1,140 of the 48,200 rows (2.37 per cent), under-billing ₹79,800.

Comparability is a modelling property

Two numbers in one column need not be the same measurement. Of Kavach's 1,38,000 HbA1c results, 86,400 came from liquid chromatography and 51,600 from an immunoassay; among the 48,000 patients with three or more results, 10,848 of the 48,000 patients (22.6 per cent) had both. Mean method bias was 0.3 percentage points against a decision step of 0.5, so a trend crossing methods can manufacture a deterioration.

7. Where product type and stage genuinely change the answer

Four things do not change anywhere: grain, identity, cardinality and time are the same questions in a consumer app and in a turbine. What changes is which bites, and what it costs. In consumer products identity dominates, because the subject shares devices and changes numbers. In B2B and enterprise the organisation chart is the model: legal entity, operating unit, site, team and individual are five entities, and a schema with only "user" and "company" cannot express an approval chain or a statutory filing; the schema is also a contract with the customer's data team, so a column rename breaks someone's board report. In platforms and marketplaces the junction table carries the economics, and the two sides overlap, as Lavani found. In hardware the object needs identity of its own — serial, lot, calibration. In AI products the split between system of record and derived store becomes central.

Stage changes the cost, not the question. At seed the model is cheap to change and the constraint is the founder's belief about what the business is. At Kavach's stage the readers have multiplied and a change is a coordination problem.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

One: pricing the remodel. Jaidev costed three paths with a pod of seven at ₹2.4 lakh per person-month, starting 20 April 2026.

OptionBuildDeliveryBuild cost (₹ lakh)DownsideExpected cost (₹ lakh)

B. Remodel patient identity first14 wks27 Jul 202658.80.30 × ₹53.2 lakh lost first-year margin74.76
C. Ship per-visit results now, remodel next quarter4 wks18 May 202616.8₹58.8 lakh remodel later + 0.45 × ₹53.2 lakh99.54

Table 3. Build cost = 7 people × months × ₹2.4 lakh: 1.5 months = 25.2, 3.5 = 58.8, 1.0 = 16.8. Option A's downside is ₹58.8 lakh of rework plus ₹37.2 lakh of credits, ₹96.0 lakh in all. First-year contribution is ₹190 lakh × 28 per cent = ₹53.2 lakh.

Option B at ₹74.76 lakh beats Option A by ₹3.24 lakh — less than the error in any of the probabilities. The model's contribution was to show that the decision could not be made on expected value, pushing the argument to the shape of the downside.

Two: the migration, costed by readers rather than rows.

Table 4. Patient rows: 5,27,360 single-person keys, plus 77,760 family keys at a callback mean of 2.4 people each (1,86,624), plus 58,880 desk-handset orders each given a provisional patient. Samples at a mean of 1.6 per order, and a 3.5 per cent repeat rate gives 1.035 runs per sample. The total is the exact sum of the five rows.

At the measured write rate of 9,000 rows a second the backfill takes 84,88,384 ÷ 9,000 = 943 seconds. It ran across three nights: the work is reconciliation across twenty-three readers and a three-week dual-write window.

Three: the failure. Jhoomar Jewellery Partners, twenty-eight stores and a web channel, set out in 2025 to build one customer record from store CRM, e-commerce accounts and its gold-savings-scheme ledger. The merge ran on 18 August 2025 on a single rule — same mobile number — collapsing 3,84,000 source records into 2,41,000 golden records. Seven weeks later, on 6 October 2025, an audit found 9,700 of the 2,41,000 golden records (4.02 per cent) were wrong merges, so instalments paid by a mother were credited against a son's entitlement.

Unmerging was impossible: the merge had overwritten source identifiers and kept no mapping. Jhoomar restored the scheme ledger alone from a backup of 1 September 2025, then rebuilt non-destructively — a hub of persons, every source record retained with its own key, candidate matches held as dated reversible assertions. Leela Khambata replaced the single rule with two factors: mobile number plus one of date of birth, PAN last four digits, or house-and-pincode. The same 3,84,000 sources produced 3,11,500 golden records with 41,400 possible-duplicate pairs for review at 180 pairs per analyst-day — 230 analyst-days, nine working weeks for five analysts, ₹7.36 lakh. A re-audit of 1,500 found 9 of the 1,500 (0.6 per cent) wrong. Jatin Bhide, the chief technology officer, put the cost of catching it late at ₹11.77 crore restated across 2,140 accounts.

9. Failure modes and the questions that catch them early

Grain drift. Sign: every feature arrives as new columns. Diagnostic: complete "one row here is exactly one ___" and listen for "and". Late, it costs a rewrite of every reader.

Identity by convenience key. Sign: support merges accounts by hand. Diagnostic: what are our false-merge and false-split rates? Late: Jhoomar's ₹11.77 crore restatement.

State without history. Sign: last month's questions are answered from a spreadsheet. Diagnostic: can we reproduce the number we reported for March, as of March?

Incomparable values in one column. Sign: a metric moves on a date matching an internal change. Diagnostic: the same measurement, unit and method for every row?

Destructive migration with no reverse map. Sign: the plan has no rollback section. Diagnostic: what do we do at hour three if the reconciliation does not tie?

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Normalise first, or design for reads. The normalisers rest on sixty years of evidence that duplicated mutable facts diverge, and that customers find the divergence first. The other camp rests on cheap columnar storage and read-dominated workloads, so one wide table per subject beats a dozen joins. It is wrong wherever that table is also written to.

Event log as system of record, or current state. The log-first position is strongest in regulated contexts: an immutable ledger makes "what did we believe on 31 May" answerable by construction. Opponents argue, from stalled projects, that deriving state from events pushes complexity into every reader.

One canonical entity, or mapped contexts. Master-data advocates point to the cost of a company that cannot count its customers; the other camp points to the graveyard of canonical-model programmes. Jhoomar supports both readings.

Rigid schemas, or schema-on-read. JSON columns let a team ship an unknown shape today, and the cost lands a quarter later on whoever must query it, as string parsing inside SQL. Flexibility defers the modelling decision at interest; the argument is about the rate.

Whether the product manager belongs here at all. One camp holds the schema an engineering detail and PM involvement interference. The other holds that grain and identity are statements about the business no engineer can settle alone.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this draws entity-relationship diagrams. Someone who has internalised it asks for the grain sentence before looking at a screen design; keeps a list of the schema assumptions most likely to expire — one customer has one account, one worker has one employer — and revisits it when the business changes shape rather than when it breaks; insists on a measured identity error rate before shipping anything that joins a person to themselves; prices migrations by readers rather than rows; and will tell a sales team holding a signed contract that a feature is impossible as designed, and name the table.

12. What Kalyani and Jigisha decided

Kalyani took Option B, then narrowed it. The remodelling went ahead for 27 July; on 1 June the corporate customer received the cohort dashboard, which aggregates and so needs no person-level identity, plus individual results per visit with no trend line. Patients on the 6,43,200 single-person orders were offered an identity confirmation that upgraded them early. Trends were drawn within one analytical method, with a visible break marker where the method changed. The expected costs were indistinguishable, so the decision belonged to the asymmetry: a delayed feature is recoverable, a wrong clinical trend is not.

Jigisha split person from employment. Attendance, overtime and statutory filings stayed at employment grain, because that is the grain statute uses; skills moved to the person; agency visibility derived from the employment window. What she refused was cross-tenant matching: Kaarya would resolve one person within one customer, never across customers.

Three questions. First, Kavach's audit cost four days and changed a ₹1.9 crore decision; what is the equivalent measurement in your own product, and why has nobody run it? Second, should Kalyani have presented the expected-value model at all, when the real argument was asymmetry? Third, when would Jigisha's refusal to match across tenants be the wrong call?

13. Going deeper

How web and mobile apps work — the server's stored data is what persists, the premise this topic examines. Databases, storage and caching — the model says what is stored, this decides how fast it is found. APIs and integration basics — an API is a schema made public, so every entity decision becomes a compatibility obligation. Cloud infrastructure basics — why storage became cheap enough for the wide-table camp to have a case. Reading an architecture diagram — which component owns which data. Scalability and performance — how grain and cardinality set query cost. Security basics for PMs — the discipline behind permission-carrying rows. Identity: auth, SSO, roles and permissions — the problem that defeated both protagonists.

Parchoon Networks: One Row Per Shop

A distribution-software company cannot say how many customers it has.

1 · The night beforeSarjapur Road, 11:40 pm

At 11:40 pm on Sunday, 29 November 2026, Bhavreen Indora stood in front of a whiteboard in her flat off Sarjapur Road in Bengaluru and looked at two numbers written a metre apart: 1,10,500 and 86,900. In nine hours a sub-committee of the Parchoon Networks board would come onto a call from Bengaluru, Edison, Toronto, Singapore and Dubai — 9 am for her, 10:30 the previous evening in New Jersey — and ask which of those two numbers the company's new credit product had been sized on, and what it would cost to be sure.

Three weeks earlier, in the fortnight around Diwali, Parchoon Beat had carried 11.4 lakh orders in a single week, the most it had ever handled, and nothing had broken. What was in front of Bhavreen now was smaller than an outage and harder to explain to a board. Parchoon's production database held 1,92,400 rows in a table called outlet. Nobody could say how many businesses that was, and two teams who had tried had come back 26,400 apart.

She had a decision memo open with four options in it. She had begun to suspect it asked the wrong question, and had until morning to decide whether to say so.

2 · Company historyEleven weeks in 2021

Parchoon Networks was founded in Bengaluru in February 2021 by Baldev Ichhogil and two classmates to sell order-taking software to FMCG distributors — the middle layer of Indian trade that moves biscuits, soap and oil from company depots to kirana shops. Its first customer was a Nagpur biscuit distributor who wanted his fifteen salesmen to stop writing orders in carbon-copy books.

Baldev built the first version in eleven weeks during the second COVID wave. The design decision that mattered was made in June 2021 and took about an hour: one row per shop. A salesman had to create a shop in four taps, so outlet carried its name, beat and distributor, the proprietor's name and phone number, a nullable gstin, a nullable pan and a credit_limit, all on one row (Exhibit 1). There was no record for the business that owned the shop, and none for the human whose phone number it was.

In March 2023, when a Coimbatore customer onboarded twelve pharmacies, an engineer added a self-referencing parent_outlet_id. It was never made mandatory. By September 2026 it was populated on 12,400 rows, of which 3,100 pointed at rows since merged or soft-deleted.

3 · The industryDistribution, rails and rules

By 2026 Indian retail distribution was unusually well instrumented and unusually crowded. UPI, on NPCI's rails, had made collection at the shop counter cashless for most of Parchoon's distributors. ONDC had begun pulling kirana inventory into a shared network, which required outlet-level serviceability and a stable identifier for a physical location. GST e-invoicing pushed invoice discipline down to firms with turnover of ₹5 crore, and the GST Act obliged them to retain records for six years. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act gave the proprietor whose phone number sat in outlet a right to its erasure.

Parchoon competed with field-force products from Bizom and FieldAssist, with Zoho's inventory suite at the low end, and indirectly with the B2B marketplaces — Udaan, Jumbotail, JioMart Partner. Quick commerce, Zepto and Blinkit, was taking the fastest-moving lines out of metro kirana baskets, which made credit and assortment, not order capture, the thing distributors now paid for. Parchoon's exposure was not only Indian: 18 per cent of FY27 revenue to date came from Gulf distributors billing in dirhams under UAE VAT, where the tax identifier is a TRN and not a GSTIN.

4 · What happenedApril to November 2026

In April 2026 Parchoon signed Pukhta General Trading LLC of Dubai, a distributor of Indian packaged foods, on a ₹1.9 crore annual contract. Pukhta bills under four legal entities and wanted one login across them. There was nowhere in the schema to put a TRN, so the integrations team put it in the gstin column for 1,840 outlet rows. The nightly GSTN checksum validator began failing those rows. Nobody minded, because nothing depended on it passing.

In July the data team re-ran validation properly and the composition of Exhibit 2 changed: the 1,840 TRN rows moved out of the validated bucket into the malformed one. In the same month Bhagyesh Ikolaha brought back a term sheet from a Mumbai NBFC for distributor-financed credit to shops, on which Parchoon would earn 1.6 per cent of the outstanding book as a platform fee. The lender's one hard requirement was that exposure be assessed and capped per borrowing entity.

In August the ONDC pilot was committed for 15 January 2027. In September Bitasta Isru's team in Toronto delivered an entity-resolution model clustering outlet rows by proprietor phone, PAN and fuzzy shop name, and the gap in Exhibit 3 appeared: Finance counted 1,67,600 billing parties, the model 1,41,200 clusters. The two disagreed about what a customer was, not about any particular shop.

The credit pilot ran anyway, in Ludhiana and Jalandhar through October and November, because the go/no-go date was 11 December. Lines were sanctioned against 612 outlet rows, totalling ₹9.18 crore, an average of ₹1.50 lakh per row. On the GSTIN rule those rows belong to 486 businesses: 378 hold one each and 108 hold two or more, the largest holding nine. Assessed at party level the same borrowers would have been capped at ₹7.42 crore, so the pilot sanctioned ₹1.76 crore more than that, concentrated in 108 borrowers — a mean excess of ₹1.63 lakh each. None had defaulted. The lender's risk team found it on 24 November.

Figure A — dates between 1 November 2026 and 30 April 2027

Scale: linear in days, 1 November 2026 at x = 60 and 30 April 2027 at x = 840 — 180 days at 4.333 px per day, ticks at month starts. The seven markers invert to days 29, 40, 75, 82, 91, 119 and 151.

5 · The peopleSeven positions

Bhavreen Indora — Director of Product, Bengaluru
Owns the credit product and the memo. Wants a decision that survives the ONDC pilot as well as the lender. Is not saying that she approved the pilot's outlet-level sanctioning in September.
Baldev Ichhogil — co-founder and CTO, Bengaluru
Argues that a mapping table maintained by operations is enough, and that the 2021 schema is why Parchoon beat better-funded rivals to 1,860 distributors. Is not saying that he has had a half-finished party table on a branch since March, untested against production volumes.
Bitasta Isru — Staff Data Scientist, Toronto
Holds that identity is a modelling problem and her clusters already solve it; a schema change would discard the signal. Her promotion case rests on the model. Is not saying that its precision was measured against a labelled set her own team produced.
Bhagyesh Ikolaha — SVP Sales, Edison, New Jersey
Wants the credit product live before the lender's December date; his FY27 target assumes it ships. Is not saying that he has already shown the lender the 26,520-shop eligible base from Exhibit 5A, or that it is in the board deck.
Bindiya Ibbanwal — Head of Customer Success, Singapore
Reports that her team already reconciles parties by hand and can carry on. Her bonus is weighted to the Pukhta renewal in April. Is not saying that the reconciliation lives in three spreadsheet versions and that fourteen months of merge decisions were never logged.
Bhuvnesh Imlahi — Engineering Manager, Ledger squad, Pune
Says dual-writing a real party entity is the only honest path and will take 46 engineer-weeks. Is not saying loudly enough that one of his four engineers resigned on 24 November, after Exhibit 6 was compiled.
Birinder Irotra — Financial Controller, Gurugram
Owns the Finance column of Exhibit 3 and insists two GSTINs are two legal persons, whatever a model says. Audit season is his risk. Is not saying that 67,600 blank-GSTIN rows are counted as one party each purely because he has nothing else to count them by.

6 · ExhibitsWhat the company can see

Source: schema dump of 30 September 2026 and the platform team's own annotations; the dangling-pointer count is from a one-off query, not a monitored check.

Exhibit 3 — how many customers does Parchoon have?

7 · VoicesIn the team's own words

“In 2021 a shop was a shop. A salesman had four taps and a 2G signal outside a paan stall. Had I asked him which legal entity he was standing in front of, we would have had no company.”

Baldev Ichhogil, schema review, 12 November 2026

“Eligible base 26,520 shops, fee ₹1.96 crore in year one. The lender has seen it. Do not send the board a smaller number six days before the board call unless you can name the shops that are not real.”

Bhagyesh Ikolaha, email, 24 November 2026, 08:14 EST

“A mapping table is a second source of truth that nothing enforces. 46 engineer-weeks, 28 of them Ledger and Platform & Data people who have read the invoice code. We do not have 28.”

Bhuvnesh Imlahi, Pune, 25 November 2026

“They are all real shops. 26,520 is 24 per cent of rows; 20,856 is 24 per cent of GSTINs, and a limit attaches to the GSTIN because that is who signs. The difference is 5,664 rows, not 5,664 shops.”

Birinder Irotra, replying to Ikolaha, 27 November 2026

“Fourteen months we have done this by hand and nobody asked. When a Jalandhar distributor says the sweet-shop and the provision store are one party, I write it in my sheet. The product has no column for what I just decided.”

Bindiya Ibbanwal, Singapore, 27 November 2026, 14:20 SGT

“Both of you are counting the wrong noun. My clusters say 79,400 in that bucket. One proprietor, one phone, one PAN, four GSTINs across two states is one credit risk and four of Birinder's parties.”

Bitasta Isru, Slack, 28 November 2026, 07:10 EST

“A party does not have a phone number. A person does, and we do not have people.”

Bhavreen Indora, memo margin, 28 November 2026

8 · The optionsAs the memo states them

Option A — a mapping table maintained by operations. Ship a party_map side table that Bindiya's team keeps current, and read credit limits through it. Six engineer-weeks, roughly ₹22 lakh a year of operations cost, available before 11 December. It makes the fourteen months of unlogged judgements official, and it does not prevent a salesman creating a 1,92,401st row tomorrow.

Option B — a real party entity, dual-written. Create party, write to both for a quarter, backfill, then move credit_limit onto it. 46 engineer-weeks of which 28 must come from Ledger and Platform & Data, which hold 26 uncommitted weeks on the face of Exhibit 6 and 21 after the Ledger resignation. Something in Figure A moves.

Option C — model it properly: party, outlet, person, role. Separate the business, the location, the human and the relationships between them, with an append-only ledger of changes. 120 engineer-weeks against 59 uncommitted, 54 after the Ledger resignation. Baldev's estimate and Bhuvnesh's agree here, which Bhavreen noted was the first time.

Option D — buy entity resolution. License a service at ₹38 lakh a year plus 11 engineer-weeks of integration, and let it decide what one customer is. Bitasta's view is that this buys a worse version of what she has built.

At the top of the memo Bhavreen had written how do we identify the party? In the margin, uncrossed, were two more questions. Does the ONDC pilot need a party or a location? Where should credit_limit live?

9 · Deadlines and constraintsWhat cannot move

The lender's go/no-go is 11 December. If Parchoon cannot deliver party-level exposure by then, the lender underwrites on its own data and Parchoon's fee falls from 1.6 per cent of book to 0.6 per cent — on Exhibit 5B's book, from ₹1.54 crore to ₹0.58 crore. Pukhta requires multi-entity billing live on 31 January, with service credits of 8 per cent of the annual fee per month of delay, ₹15.2 lakh a month against a ₹1.9 crore contract; the renewal is in April. The 15 January ONDC date was committed in writing.

FY26 exit ARR was ₹52 crore against an FY27 plan of ₹71 crore, on ₹46 crore of Series B cash, with the board expecting EBITDA breakeven in Q4 FY28. The hiring freeze runs to 1 April 2027. The GST Act requires six years of invoice retention; the distributors' DPDP obligation requires erasure in thirty days; Parchoon is the processor in both cases and has contracted to support both.

At 12:20 am her phone lit up: Bitasta, 1:50 pm in Toronto, asking whether to put 79,400 in the deck as a third number or leave it out. On the whiteboard there were now three numbers and a fourth, 1,92,400, underlined twice. The rain had started again over Sarjapur Road. The call was in eight hours and forty minutes, and the memo still had four options in it.

10 · Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 3 counts the same 1,92,400 rows twice. State what each column counts, and name one thing neither tells you about a shop that owes money.
  2. Exhibits 5A and 5B differ by ₹26.16 crore of book. Reconstruct both chains and say what would have to be true of Parchoon's data for 5A to be the right number to give the lender.
  3. The Ludhiana pilot sanctioned ₹1.76 crore more than a party-level cap would have allowed, across 108 borrowers, with no default. Was that a data-modelling failure, a credit-policy failure, or neither? What evidence here decides it?
  4. Which consequences in Exhibit 2 follow from the 2021 schema and which from how the field and integrations teams used it? Does the distinction change which option you fund?
  5. Under Option A, what happens to the 176 open requests in Exhibit 4, and who carries the risk if a distributor's thirty-day obligation is missed? Price that against ₹22 lakh a year.
