exp20v2-tech.data.model:
Data Modelling for PMs

Entities, relationships, and why the shape of a schema decides which features are cheap, which are expensive, and which are quietly impossible.

1. The basket that could not be bought

On 9 March 2026, Aditi Joglekar, head of product at Anaaj Direct Exchange, sat in a conference room in Pune with a request she could not refuse and could not simply grant. Anaaj runs a business-to-business marketplace on which restaurants and neighbourhood kirana stores order staples such as rice, dal, edible oil and sugar from regional wholesalers. A restaurant group with forty outlets had offered to move its entire procurement onto the platform from 1 June, on one condition: its cooks must be able to build a single basket of items from several wholesalers, pay once, and receive a separate delivery and a separate GST invoice from each.

Aditi's engineering lead, Bhaskar Wagh, said this was not a screen design. Anaaj's database had been designed in 2024 around a simple belief that one order meant one item from one wholesaler. The platform held 1,80,000 such orders. Bhaskar offered two options. A patch that bolted a "basket" label onto the existing rows would take three weeks. A proper restructuring of the data would take nine weeks, and would end on 11 May, leaving three weeks before the restaurant group's start date for migration and testing.

Camila Duarte, the analyst in Lisbon, had warned that a patch would double-count deliveries in her reports. If Aditi chose the patch and the structure proved wrong, Anaaj would pay in invoices that did not reconcile and refunds handled by hand. If she chose the restructuring and misjudged the scope, she would miss 1 June. The decision turned on one question: how does the shape of our data constrain what we can build?

2. The idea

A data model is the agreed description of the things a product keeps records about, the facts it stores about each, and the connections between them. Three terms carry most of the weight. An entity is a kind of thing the business needs to remember: a buyer, a wholesaler, an order. An attribute is a fact about an entity, such as a price or a delivery address. A relationship is a rule connecting entities, for instance that a wholesaler supplies many items. A schema is the data model as actually implemented in a database: its tables, columns and the links between them.

The discipline grew from a practical problem: in the 1960s, each program stored data in its own private layout. In 1970, Edgar Codd, an IBM researcher, proposed the relational model, in which data lives in tables whose connections are stated explicitly and independently of any application. In 1976, Peter Chen introduced the entity-relationship diagram, a way for business and technical people to agree on entities and relationships before building.

The sentence Aditi could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "A schema is a list of what the product is allowed to know, and a feature we cannot express in that list is a feature we are not really building."

3. How it actually works

Bhaskar drew Anaaj's existing model on the whiteboard. It had three entities. A buyer and a wholesaler each had a row of their own. The third, the order, held everything else: the item, the quantity, the price, the delivery address, the status, and a single wholesaler identifier. Each order pointed to exactly one buyer and one wholesaler. This is a one-to-many relationship: one buyer may have many orders, but each order has one buyer. Figure 1 shows it.

Practitioners usually leave three things implicit. Every entity needs a key, an identifier that is unique and never changes, so that other tables can refer to it without copying its details. A relationship is stored as a key held in another table: the wholesaler identifier inside the order row is the whole mechanism by which an order belongs to a wholesaler. And every column implies a decision about which entity the fact is really about. Anaaj stored fee and status on the order because an order and a delivery were then the same event.

That last assumption is the one that failed. Each fact has a home, and the home determines how many of that fact can exist. A status that lives on the order row can take one value per order. If a basket contains three wholesalers who ship on three different days, there is no place for three statuses. No interface design changes that.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

Camila built a sample basket of five lines from three wholesalers.

LineWholesalerItemQtyUnit price (₹)Line total (₹)
1Bhavani Grain PartnersRice, 25 kg bag41,4505,800
2Bhavani Grain PartnersToor dal, 30 kg bag23,9007,800
3Chandra Foods GroupRefined oil, 15 L tin32,1006,300
4Chandra Foods GroupAtta, 50 kg bag22,1504,300
5Charan Sugar IndustriesSugar, 50 kg bag12,3002,300
Basket total (sum of the five line totals)26,500

Table 1. Line totals are quantity times unit price. Per-wholesaler subtotals: Bhavani 13,600; Chandra 10,600; Charan 2,300; together 26,500.

Under the old schema, each of the five lines must be a separate order, because an order can hold only one item. Anaaj charges ₹150 per order as a delivery fee, so the basket would carry 5 × 150 = ₹750 in fees, which is 2.83 per cent of the ₹26,500 goods value. The restaurant's accountant would receive five invoices where three are correct.

Under a restructured schema, the model has four entities: an order (the basket, with the buyer and the payment), an order line (one item, one quantity, one price), a shipment (what one wholesaler sends in one delivery) and the existing buyer and wholesaler. Fees attach to shipments: 3 × 150 = ₹450, or 1.70 per cent of ₹26,500. Invoices attach to shipments, giving three, one per wholesaler.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose Chandra Foods can ship only two of the three oil tins. In the new model this is a single edit: line 3 shows 2 shipped, so its value becomes 2 × 2,100 = ₹4,200, a reduction of ₹2,100. Chandra's invoice falls from ₹10,600 to ₹8,500, and the basket falls from ₹26,500 to ₹24,400. Check: 13,600 + 8,500 + 2,300 = 24,400. Under the old schema, support staff would edit the quantity by hand and the original order would be lost.

The same arithmetic governed the migration. Camila searched the 1,80,000 old rows for orders from the same buyer placed within ten minutes of each other, which were probably one basket split by the old system. She found 54,000 such rows forming 21,600 baskets, a mean of 2.5 rows per basket. Every old row becomes one order line and one shipment. Headers (orders) equal the 1,26,000 standalone rows plus the 21,600 baskets, which is 1,47,600. The backfill therefore writes 1,47,600 + 1,80,000 + 1,80,000 = 5,07,600 rows. Widen the window to sixty minutes and she found 61,200 rows in 24,000 baskets, a mean of 2.55. Headers become 1,18,800 + 24,000 = 1,42,800, and the total 5,02,800. The wider window groups 7,200 additional rows, 4.0 per cent of the table, on a guess no schema can verify.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

An entity is a decision, not a discovery

The entities are not obvious. Anaaj's founders treated an order and a delivery as one thing because, in their first customer's life, it was. Deciding what counts as a thing worth its own table is a claim about the business, and it is the claim most likely to expire.

Cardinality is the most consequential fact in the diagram

Cardinality is how many of one entity may relate to one of another: one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many. When two entities are many-to-many, as baskets and wholesalers now are, the relational model needs a third table between them. Here the shipment plays that role. Asking "can one of these ever have several of those?" finds missing tables cheaply.

Attributes live somewhere, and "where" is a business rule

The unit price on an order line is deliberately a copy of the product's price at the moment of purchase, not a link to today's price. If it were a link, last month's invoice would change whenever a wholesaler revised a rate. Which facts to freeze is a product decision.

State is not history

A status column holds only the latest value. If Anaaj wants to know how long a shipment waited between "packed" and "dispatched", it needs a record of each change. Data not recorded cannot be recovered later.

Normalisation versus convenience

Normalisation is the practice of storing each fact once, in the one place it belongs, and referring to it elsewhere by key. It prevents contradictions. The opposite practice, denormalisation, copies facts to make reading faster. Neither is correct in itself; the trade-off returns in the next topic.

A data model is not a user interface, and not an analytics model

The screen may show one "basket" while the database stores four tables. Reports often need yet another shape, which is why Camila's dashboards sit on a separate copy.

What the model cannot tell you

A schema can show what is possible to record. It cannot show whether anyone wants the feature, how fast a query will run, or whether the wholesalers will actually accept split deliveries. Those answers come from customers and tests.

Questions to ask before relying on a diagram

Ask which entities the diagram omits, and what the team would do if the most important relationship became many-to-many tomorrow.

6. How it differs by product type and by stage

In a consumer product, the stress is usually identity: one household sharing an account, or one person with two phones. In a B2B product such as Anaaj's, the stress comes from organisational structure. A restaurant group has outlets, cooks, approvers and a finance team, and a model with only "user" and "company" cannot hold them. In a marketplace, there are two or more sides, and the data model decides how many of each side can meet in one transaction. Anaaj's difficulty was precisely this: its model supported a one-sided meeting only.

Stage changes the economics. In an early-stage company a wrong model is cheap to change, so a rough design is justified. At Anaaj's size of 1,80,000 orders, a change touches reports, invoices, customer support tools and partner integrations. In a large company with many teams reading the same tables, the model is a public contract.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake 1: building the feature on the screen, not on the model

Symptom: estimates keep growing after design sign-off. Misunderstanding: that the interface is where features live. Diagnostic: ask the engineer to point to the table and column where each new fact will be stored; hesitation signals a missing entity.

Mistake 2: patching with labels

Symptom: support teams keep a spreadsheet to reconcile what the system cannot. Misunderstanding: that a flag or a free-text field can stand in for a relationship. Diagnostic: count the manual corrections in one week; a steady number means the model is leaking.

Mistake 3: assuming the old data fits the new shape

Symptom: a migration that is "almost done" for weeks. Misunderstanding: that history carries the distinctions the new model needs. Diagnostic: take a hundred old rows and try to classify them by hand, as Camila did.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled decision begins with one page from Bhaskar and Camila: the entities the feature requires, each relationship's cardinality, and the fields frozen at purchase. Aditi tests it against Table 1, the partial-shipment case and the migration counts before committing a date. The team ships the new model beside the old, backfills, compares totals, and moves buyers across in stages.

9. What Aditi decided

She chose the nine-week restructuring. The reasoning was threefold. The patch would have given Anaaj five invoices where the restaurant group's accountant expected three, and ₹750 in fees against ₹450 on the sample basket. The partial-shipment case, which she expected weekly at scale, had no home in the old model. And the three-week gap between 11 May and 1 June, while tight, was enough to run the backfill of 5,07,600 rows twice and reconcile it against the old totals. Camila kept the ten-minute rule and reported the sixty-minute variant as a sensitivity, so the 7,200 ambiguous rows were reviewed, not assumed.

Next comes Databases, storage and caching: the model says what is stored, the database determines how fast it is found. Two questions to sit with. First, which assumption in your own product's data, that one customer has one account or one order has one delivery, would be hardest to give up? Second, if a competitor offered a feature your schema cannot express, how would you discover that before your customers did?
case20v1-tech.auth:
Jivika Desk: The Identity Question

A decision case on SSO, SCIM and permissions

1. Opening

At 8:00 pm on Monday, 19 October 2026, Smruti Chandaria sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of Jivika Desk's Pune office with a security questionnaire open on her laptop. Question 14 read: "Does the vendor support SAML 2.0 single sign-on with our identity provider, automated user provisioning through SCIM, and customer-defined roles?" The honest answer, for all three parts, was no.

The questionnaire came from a Dubai retail group negotiating a ₹2.4 crore annual contract, the largest Jivika Desk had ever been close to signing. Its security committee would meet on Monday, 30 November. Smruti, Head of Product, had until Friday, 23 October to tell engineering what the squad starting on 26 October would build.

2. Company background

Jivika Desk, founded in Pune in 2017, sells a customer-support and service-workflow platform to Indian mid-market companies: distributors, NBFCs, regional manufacturers and consumer brands that had outgrown shared inboxes. It has 412 paying accounts and annual recurring revenue of ₹38 crore, with 210 employees across Pune, Bengaluru and a small sales office in New Jersey.

Buyers routinely shortlist Jivika Desk beside Freshworks and Zoho, both Indian-founded and both familiar to every procurement team. Jivika's pitch has been speed of set-up and price. Until this year that was enough, because small buyers log in with an email and a password and ask no questions about it.

3. The situation

Larger buyers behave differently. Their IT teams run Microsoft Entra ID or Google Workspace as the single place where employees are created and removed. They want staff to sign in through that system (single sign-on, or SSO, here over the SAML standard), want accounts created and deactivated automatically when HR changes a record (SCIM), and want to decide which employee may see or change what (role-based access). Jivika Desk offers three fixed roles: Admin, Agent and Viewer. Accounts are created by hand, and nobody is removed unless an administrator remembers.

Sakshi Chovatia, who leads customer success from Singapore, had been logging the pattern for two quarters. Exhibit 1 collects the seven open enterprise deals. Six carry at least one identity requirement. Only one, a Gurugram edtech firm, would sign today.

The Dubai group's chief information security officer, Sachin Chhajed, was courteous but fixed. His committee would not approve a vendor that could not show SSO working in a staging environment by 30 November, and wanted dated, contractual commitments for SCIM and custom roles by 31 March 2027. He also asked where user data is stored, a question that, since the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Indian buyers now ask as well.

Smruti had also asked Pune engineering how the product would need to change. Saumil's team found that roles are the hardest part: every screen checks the three fixed roles in code, so customer-defined roles mean rewriting those checks to read a permission table instead. Sign-in, by contrast, touches one service. That difference shaped the routes below.

Smruti had costed three routes (Exhibit 2). The calendar made the choice harder: the squad starts on 26 October and Diwali falls on Sunday, 8 November, so real working time before 30 November is short (Exhibit 3).

4. The people

Saumil Chitalia, VP Engineering in Pune, would rather build. He has watched the team inherit three vendor integrations that later became maintenance burdens, and he distrusts a dependency that sits in the login path of every customer. He also worries that 24 engineer-weeks is optimistic.

Sushant Champaneri, head of sales for North America in New Jersey, dialled in at 10:30 am his time. He wants anything that gets a "yes" onto the next questionnaire and will not defend a roadmap slide to a buyer.

Sakshi Chovatia, in Singapore, where it was 10:30 pm, supports the Singapore logistics prospect directly. She worries about the 412 existing customers: some already ask for SSO at renewal, and a rushed launch that locks people out of their helpdesk would cost her more than a lost deal.

Sachin Chhajed, in Dubai, owns the decision on the buyer's side and rewards candour. He has said he prefers a smaller feature set shipped on time to a larger one promised.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets out what each open deal requires. Smruti read it twice: SSO appears in five of the seven deals, custom roles in four, SCIM in three.

Exhibit 2 compares the routes. An engineer-week is costed at ₹1.25 lakh fully loaded, which is a ₹65 lakh annual cost spread over 52 weeks.

Exhibit 3 places each route against the committee date. The bars use a scale of 8 pixels per day from 19 October.

6. The options

Route 1: build everything in-house. It keeps control of the login path and costs the least of the routes that serve the whole pipeline, ₹30 lakh. Its cost is time. The squad would work SAML, SCIM and a rewrite of every role check in parallel, so SSO lands only with the rest on 7 December, a week after the committee, so the Dubai group would be asked to approve a promise.

Route 2: buy SSO and SCIM from an identity broker, build roles in-house. SAML and SCIM are standard plumbing that every vendor must get right and none can differentiate on, whereas roles are specific to Jivika's own objects, such as tickets, queues and customer records. The broker puts SSO and SCIM in staging by 20 November, but it costs ₹36.75 lakh in year one, recurs at ₹18 lakh a year, and places a third party in every customer's login.

Route 3: SSO only, in-house. It is the cheapest at ₹10 lakh and reaches staging by 23 November. But it fully serves only the ₹54 lakh Bengaluru deal, because every other deal with an identity requirement also asks for SCIM or roles, and it spends the Dubai group's goodwill.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Why do enterprise buyers treat SSO, SCIM and role-based access as gates rather than features? What risk does each one remove for the buyer's IT team?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, which requirements decide the most pipeline value, and how does your answer change if the Dubai deal is excluded?
  3. Compare the routes in Exhibits 2 and 3 on cost, date and the deals fully met. What does each give up?
  4. Which route would you commit to by 23 October, what would you tell Sachin Chhajed, and what evidence would make you change course?

8. A note for the learner

Identity is the front door of enterprise security, and a buyer's security team can only say yes if three questions have answers: who is signing in (SSO), who still works here (SCIM), and who may do what (roles). A missing answer is a veto, so these features decide deals long before anyone compares screens.

A well-reasoned answer separates what is standard from what is distinctive. Exhibit 1 shows that SSO or SCIM is required in five deals between them, and the plumbing is the same everywhere; roles must match the product. One defensible path is Route 2. It is the only route that puts both SSO and SCIM in staging before the committee meets, on 20 November, and still covers all six identity-bound deals by 31 March. Its extra ₹6.75 lakh over Route 1 (36.75 less 30) buys 17 days, from 7 December back to 20 November, and turns a promise into a staging demo for a ₹240 lakh deal. Smruti should also tell Sachin plainly that roles will arrive after the committee date, and why.

It carries real risks Smruti should name: the broker's recurring fee, the lock-in, and where it stores identity data under the DPDP Act. Her mitigations are a pilot with two existing customers who have asked for SSO at renewal, an Indian data-residency clause, an exit plan, and a firm commitment of 24 December for roles, offered to Sachin as a dated contract term. Saumil's concern about 24 engineer-weeks is a reason to prefer Route 2's 15. Route 3 is rejected on arithmetic: 18.5 per cent of the value it unlocks, against 5.7 per cent.
exp20v2-tech.auth:
Identity: auth, SSO, roles and permissions

Why enterprise deals hinge on a login screen nobody admires

1. The questionnaire

On Tuesday 14 July 2026, Divya Kothari, head of product at Dhriti Payroll Systems, a Pune company selling payroll and attendance software to mid-sized employers, opened an email from Farhan Siddiqui, chief information security officer of Ekam Steel Industries. Ekam had been a pilot customer for eleven weeks, with 400 supervisors on the product. It now wanted 8,000 employees on it. Siddiqui attached a 61-question security questionnaire and a deadline of 31 July, seventeen days away.

Question 7 asked whether employees could sign in with Ekam’s own corporate login. Question 12 asked whether an employee who leaves Ekam is automatically removed from Dhriti. Question 19 asked whether a plant accountant could be given the right to approve payroll without the right to change bank details. Dhriti’s honest answer to all three was no. It had email-and-password login, accounts that someone at Ekam created by hand, and two roles: Admin and User.

The commercial stakes were easy to state. The Ekam contract was worth 8,000 seats at ₹480 per seat per year, ₹38,40,000 or 38.4 lakh. It was one of five stalled enterprise deals, all with similar lists. Eshaan Dandekar, the chief technology officer, had a fix in mind but asked whether it justified a quarter of his team. Divya had to decide what to build, in what order, and whether to promise it before it existed.

2. The idea

Identity management answers three separate questions, and the central discipline of this topic is keeping them apart. Authentication (often shortened to authn) asks: who is this? Authorisation (authz) asks: what may this person do? Provisioning asks: should this person have an account at all, today? A login screen answers only the first.

The problem these ideas solved is credential sprawl: without coordination, each staff member holds a separate password in every subscription, and each is a place where a leaver keeps access. The remedy is to keep one authoritative record of each person, held by an identity provider (IdP), such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta or Google Workspace, and to let every application, called a service provider in the jargon, trust that record instead of keeping its own.

The standards arrived in layers. SAML 2.0, published by the OASIS standards body in 2005, lets an IdP hand a service provider a signed statement that a named person has authenticated. OAuth 2.0, published as RFC 6749 in 2012, was designed for something different: letting one application act on your behalf in another without learning your password. OpenID Connect (OIDC), finalised in 2014, added an identity layer on top of OAuth and is the modern, lighter-weight alternative to SAML. SCIM, the System for Cross-domain Identity Management, begun around 2011 and standardised by the IETF in 2015, handles provisioning: creating, updating and deleting accounts automatically. Role-based access control (RBAC), formalised by David Ferraiolo and Richard Kuhn at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology in 1992, assigns permissions to roles rather than to individuals.

The sentence Divya could repeat in any meeting: “Single sign-on proves who the person is, provisioning decides whether they exist, and roles decide what they can touch; Ekam’s security team will not sign unless all three live in their hands, not ours.”

3. How it actually works

Figure 1 shows the common SAML path. An employee opens Dhriti and, because Dhriti recognises her company, is redirected to Ekam’s identity provider. She signs in there, with whatever Ekam requires, such as a second factor on her phone. The IdP returns a signed assertion: a small document stating her name, email and group memberships. Dhriti checks the signature against a certificate Ekam gave it in advance, and opens a session. Trust is established once, by exchanging certificates, not at each login.

Two steps are usually left implicit. First, matching: Dhriti must decide which of its own records the assertion refers to, usually by email address, and what to do if no record exists. Second, session lifetime: when Ekam disables a leaver at the IdP, Dhriti’s session may continue for hours unless it is told to expire, which is why many buyers ask for short sessions.

SCIM fills the gap in the story. SSO controls who can get in; it does not create or remove accounts in Dhriti. With SCIM, Ekam’s IdP calls a Dhriti interface and says: create this user, change this department, deactivate that one. Deactivation, not deletion, is the standard action, because payroll records must be kept. Then RBAC takes over inside the product. Ekam’s IdP can send a group such as “Plant-Accountants”, and Dhriti maps that group to a role, which is a named bundle of permissions. The permission to “approve payroll run” is separate from “edit bank details”, and a role lists which of these it carries.

PermissionAdminPayroll approverPlant accountantAuditor
View payslipsYesYesYesYes
Approve payroll runYesYesNoNo
Edit bank detailsYesNoNoNo
Export reportsYesYesYesYes
Manage users and rolesYesNoNoNo
Read audit logYesNoNoYes

Table 1. A role matrix for Dhriti. The separation between approving a run and editing bank details is what question 19 was probing.

The accountant who prepares payroll cannot also redirect a salary to another account, the oldest fraud in the book and the reason auditors insist on segregation of duties. Two roles, Admin and User, could never satisfy Ekam.

4. A worked example

Divya started with the money at risk. She listed the five stalled deals, multiplied seats by the quoted price, and kept every figure in lakh.

Table 2. Stalled pipeline. The total is the exact sum of the rows; the price column is not summed because it is a rate. 107.3 lakh is ₹1.073 crore.

Next she asked Dandekar for effort estimates, priced at ₹1.1 lakh per engineer-week fully loaded.

The answer flips at a share just above 43 per cent: 46.2 divided by 107.3 is 0.4306. Divya read this as: the build pays back in year one if signed deals exceed 46.2 lakh, and later years are nearly free of the fixed cost. The table omits that the features are reusable across customers.

The SCIM figure deserves its own arithmetic, because it is the one security teams press hardest. Ekam loses roughly 18 per cent of its workforce a year. On 8,000 staff that is 1,440 leavers. If departed employees’ accounts are removed by hand and the average account survives 21 days, that is 1,440 × 21 = 30,240 account-days of exposure. With SCIM deactivating within one day, it falls to 1,440 account-days, a twenty-one-fold reduction.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Authentication is not authorisation

Proving who someone is says nothing about what they may do. Finishing SSO finishes one of three jobs.

OAuth is not a login protocol

OAuth 2.0 grants an application a token to access something on your behalf, such as reading your calendar. Using it as proof of identity is a classic error, and the reason OpenID Connect exists. When a vendor says “we support OAuth”, ask which job they mean.

SAML and OIDC are rivals, not layers

SAML, built on XML, dominates older enterprise estates; OIDC, built on JSON, newer ones. An enterprise product usually needs both, because the buyer’s IdP decides.

SSO does not remove leavers

A disabled IdP account blocks the next login but may leave sessions and API keys alive. Only provisioning and short sessions close that gap.

RBAC has a limit, and the limit is a count

With 14 independent permissions there are 214 = 16,384 possible permission sets. Arbitrary custom roles sound generous and become a support burden. Where rules depend on context, such as “approve only your own plant’s payroll”, pure RBAC strains.

Tenant boundaries are not roles

An Ekam admin must administer Ekam’s data only. Role checks that forget the tenant (the customer’s separate data space) let a valid user read another company’s records.

Identity cannot tell you intent

A correctly roled accountant can still export every salary in the company. Audit logs and alerts address misuse; identity does not.

Questions a newcomer should ask

Which identity providers do our buyers run? Who administers roles at the customer? What happens to a session when a person is disabled? Is SSO a paid add-on or table stakes?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products, identity is mainly a conversion problem. A phone number and a one-time code, or “sign in with Google”, lower friction; roles are nearly absent because each account is one person. Social login matters most; SAML almost never appears.

In B2B software, the buyer is an organisation, and identity becomes a procurement gate. The administrator, not the user, is the customer for these features, and the checklist is as predictable as a tax form.

In marketplaces, one human may be a buyer in one transaction and a seller in the next. Permissions attach to the relationship, not just the person, and a seller’s staff need roles within the seller’s account.

Company size changes the sequence. An early-stage company with five customers can answer the questionnaire with a roadmap and a call; one with 500 customers cannot, because its sales team meets the question weekly. Large companies also inherit the cost of changing a role model customers rely on.

7. Common mistakes

Building SSO and stopping. The symptom: a buyer signs, then asks about leavers in month three. The misunderstanding is treating sign-on as the whole subject. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask the customer’s IT administrator to disable a test user and time how long Dhriti takes to refuse that person.

Hard-coding roles in the product. The symptom: every new customer request needs an engineer. The misunderstanding is that roles are product behaviour rather than data. The diagnostic is to count how many role changes in the last quarter needed a code release.

Trusting the claim, not the check. The symptom: a forged assertion is accepted. The misunderstanding is that a well-formed assertion is a true one. The diagnostic is to submit an assertion with an invalid signature in a test environment and confirm it is refused.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Divya’s situation has a short life. On 15 July the answers to the 61 questions are sorted into those already true, those buildable inside a quarter, and those never to be promised. The sales team receives a one-page statement of exactly which standards are supported, SAML 2.0, OIDC, SCIM 2.0, and on which date. Integrations are tested with Entra ID and Okta before launch. The customer’s administrator, not Dhriti, assigns roles. No commitment in the reply exceeds what engineering has estimated.

9. What Divya decided

She did not ask for the full 42 weeks at once. She proposed the order of Table 3 by blocking power: roles first, because Ekam’s question 19 was the most specific; SSO second; SCIM third; the audit log folded into the roles work. She told Siddiqui in writing that SSO and role separation would be generally available by 30 September, and that SCIM would follow in a dated pilot for Ekam. Her reasoning: a dated, narrow promise carries less risk than a broad one, and the cautious scenario in Table 4, a 3.28 lakh shortfall, was a small price for a capability every future enterprise customer would require.

Learn next: enterprise security requirements, the questionnaire these answers sit inside; admin, roles and permissions, to design the matrix well; and API keys, rate limits and quotas, because machine access has its own identity rules.

Two questions to sit with. If Ekam’s own identity provider were breached tomorrow, which of your controls would still protect your customer’s data, and which would fail with it? And at what share of closed deals would you refuse to build, and what would you ask the sales team to prove before you believed that number?

Identity: auth, SSO, roles and permissions

Near-expert depth: the login screen is the cheap part, and the authority model is the expensive one

1. Two decisions, thirty-one days apart

On Monday 9 February 2026, Nandita Mukherjee, vice-president of product at Manthan Health Works — a Hyderabad company whose clinical documentation software runs in 310 hospitals across 38 groups — opened a renewal she had assumed was routine. Madhuvan Hospitals Group, eleven hospitals across Maharashtra and Gujarat, was the second largest contract on Manthan's books.

Seat typeSeatsPrice per seat per year (₹)Annual value (₹ lakh)
Licensed clinician4,8002,100100.80

Total14,200–143.10

Table 1. The price column is a rate and is not summed. 100.80 + 42.30 = 143.10 lakh, or ₹1.431 crore — 3.1 per cent of Manthan's ₹46.2 crore of recurring revenue.

Niranjan Oza, Madhuvan's head of information technology, was not asking for single sign-on; Madhuvan had run on Microsoft Entra ID since its first month. He asked three harder questions. Could a hospital's administrator manage roles for that hospital alone? When a consultant was disabled in Entra ID at nine in the morning, at what minute did she stop being able to open a chart? And when a junior doctor in a cardiac arrest needed a record she had no standing right to see, what happened, and who found out?

Oza attached a log: 611 accounts disabled over the previous quarter. Manthan's connector polled every four hours, and nobody could say when any of the 611 had actually lost their session. Dr Neelima Ogale, Madhuvan's chief medical information officer, summed it up: “You have proved you can let people in. Not that you can get anyone out.”

Thirty-one days later, on Thursday 12 March 2026, Niketa Oberoi, who ran platform product at Medhini AI Labs in Bengaluru, met the same subject from the far end. Medhini's agent platform read a document, called internal systems and drafted work for a human to approve. Mudrank Finance Group, a large retail non-banking financial company, had a ₹2.4 crore annual agreement in negotiation — 7.6 per cent of Medhini's ₹31.6 crore of recurring revenue, its largest ever. Nilesh Mogre, its head of information security, had stopped the deal on one objection.

The agent authenticated to Mudrank's systems as a service account that could read all 1.84 crore customer files. A relationship manager such as Meenal Narvekar could read 412. Mogre's position: an agent acting for Narvekar must reach what Narvekar reaches and nothing more — a blast radius smaller by a factor of about 44,700. Milind Natarajan, Medhini's principal engineer, observed that nothing in the product had been built that way.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Identity resolves four questions routinely collapsed into one. Authentication establishes which principal is present. Authorisation decides whether it may perform a given operation on a given resource. Provisioning governs whether it has an account today, and audit records what was decided and why. A principal need not be human: a service, a job, an agent run and a device all qualify, and they now vastly outnumber people.

The history is one of removing trust from the wrong places. Kerberos, at MIT in the 1980s, replaced passwords on the wire with tickets from a trusted third party. SAML 2.0 (OASIS, 2005) carried that across organisational boundaries with signed assertions. OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749, 2012) solved a different problem — letting one application act in another on a user's behalf without learning the password — and OpenID Connect, final in 2014, put an identity layer back on top. SCIM became an IETF standard for provisioning in 2015; role-based access control was formalised by David Ferraiolo and Richard Kuhn at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology in 1992, as an explicit rejection of per-user access lists.

Three schools now disagree substantively. The directory school holds that the enterprise directory is the single source of truth: groups in Entra ID or Okta are the authority model, applications merely render it, and anything configured inside your product is a defect. It will sign that an application holds no user records beyond a cached projection; not that it may define permissions the directory cannot express.

The policy school, whose canonical artefact is Google's Zanzibar paper of 2019, holds that authorisation is a graph question — can this subject reach this object through some relationship? — belonging in a decision service queried at every access. It will sign that roles are a user interface over policy, never the storage format; it will not sign that customer administrators should author policy directly, which yields rules nobody can audit.

The product school holds that the authority model is part of the product's domain language — “attending physician on this admission” is a clinical concept before it is a permission — and that outsourcing it yields correct systems clinicians route around. It will sign that the role catalogue is designed with customers and versioned; not that permissions are plumbing.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Start with one agent action at Medhini: it contains every mechanism in the topic, where a browser redirect contains one.

Step three is what most teams leave implicit, and it is the whole of Mogre's objection. Under RFC 8693 token exchange, the application presents the user's token and asks the authorisation server for a new one carrying the user as subject, the agent as actor, and a scope narrowed to the task: Medhini acting for Narvekar, on task 7741-C, to read a profile and a statement. Narvekar's authority covers 9 of Mudrank's 18 permissions, or 50 per cent; the token carries 2, or 11 per cent. Only a service account widens that to everything.

The second mechanism is the cost of asking: authorisation is many questions per request, not one. Manthan instrumented a single chart open at Madhuvan in January 2026.

DecisionChecksp95 ms per checkMilliseconds
Tenant: which hospital group owns the record10.400.4
Role to permission lookup11.201.2
Facility scope: one of eleven hospitals11.101.1
Care relationship: on this admission or not16.806.8
Consent and sensitivity category32.507.5
Field-level masking decisions280.359.8
Total35–26.8

Table 2. The middle column is a rate and is not summed. 26.8 ms of the 400 ms page budget is 6.7 per cent.

Thirty-five decisions, 26.8 milliseconds. Mahesh Nadkarni, Manthan's engineering head, cached the three stable lookups — role, facility and care relationship, 9.1 ms together — behind a cache answering in 0.2 ms per lookup at a 92 per cent hit rate. Expected cost falls to 0.08 × 9.1 + 0.92 × (3 × 0.2) = 1.28 ms, and the page's authorisation cost to 19.0 ms, a reduction of 29 per cent. The second-order effect matters more: five minutes of caching means a revoked permission keeps working for up to five minutes, so the time-to-live is a security parameter. Nobody in the review called it one.

The third mechanism is revocation, and the formal point is that revocation lag is a maximum over independent channels — not an average, never a sum. A principal loses access only when the slowest surviving path closes.

Setting aside personal access tokens, which never expired, Manthan's governing lag in February was 20,160 minutes — fourteen days, the mobile refresh token's lifetime. Oza's four-hourly poll, the number both sides quoted, was not the binding constraint. The target binds at 15 minutes, the interval at which the mobile client re-checks revocation: a factor of 1,344, won by fixing channels nobody watched.

The fourth mechanism is the model's shape. Manthan defines 23 permissions, so there are 223 = 8,388,608 possible subsets. Nobody enumerates those; Manthan ships nine roles. The question is what happens when customers want them scoped.

Roles scoped per hospital (11)9917,672No

Table 3. Madhuvan's 14,200 accounts under four models. Row 2: 2,480 staff work at an average of 2.4 hospitals, so 11,720 + 2,480 × 2.4 = 17,672. Row 3: of those, 4,310 span an average of 2.5 departments, so 13,362 + 4,310 × 2.5 = 24,137.

Scoping multiplies the catalogue by the scope cardinality and inflates assignments by 70 per cent, yet still cannot express the one rule clinicians live by. That is the empirical case for the policy school; the counter-case is that the fourth row holds only if someone can explain its four rules to an auditor.

4. When the standard answer applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. First: the buying organisation, not the user, bears the cost of a wrong grant. True at Madhuvan, where a disclosed psychiatric note is the hospital's exposure under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; true at Mudrank, which answers to the Reserve Bank of India. Where it is false, as in consumer products, most of this is over-engineering.

Second: principals change faster than a product team can respond. Madhuvan disabled 611 accounts in a quarter, so provisioning must be automatic; Medhini's agent runs create tens of thousands of short-lived principals a day.

Third: permissions are legible to the customer's domain experts. True at Madhuvan, where Dr Ogale can read a role matrix and say what is wrong with it. False at Mudrank, where the thing authorised is a sequence of tool calls chosen at runtime. Where it fails, role catalogues become theatre and the real control is the token's scope.

Fourth: the identity provider is more trustworthy than your own store. Usually true, and the reason federation is demanded, but it misleads twice. A product sold to small businesses with no directory loses sales by insisting on it. And delegating authentication makes the customer's outage your outage: a directory at 99.9 per cent availability is unreachable for 43.2 minutes in a thirty-day month, and a hospital still has patients during them.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product companies find identity the first thing shared and the last unified. Manthan sells a chart product and a billing product acquired in 2024, and Madhuvan's administrators maintain two role models for the same people. The honest treatment is a ladder of scopes.

Regulated settings add a requirement access control cannot express: emergency override, which clinicians call break-glass. The right design grants the access, records it loudly, and routes it for review within a fixed window — Madhuvan's was 24 hours. Manthan had none, so eleven ward sisters held a standing elevated role “just in case”: a far worse control, and what every product without an override eventually grows.

Shared hardware breaks the assumption that a session belongs to a person. A nursing-station terminal serves nine people in a shift; badge-tap re-authentication with a 90-second lock is the mature answer, a shared login the immature one that destroys the audit trail where regulators look first. Two-sided cases add an axis: at Medhini a model provider's engineers see telemetry for their own model only, so the question concerns two organisations, not a role within one.

At the organisational seam the pattern rarely matches what companies say. Identity sits with a platform team that has no customer-facing roadmap; revenue pressure arrives through sales, audit obligation through security, and nobody owns the catalogue as a product. Those who handle it well give it an owner and a version number, and refuse to let a deal add a role that is not in it.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Revocation lag is a maximum, not an average. The tell-tale is a vendor who answers “how fast do you revoke?” with one number, usually the provisioning interval. That reading was wrong at Manthan by a factor of 84: the poll was 240 minutes, the refresh token 20,160. Experts ask for the channel list first.

“Supports SSO” is not a specification. The tell-tale is a one-word answer in a questionnaire. Flow direction, assertion signing, assertion encryption, single logout, certificate rotation and multiple domains per tenant are six commitments. Manthan supported four; the other two generated most of its support tickets.

The customer's groups are not your roles. The tell-tale is a product asking the customer to create directory groups named after your roles. That inverts the burden: a 14,000-person hospital group will not restructure its directory for one vendor. Experts ship a many-to-many mapping screen instead.

Just-in-time provisioning is asymmetric. Creating an account on first login is only the creation half. The tell-tale is a tenant whose account count rises monotonically and has never fallen. Madhuvan's held 14,200 accounts against a headcount near 12,900 — a gap that was almost entirely leavers.

Permission caching is a security parameter. The tell-tale is that nobody present can state the time-to-live, because caching reads as a performance concern. In fact it is the floor on how fast a demotion takes effect, and a 300-second cache quietly contradicts any promise of immediate revocation.

Tenancy is enforced in the data layer or not at all. The tell-tale is a tenant identifier arriving in the request body or a header rather than derived from the session. Every cross-tenant exposure of the last decade has one shape: a check that asked “may this role read invoices?” and never “whose invoices?”.

Role inheritance creates grants nobody intended. The tell-tale is a “deny” checkbox in the admin screen, almost always a patch over a hierarchy that over-grants. Experts prefer a flat catalogue, because it renders as a matrix a compliance officer will read and a six-level hierarchy does not.

Email is a terrible join key and the default one. The tell-tale is a migration plan that matches on email address. People change surnames, hospitals merge domains, consultants carry three addresses. Of Manthan's 1,150 visiting consultants, 174 held two accounts with different roles.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the subject barely exists: one principal per account, no administrator, and the live questions are conversion and recovery. In business software the buyer is an organisation, identity becomes a procurement gate, and the administrator rather than the user is the customer. In enterprise deals that gate has teeth: a questionnaire, a penetration test report, a clause on revocation time.

Platforms and marketplaces differ in kind, because authority follows a relationship rather than a role. Medhini's model providers, Mudrank's channel partners and a hospital's visiting consultants are one shape: a principal whose rights derive from an edge in a graph. Platform companies therefore reach for policy engines earlier.

Hardware changes the session model, not the authority model: badge taps and kiosk modes are authentication problems, and what a nurse may do with a chart is the same question at a workstation or a tablet. Artificial-intelligence products change more, introducing a principal that is neither person nor fixed service, acts on someone's behalf, chooses its own actions and lives for seconds. Everything here still applies; what changes is that the token, not the role, is the unit of control.

Stage matters in one way. An early company answers the questionnaire with a roadmap because it has five customers; one with 142 accounts meets the question weekly and needs a policy. The expensive stage is the third, where hundreds of customers depend on a role model you now know is wrong, and the migration rather than the design is the hard problem.

8. Three worked examples

Delegated administration at Manthan. Every role assignment at Madhuvan had gone through a support ticket: 1,340 in the quarter, averaging 11 minutes, or 245.7 hours. At ₹900 per support hour that is ₹2.21 lakh a quarter, ₹8.84 lakh a year, against a ₹143.10 lakh contract. Afterwards 1,180 of the 1,340 assignments were made by hospital administrators and the ticket load fell to 160, a reduction of 88 per cent. The deeper gain: a hospital's administrator could not touch the other ten.

Scope narrowing at Medhini. Natarajan rebuilt the agent on token exchange. An average task made 41 tool calls, 29 of which touched customer data. Under the service account each of the 29 was authorised against 1.84 crore files; under delegated tokens, against one file and two permissions. Mudrank re-ran 84 adversarial prompts designed to make the agent fetch a file outside Narvekar's book; all 84 retrieved nothing, because the token could not express the request. That is the case for enforcing at the boundary rather than instructing the model.

The role migration that failed. On 7 July 2026 Manthan migrated Madhuvan from two roles to nine, mapping accounts by job-title text. Of 14,200 accounts, 1,860 — 13.1 per cent — matched no rule and fell to the default, “Clinician, full chart access”. The defect surfaced 23 days later, on 30 July, when a ward clerk at the Nashik hospital opened a psychiatry note. Reclassification took nine days; 212 of the 1,860 had opened a record they should not have, 41 of those in a sensitive category.

Cost of the failed migration₹ lakh

Service credits, 10 per cent of annual contract value14.31
Two prospective deals delayed one quarter10.80
Total50.11

Table 4. 15.40 + 9.60 + 14.31 + 10.80 = 50.11 lakh. Credits are 10 per cent of ₹143.10 lakh; the delay figure is one quarter of two deals worth ₹25.20 lakh and ₹18.00 lakh a year.

What mattered was not the nine days of reclassification but the rule Nadkarni wrote afterwards: no identity migration ships without a dry run reporting how many accounts hit the default, and a two-week shadow period in which both models run and disagreements are logged unenforced. That costs about 4 engineer-weeks, ₹5.60 lakh — roughly one-ninth of ₹50.11 lakh — and would have surfaced all 1,860 accounts before one was granted.

9. Failure modes and their diagnostics

Table 5. Every diagnostic in the third column is answerable within a day by anyone with a test tenant.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should single sign-on be a paid feature? The case for charging is that it is bought by a different buyer with a different budget, and supporting a dozen providers has real cost. The case against is that a security control, once priced, pushes small customers into worse configurations. Medhini has evidence from its own price list: 38 Business-plan accounts at ₹8.40 lakh asked for federation that year, Enterprise carrying a 40 per cent uplift at ₹11.76 lakh.

Outcome for the 38 accounts asking for SSOAccountsRevenue effect each (₹ lakh)Annual effect (₹ lakh)
Upgraded to Enterprise12+3.36+40.32
Stayed, accepted a workaround90.000.00
Lost, attributed to the paywall10.2−8.40−85.68
Lost, would have churned anyway6.80.000.00
Total38–−45.36

Table 6. 12 + 9 + 10.2 + 6.8 = 38; +40.32 − 85.68 = −45.36 lakh. The paywall is assumed to cause 60 per cent of the 17 losses, and that share is the contested input: at 28 per cent the policy breaks even, and if it caused all 17 the cost is ₹102.48 lakh.

The charging position fails if attribution is much lower, or if the twelve upgrades brought expansion revenue the table ignores. Oberoi's honest reading was that Medhini had asserted an attribution rate it never measured.

Roles or policy? The role school rests on auditability: a matrix can be reviewed by a compliance officer, and reviewability is the point of access control. The policy school rests on expressiveness, and on Zanzibar-scale evidence that relationship queries are the general case. The role position fails if customers routinely need conditions roles cannot express, which Table 3 suggests is already true at Madhuvan. The policy position fails if policy sets become unreviewable; nobody has published a convincing study of audit quality under either.

Buy or build? Buying an identity platform converts a multi-quarter build into configuration and transfers the burden of supporting every provider. Building keeps the authority model inside the domain, which matters most where that model is the product. The buy position weakens when the questions are relational and clinical; the build position weakens the moment a questionnaire asks for something standard you have half-built.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in three ways. They ask for the channel list before accepting a revocation number, and test it in a customer's tenant rather than trusting a document. They treat the role catalogue as a versioned artefact with an owner, and can refuse a deal-specific role without losing the deal, because they can show where the requirement already lands. And they separate what the product proves from what it asserts: an audit log that answers a regulator in minutes is a different asset from a log file an engineer can query. The studied practitioner knows the acronyms; the master knows which one binds this deal.

12. What each of them decided

Mukherjee did not promise instantaneous revocation. She committed to a published figure — 15 minutes across all channels — and to a quarterly joint test in which Madhuvan disabled a seeded account and Manthan reported the measured lag on every client. She shipped delegated administration and break-glass with 24-hour review before the renewal, and deferred department-level scoping because Table 3 showed it adding 6,465 assignments without answering the question clinicians ask. A measured, falsifiable number is worth more to a security team than a better unmeasured one.

Oberoi rebuilt the authority model rather than special-casing Mudrank, and changed the sales posture to match: the intersection of agent grant, user authority and task scope became the stated security model, documented and demonstrable. She left pricing open, commissioning a study of the 17 lost accounts.

Discussion questions. First: Manthan's 15-minute figure depends on a mobile client checking in. What should it do about a device switched off for a week, and does that change the published number? Second: Table 6 turns on an attribution share nobody has measured. What experiment would you run, and what would you charge meanwhile? Third: if Mudrank's identity provider went dark for 43.2 minutes, which of Medhini's controls would hold — and should the system fail open or closed?

13. Going deeper

  • Security basics for PMs — the threat-modelling vocabulary that makes these arguments precise.
  • Enterprise security requirements — the questionnaire regime these commitments sit inside.
  • Admin, roles and permissions — designing the catalogue and delegation screens Table 3 implies.
  • Auth, keys, rate limits and quotas — machine identity, and the unexpiring tokens that were Manthan's worst channel.
  • How web and mobile apps work — why a refresh token behaves unlike a browser session, which is Figure 2.
  • APIs and integration basics — token exchange, scopes and the on-behalf-of pattern of Figure 1.
  • Data modelling for PMs — "attending on this admission" is a modelling decision first.
  • Databases, storage and caching — where the 92 per cent hit rate and its time-to-live live.
  • Cloud infrastructure basics — workload identity, secrets, and what a service proves about itself.
  • Reading an architecture diagram — fluency to spot a tenant check in the wrong layer.

Kunji Shiftworks: Who Pressed the Button?

A Bengaluru frontline-workforce company has seven weeks to sign a security addendum it may not be able to honour, and an identity model that is the reason it won in the first place.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

At twenty past eleven on Sunday 11 October 2026, Tanishi Dedhia had two documents open on a kitchen table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru: an eleven-page Information Security Addendum from Kashida Retail Group, and a page blank but for a heading, Identity: recommendation for Monday.

Clause 7.4 ran to two sentences. Each of fourteen named privileged actions — stock adjustment, price override, roster edit, eleven others — had to be attributable in Kunji Shiftworks' audit log to one named individual, and the attribution had to survive that individual's leaving. Clause 7.5 gave four hours to remove access after a termination in Kashida's HR system; clause 7.6 required SAML 2.0 against the group's identity provider for every user with a group mailbox.

Kunji had to sign, or refuse, by Monday 30 November 2026 and comply by 31 March 2027; the board would meet on 26 November. On Kashida alone ₹682 lakh was at stake, of which ₹270 lakh already books, against a ₹17.52 crore run-rate (Exhibit 1). Tanishi had four options, three sets of numbers that disagreed, and a suspicion that she had been asked the wrong question.

2. The company, and the decision of June 2018

Kunji Shiftworks Private Limited was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Trilochan Dattani and Tushaar Doshi. The product is unglamorous: attendance, rostering, tasks and stock counts for frontline crews. By September 2026 it ran in 71 tenants, 4,251 sites and 7,894 shared devices, on ₹14.6 crore of cash.

The decision that shapes this case was taken in June 2018 and was then correct. Kunji's users had no company email, no personal smartphones at work and often nothing better than 2G; a crew of fourteen shared two tablets across three shifts. Doshi made the login an outlet code and a four-digit PIN, and the identity key the triple of tenant, outlet and PIN. Sign-in took under three seconds, and Kunji won its first forty logos on that difference.

Two later decisions compounded it. In 2018 the tenant was a customer identifier stamped on each row; the March 2021 rewrite made it a level in the hierarchy, above outlet, but left the identity key itself untouched, so a transferred person acquired a second PIN. In September 2023, asked for single sign-on by Kalavati Hypermart, Kunji shipped an OAuth login against Google Workspace for the back office only, and began writing "SSO available" on its RFP responses.

3. The industry

Organised retail, pharmacy chains, dark stores and 3PL hubs have multiplied — Reliance Retail, Trent, DMart and Flipkart have put an enormous frontline workforce behind a device — and procurement has matured faster than the products: a 2026 deal needs a 180-line security questionnaire and, increasingly, SOC 2 Type II. Buyers compare Kunji with Darwinbox, Zoho People and Keka, whose enterprise tiers they expect to carry SAML and directory-driven provisioning. Regulation pulls the same way: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 attaches notice and purpose-limitation duties to any new inference about an identified worker.

The team is scattered in a way the 2018 architecture never anticipated: engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, a designer in Berlin three and a half hours behind IST until the clocks change on 25 October, a data scientist in Toronto and a sales head in New Jersey both nine and a half hours behind until 1 November, customer success in Singapore, and the largest contract administered from Dubai. In July, Kaarigar Workforce Cloud took a ₹96 lakh Pune 3PL deal with an RFP response that answered SCIM 2.0 in one word: yes.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Kashida Retail Group, a 640-site grocery and general-merchandise group trading in the UAE and Oman, signed for 212 sites in November 2024. Kunji's questionnaire answer read "role-based access control with per-user audit logging": true of the back office, false of the floor, unnoticed on both sides for fifteen months.

In February 2026 Kashida's group internal audit visited two Dubai distribution centres and asked who had made 46 particular stock adjustments. Kunji could produce a site and a PIN, not a person. The audit raised a finding; the finding produced September's addendum. In April, Kunji shipped an OIDC login against Microsoft Entra ID for two tenants' back offices and told the market that enterprise SSO was live.

Three things have since turned out to be wrong (Figure 1). On 2 October, Doshi's team established that PINs are recycled — the console suggests the lowest free PIN, so a leaver's credential is often reissued within days — and that 1,418 of Kashida's 9,740 live PINs, 14.6 per cent, have been held by more than one person since November 2024, so actions under those PINs cannot be attributed even retrospectively. On 7 October, Tapasi Dhanani's model attributed 88 per cent of frontline actions to a single named person, but only at those two distribution centres: 1.46 lakh of September's 59.60 lakh actions, and the only sites where devices are issued one to a supervisor. Across three Indian tenants it reached 54 per cent. On 8 October, Tejomay Didwania noted that Kunji's ISO 27001 scope excludes the frontline PIN service.

5. The people

Tanishi Dedhia, VP Product, Bengaluru, owns Monday's page and says Kunji should promise only what it can evidence; her roadmap is already promised to three other tenants. She has not mentioned telling Kashida's group CIO, Toshika Dharamshi, in February that named-user trails were "on this year's roadmap".

Trilochan Dattani, co-founder and CEO, wants the addendum signed and the thin option shipped: a Series B conversation is live at an indicative ₹140 crore pre-money, eight times the run-rate. He does not mention that he approved the 2018 design himself.

Tushaar Doshi, Director of Engineering, Platform and Identity, Pune, argues for a rebuild — one person, one identity — and has lost two engineers this year. He does not say that his own 2021 rewrite left the outlet-scoped key in place to hit a date.

Tarana Dhariwal, Customer Success, Singapore, carries Kashida and Kalavati, is bonused on gross retention and wants no migration near the peak. She has written to Kashida's IT head that SCIM would be "available in the first quarter" — meaning Kunji's, which begins in April.

Toshan Dagli, SVP Sales, Newark, wants a SAML button and a SOC 2 letter to attach to questionnaires by December. He does not volunteer that his team fills in the CRM's "primary blocker" field, or that three of its eleven identity losses were lost on price after discounting below floor.

Tapasi Dhanani, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto, built the roster-inference model and is its loudest sceptic: inference is a statistical claim and should be labelled one. It is also the most visible thing she has built here.

Tejomay Didwania, Information Security and Compliance, Mumbai, is fractional at three days a week and must sign the compliance schedule, which is why he will not attest to clause 7.4: an inference about an identified worker is a new purpose with a notice attached. He has not told the board that the 2024 questionnaire answer was already a stretch.

6. Exhibits

Option B, the rebuild: one person, one identity, roles reattached, PINs demoted. It answers everything and arrives on 23 August 2027, almost five months after the compliance date, at ₹248 lakh.

Option C, embed a vendor: 22 March 2027, nine days inside the date, but it moves a core competence and a per-identity meter into someone else's business model: harmless at 3,624 identities, not at 1,29,724.

Option D, the supervisor tier: SSO for supervisors, the floor on PINs, the audit trail completed by joining the roster. It arrives 12 April 2027, twelve days late, and rests on a model validated where devices are one to a person.

What Tanishi could not settle was whether these were four options or four versions of one assumption. Clause 7.4 covers fourteen action types, 2.3 per cent of the floor's actions (Exhibit 6); she had not asked Dharamshi whether attributing those fourteen to the supervisor who authorised them would close the finding, and she could not remember anyone costing what a named-user model would do to a price list quoted per device.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The addendum must be signed by Monday 30 November 2026 and performed by 31 March 2027; the board meets on 26 November with the Series B diligence pack. Tenant change freezes run from 24 October to 16 November, around Diwali on 8 November, removing three working weeks. Kunji holds ₹14.6 crore of cash against a burn of ₹2.3 crore a quarter, and a plan to reach EBITDA breakeven in the January–March 2027 quarter. There are 26 engineers and a hiring freeze until the round closes. The Kashida MSA carries a 99.5 per cent availability commitment with credits of up to 8 per cent of a quarter's fees, about ₹5.4 lakh on the existing contract. Kalavati renews on 31 March 2027 having asked for the same clause.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does clause 7.4 actually require, in terms an engineer could implement and Didwania could attest to? Write it as an acceptance test.
  2. Exhibit 2 reports all 318 of Kashida's accounts SSO-eligible (2,763 of 3,624 across the base); Kashida's own directory returns 207 of the 318. Which number should a SCIM design use, and what breaks at cutover under each?
  3. Exhibits 5a and 5b disagree about what identity has cost. What would settle it, and until then, should it change Monday's recommendation at all?
  4. Exhibit 3 cannot say how many accounts hold more than one role. Is that a reporting, design or procurement defect, and who should have caught it?
  5. Kunji bills by device; its buyers license by named user. Is this an architecture, pricing, contracting or compliance problem, and whose budget pays?
  6. It is nine o'clock on Monday 12 October 2026. What goes on Tanishi's page, what does she commit to Dharamshi before 30 November, and what does she tell a board that is also reading a term sheet?

11. Sunday night, continued

At ten past midnight Tanishi wrote one sentence on the blank page — "We can sign 7.5, we can sign 7.6 for the accounts in your directory, and we cannot sign 7.4 as written" — and looked at it. It would be read in Dubai as a refusal, in Newark as a lost quarter and in Pune as permission to start the rebuild nobody had funded. Then she deleted it, because she could not tell whether it was the honest answer or the easiest one to defend, and the cursor sat blinking at the top of an empty page.
exp40v2-tech.llm.feature:
Adding an LLM Feature

Wiring a model API into a product: prompts, tokens, cost, and what decides whether the feature pays

1. Two companies, one February

On Thursday 5 February 2026, in Bengaluru, Ela Edulji put one number on the screen: ₹13.80 lakh. She is vice-president of product at Ekatva Compliance Systems, a fictional vertical software firm selling to Indian chartered accountancy practices: 1,850 firms, 14,200 seats at ₹2,400 a seat a month, ₹3.408 crore of monthly revenue. The ₹13.80 lakh was February's model bill for a drafting assistant that reads a GST or income-tax notice and drafts a reply with citations. Omana Oommen, the chief financial officer, did not object to 4.05 per cent of revenue; she objected to its shape. The 480 seats in the heaviest five per cent each consumed ₹977.73 of model spend against ₹2,400 of revenue, beside ₹143.78 for the average seat — and Ekatva's largest renewal, a 340-seat firm in Chennai, sat in that band.

Four days later, on Monday 9 February, Oviya Easwaran met a worse version in Hyderabad. She is chief product officer at Ojaswi Learning Network, a fictional exam-preparation app with 1.1 crore monthly active users, of whom 3,40,000 pay ₹249 a month — ₹8.466 crore of monthly subscription revenue. Its doubt-solving assistant answers 3,92,92,000 questions a month. On 23 January, Ekta Odedra in analytics reconciled the usage records against the January forecast and found it had assumed every question looked like an English one. The true run-rate was ₹10.73 crore a month, or 126.7 per cent of what paying users paid. Both had eight weeks: Ekatva's pricing committee met on Thursday 2 April, Ojaswi's board on Monday 6 April.

2. The idea, and the four camps

Adding an LLM feature means sending assembled text to a language model across an application programming interface and building product behaviour on what returns. A prompt is the complete text sent on one call; the model holds no memory between calls, so all it must know travels every time. A token is the billing unit, a fragment of characters, and input and output are priced separately — output dearer, because generating is sequential while reading is parallel.

The invention solved an economic problem. Until about 2018, language capability needed a research team, labelled data and months of work; transformers from 2017 and the inference APIs that followed from 2020 replaced that fixed cost with a variable one. Hence this page's subject: building a language feature collapsed to days of work, while running it became a per-call charge that scales with success. A feature that works too well can bankrupt the line that owns it.

Four camps disagree about what follows. The orchestration camp holds that the model is a utility and value sits in workflow, data and distribution; it signs "train nothing until an evaluation set shows the hosted ceiling", and refuses "model choice is a moat". The systems camp holds that the model is an unreliable component and quality comes from scaffolding — retrieval, constrained output, verification, routing; it signs "scaffolding beats model selection", and refuses "a better model removes the need for verification". The weights camp holds that at scale you must own or adapt a model for cost, latency and residency; it signs "at 4 crore calls a month, inference economics justify a fine-tuned small model", and refuses "prices will fall fast enough to wait". The frontier camp holds that scaffolding depreciates because the next release deletes it; it signs "prompt engineering is a depreciating asset", and refuses "optimise cost before the frontier stops moving". Ekansh Oak, who leads applied machine learning at Ekatva, was a weights man with the scar tissue to prove it; Odhav Elavia, Ojaswi's chief technology officer, was a systems man who had never fine-tuned anything.

3. Mechanics: the call, the prefix and the meter

Figure 1 shows one Ekatva call drawn to scale by tokens. The illustrative prices used throughout, no real provider's, are: large model input ₹420 per million tokens and output ₹1,680; cached input re-read at ₹42, one-tenth of input; a cache write at ₹525, 1.25 times input; a small model at ₹70 input and ₹280 output, one-sixth of the large; embeddings at ₹14.

Two steps are usually implicit, and both decide the money. The first is context assembly: code, not the model, chooses what to send, and Ekatva's assembler spends a fixed ceiling on whatever has the highest marginal value.

The second is caching, the only nearly-free lever here. Providers hold the computed state of an unchanged prefix and re-read it cheaply. The prefix must be byte-identical and come first, which makes prompt ordering architectural rather than stylistic; Ekatva reordered its assembler in January 2025 so the stable blocks lead. Writes cost more than reading fresh, and entries expire: logs showed one write per twelve calls, so it amortises at ₹5.25 ÷ 12 = ₹0.4375 a call.

From ₹5.4775 the business arithmetic follows. Logs showed 2.4 calls per notice, counting verification retries and reviewer regenerations, so a notice costs 2.4 × ₹5.4775 = ₹13.146. At 1,05,000 notices a month that is 2,52,000 calls and ₹13,80,330. Uncached it would have been ₹22,22,640, or ₹22.23 lakh: 6.52 per cent of revenue rather than 4.05. Eknath Ovhal's time study found manual drafting took 70 minutes and reviewing a draft 11, so each accepted draft saves 59 minutes at a loaded ₹9 a minute, or ₹531 — forty times its cost.

4. The conditions, stated as tests

Five claims must hold. The task is text-to-text with a bounded acceptance standard: true at Ekatva, where an accountant signs every reply, and at Ojaswi, where a wrong step is visible but not dangerous. Value per call exceeds cost per call by a margin that survives the retry multiplier: Ekatva's ratio is 531 ÷ 13.146 = 40.4 to one, while Ojaswi's free user generates no rupee, so its case rests on retention and cost must reach paise. Failure is visible and recoverable. The context you need fits a prompt you can afford: the binding constraint is usually your cost and rate-limit budget, not the context window. You can measure acceptance, which needs an evaluation set.

The idea actively misleads in two cases. Where the right answer is a lookup with one correct value — a balance, a price — a model buys a probability of being wrong in exchange for nothing, and the right engineering is a query. And where per-call cost is small but the consequential cost of a wrong answer is unbounded, the arithmetic flatters the decision: ₹5.4775 is irrelevant beside the penalty for a misquoted section in a filed reply.

5. Edge cases and organisational seams

In a multi-product company the model bill arrives as one invoice and the products as separate profit and loss statements. Ojaswi's three surfaces shared one quota of 90,00,000 input tokens a minute. At the blended prompt size of 3,700 tokens that serves 90,00,000 ÷ 3,700 = 2,432.4 calls a minute against an evening peak of 7,200 doubts a minute: short by a factor of 2.96. The limit is denominated in tokens, so shortening a prompt buys throughput as well as rupees.

In a two-sided setting the generated text crosses the seam, and the cheaper side's economics do not govern it. In a regulated setting the question is lawful processing: under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sending a client's ledger extract to a third-party model needs a basis, a contract and a retention position, and Ewa Olszewska, Ekatva's infrastructure engineer in Warsaw, forced a regional endpoint at a nine per cent premium. For hardware, an on-device model has near-zero marginal cost and a fixed engineering cost, so break-even is a volume, not a rate. In AI-native products the bill is cost of goods sold.

The seam mature companies manage rather than describe is ownership: Ekatva's model bill sits in Ela Edulji's budget, while the reviewer minutes those drafts consume sit on the client's payroll.

6. What separates an expert

Tokens are not words, and Indic scripts are expensive

Tokenisers are fitted to their training corpus, so Devanagari or Telugu script fragments into far more tokens than its English equivalent. Exhibit 3 is Ekta Odedra's audit. The tell-tale sign of a team that has not learned this is a cost model with a single average prompt size. Local tokeniser estimates also drift from what the provider charges, so experts reconcile the invoice to logged usage records monthly.

Exhibit 3. Cost is input tokens × ₹420 ÷ 1,000,000 plus output tokens × ₹1,680 ÷ 1,000,000. The contribution column is share × cost and sums to ₹2.7300, which is also the cost of the weighted-mean counts 3,700 and 700. The English-only ₹1.932 understated the mean by 29.23 per cent, a factor of 1.4130: ₹7.59 crore forecast against ₹10.73 crore actual, a gap of ₹3.14 crore a month.

Output length is a latency lever and only a minor cost lever

Generation is sequential, so latency scales with output tokens while cost is dominated by the larger input. Ekatva's 1,250 output tokens at 45 tokens a second take 27.78 seconds; prefilling 16,000 input tokens at 9,000 a second adds 1.78, giving 29.56 seconds. A warm cache cuts prefill to 0.67 and the total to 28.44, a 3.8 per cent gain. Cutting output to 700 tokens, down 44 per cent, cuts the total to 16.22 seconds, 43.0 per cent faster, but cuts cost only ₹0.924, 16.87 per cent of ₹5.4775. Shorten answers to save time, not money.

Calls per completed task, not calls per click

The multiplier of 2.4 is the most load-bearing number in Ekatva's model, and a product variable: tighten the verifier and it rises. A cost regression usually arrives as a rising multiplier, not a rising price.

Rate chains compound, and escalation is paid twice

In Ojaswi's router, 20 per cent of doubts are served from a cache of canonical answers and 80 per cent go to the small model, of which 31.25 per cent fail the verifier. The escalated share of all doubts is 80 × 31.25 = 25 per cent, not 31.25, and those pay for the small call, the verifier call and the large call. Latency is paid twice too: 4.54 seconds of small model, 0.4 of verifier and 15.97 of large model is 20.91 seconds, 30.9 per cent worse than going straight to the large model.

Caching hides prompt bloat, so bloat accelerates

Between February and August 2025 Ekatva's statutory extract block grew from 4,700 to 6,200 tokens as circulars were appended after each incident. Being cached, the extra 1,500 tokens cost ₹0.128625 a call, which at the current 2,52,000 calls is ₹32,413.50 a month. Uncached the same creep would have cost ₹0.63 a call and ₹1,58,760 a month. Caching absorbed 79.6 per cent of the signal, so nobody noticed until retrieval quality fell.

Model upgrades are breaking changes dressed as gifts

A new version changes format, verbosity and refusal behaviour. Pin versions, keep a deprecation calendar, and re-run the evaluation set and the cost measurement on every upgrade: a model cleverer per token is often dearer per task.

Temperature zero is not determinism

Batching, expert routing and floating-point non-associativity mean identical inputs can give different outputs. A team can promise a regulated customer not reproducibility but a logged input, a logged output and a verifier.

Success raises the total bill while cutting the unit cost

As acceptance rose, drafts per active seat went from 8.2 to 10.9375, up 33.4 per cent, lifting the bill from ₹10.35 lakh to ₹13.80 lakh even as cost per accepted draft fell. Budget alarms therefore belong per user and per task: a global threshold cannot tell a leak from a triumph.

The evaluation set appreciates; the prompt depreciates

Prompts are rewritten with every model change. The set of real inputs with agreed answers survives them all, and alone makes the frontier camp's argument testable rather than a matter of taste.

7. By product type and by stage

The real differences lie in who pays per unit and how it relates to a call. Exhibit 4 sets the two side by side, Ojaswi's rows using the post-router ₹1.1095 a doubt of section 8.
