The B2B pattern is that a seat price caps model spend per seat, so the distribution matters more than the mean and the answer is a fair-use allowance, not a cheaper model. The consumer pattern is that most units pay nothing, leaving caching, routing and a usage ceiling. Stage decides whether optimising is rational at all. At ₹5.4775 a call, 60,000 calls a month costs ₹3.2865 lakh and a ten per cent cut is worth ₹0.3287 lakh, less than an engineer-week; 24,00,000 calls costs ₹131.46 lakh and the cut is worth ₹13.146 lakh, which funds a small team; 4,20,00,000 calls costs ₹2,300.55 lakh and the cut is worth ₹230.055 lakh, which funds a negotiated contract. Only the rationality of optimising changes.

8. Three worked examples

Ekatva: reordering the prompt

Reordering the assembler so the stable blocks lead took Ekatva from ₹8.82 to ₹5.4775 a call — ₹22.23 lakh to ₹13.80 lakh a month, saving ₹8.42 lakh for three engineer-weeks, with no model change and no quality trade-off.

Ojaswi: the router

Ojaswi's router was piloted from 16 February. Every doubt is embedded, at 100 tokens and ₹0.0014, and matched against a cache of canonical answers; 20 per cent hit. The rest go to the small model at ₹0.455 a call, checked by a verifier at ₹0.077; failures escalate to the large model at ₹2.730.

Ekatva's fine-tune: the one that failed

Exhibit 6. Reviewer minutes are expected values: path A is 0.88 × 11 + 0.12 × 70 = 18.08; path C is 0.71 × 34 + 0.29 × 18.08 = 29.3832. Each fully loaded figure is model cost plus minutes × ₹9 and adds exactly as shown. Path C cut Ekatva's model cost 42.3 per cent while raising fully loaded cost 54.7 per cent.

That divergence is the lesson. Ekatva's dashboard, built from Ekatva's invoice, showed a 42.3 per cent win; the ₹101.73 of extra reviewer time per notice landed on the client firms. On 18,900 notices a month that was ₹19.23 lakh of their time, which with ₹10.5 lakh of build makes ₹29.73 lakh spent against ₹1.05 lakh of fees saved. It ran five weeks and was withdrawn on Monday 6 October 2025, after two firms abandoned the button. The sign had been in the logs throughout: edit distance between draft and sent reply. The recovery, shipped 15 January 2026, kept the fine-tuned model only for the three classes where acceptance matched at 86 per cent and review took 12 minutes — 31 per cent of volume — for a blended ₹158.94 against ₹175.87, a 9.63 per cent gain.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Costing from the demo. Sign: the first invoice exceeds forecast by more than half. Diagnostic: what is the mean of the logged usage records, by language and task type? Caught late, it is a repriced product.

Unbounded user input. Sign: a long tail in the input-token histogram. One client's 94-page assessment order ran to 56,400 tokens in place of the usual 2,900, taking fresh input to 59,500 and the call to ₹27.9475, 5.10 times normal. Diagnostic: what is the 99th percentile input, and what truncates it?

Retry storms. Sign: calls per task spikes while tasks stay flat. On Friday 6 March 2026 a provider throttle plus retries without jitter took Ekatva's multiplier from 2.4 to 5.1 for forty minutes: about 353.5 notices, 954.5 extra calls, ₹5,228.52.

Verifier drift. Sign: acceptance rises while complaints also rise. Diagnostic: when was the verifier last checked against human judgement?

Evaluation-set overfitting. Sign: the set is small, unchanged for months, and every change improves it. Diagnostic: refresh it monthly from production.

Silent model deprecation. Sign: a pinned version with an end-of-life date nobody owns. Caught late, it forces a migration re-running every prompt and price.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The weights position, steelmanned: at scale, inference is cost of goods sold, and a company that does not control it cannot defend its gross margin or its latency and is hostage to a supplier's pricing and deprecation choices. Its evidence is section 7: at ₹2,300.55 lakh a month, a fifth off the bill is a strategic asset. It is wrong if adaptation cannot hold quality at task level, as Exhibit 6 showed for eleven of fourteen notice classes.

The orchestration position: every rupee spent on weights is a rupee not spent on the workflow, data and distribution customers renew for, and model quality converges while workflow advantage compounds. Its evidence is Ekatva's two largest wins — a reordering worth ₹8.42 lakh a month and a 59-minute saving — which touched no model. It is wrong where a tuned model reaches a plateau no prompt can reach.

The frontier position: scaffolding built for today's model is written off by the next release, so thin integration and patience are optimal. Its evidence is that whole prompt techniques became obsolete within two years. It is wrong wherever scaffolding encodes what models never supply: your retrieval corpus, your acceptance standard, your audit trail. Odhav Elavia's rejoinder was that a verifier is policy, and policy does not depreciate.

The fourth disagreement is about when unit cost deserves attention. One camp holds that optimising before product-market fit destroys the learning rate; the other, that negative unit economics at launch establish a usage pattern you cannot withdraw. Ojaswi is the experiment: shipping first cost it a quarter at 126.7 per cent of subscription revenue, but it now knows which 20 per cent of doubts are cacheable. A team that optimised first would have guessed.

11. What mastery looks like

Four habits. They quote cost per completed task, never per call, and can name the retry multiplier. They ask for the input-token distribution, split by language, not the mean. They treat prompt order as architectural and know what fraction is a stable prefix. And they keep separate the three questions amateurs merge: is the output good enough, what does it cost us, and what does it cost whoever checks it. The third caught Ekatva out, because dashboards are built from invoices.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Thursday 2 April 2026 Ela Edulji did not propose a cheaper model. She proposed a fair-use allowance of 30 notices per seat per month with overage at ₹45 a notice, a little over three times the ₹13.146 it costs, and kept the fine-tuned model on its three classes. Her argument was that a feature returning ₹531 of client time for ₹13.146 of spend should be sold harder, not throttled, and that heavy seats at 40.7 per cent of revenue were a pricing defect.

On Monday 6 April Oviya Easwaran took the router to full rollout, moving the bill from ₹10.73 crore to ₹4.36 crore, and accepted the 30.9 per cent latency penalty on the escalated quarter rather than weaken the verifier. She deferred Orla O'Donnell's proposal, from Dublin, to distil a model for Telugu and Devanagari traffic until per-class acceptance numbers existed, and set the company's first per-user ceiling, at 60 doubts a month.

Three questions. If the allowance moves heavy firms onto overage, what happens to the multiplier of 2.4, and which way does that move the ₹45? Ojaswi's router saves 59.36 per cent of cost and makes a quarter of answers 30.9 per cent slower: what would tell you whether that damaged retention, and why can the invoice never tell you? Exhibit 6 shows Ekatva winning on its invoice while losing on the client's clock: which figure in your product behaves that way, and who owns it?

13. Going deeper

AI-assisted building covers the tooling these features are built with, and How LLMs work, for PMs explains why prefill is parallel and decoding sequential — the physical reason output is dearer and slower. AI cost-to-serve and pricing turns ₹1.1095 a doubt and ₹5.4775 a call into allowances and margins. What's different when the feature is a model treats acceptance and non-determinism as product properties, and AI bias and fairness matters because Exhibit 3's language mix is also a quality distribution. Moats in the AI era adjudicates the four camps. AI infrastructure basics for PMs, Cloud infrastructure basics and Databases, storage and caching cover quotas, regional endpoints and caching; APIs and integration basics, How web and mobile apps work, Data modelling for PMs and Reading an architecture diagram are the fluency to argue about Figure 1 with its author.
case40v1-tech.llm.feature:
Maatram: What It Costs to Write a Listing

A case on putting a model into the product — and on who pays for every call it makes.

1. Sunday night, Guindy

At nine in the evening on Sunday 25 October 2026, Yadunandan Gangadharan was still in the Guindy office of Maatram Catalogue Systems, with a board deck of nineteen slides open in front of him. Eighteen were finished. The nineteenth was titled Recommendation and was empty.

The board met at eleven the next morning. It wanted one line from its chief product officer: whether Maatram would put a language model inside its product, and on whose bill. The feature had a name inside the company — the writer — and a demonstration that never failed. Feed it a supplier's spec sheet and it returned a marketplace listing in English, Hindi, Tamil and Telugu, in the brand's own tone, with thirty-four attribute fields filled in. Customers had been asking since March.

What Gangadharan did not have was a cost he was willing to defend in front of six directors. His engineering head's figure was ₹4.98 a listing. The provider's invoice for the pilot window, reconciled three weeks earlier, implied ₹6.60. At September's volume those two numbers came to ₹30.88 lakh and ₹40.92 lakh a month against revenue of ₹3.10 crore, and either of them broke a commitment the board had put in writing to its investors.

The weekly global call had been fixed for seven that evening, IST. Berlin's clocks had gone back that morning, so it reached Yojana Geevarghese at half past two in the afternoon rather than half past three (Figure 2). It had ended an hour ago without agreement.

2. The company, and a decision taken in 2021

Maatram was founded in Chennai in 2016 by Yogalakshmi Gopinathan and two colleagues from a catalogue services firm. It sells catalogue operations software to brands and marketplace sellers: it ingests supplier data in whatever shape it arrives, normalises attributes, writes and versions listing content, and publishes to Flipkart, Meesho, Nykaa, JioMart and the ONDC network. In September 2026 it had 310 paying accounts at an average of ₹1.00 lakh a month — ₹3.10 crore of monthly revenue and ₹37.20 crore of annualised revenue. Gross margin ran at 74 per cent and the company earned about ₹18.00 lakh of monthly EBITDA. A Series B of ₹86 crore closed in November 2024; ₹61 crore of it was still in the bank on 30 September 2026.

In 2021 the founders made the decision that now bounds every option. Rather than license a commercial taxonomy, they built their own — 1,100 hand-written category rules, maintained by a 34-person team in Chennai, which the company calls the grammar. It is why marketplaces accept Maatram's feeds with little rejection, and it is why nothing the writer produces may reach a channel without passing it. The grammar covers categories accounting for 68 per cent of the SKUs on the platform. For the remaining 32 per cent there is nothing to validate against.

3. The industry

Maatram's market is the long tail of Indian sellers and the mid-sized D2C brands above them. A seller who lists badly is not fined; the listing is simply suppressed, and in a festive week suppression is the whole loss. The Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules require net quantity, country of origin and the importer's name to appear on an e-commerce listing; packaged food carries FSSAI particulars and several goods carry BIS marks. A fluent sentence with the wrong net quantity is a compliance exposure, not a typo, and the liability sits with the seller who published it — Maatram's customer.

Competition comes from three directions: catalogue tools bundling model-written copy at no charge, the marketplaces' own free listing assistants, and the agencies that still do the work by hand in Coimbatore and Surat at ₹18 to ₹40 a SKU. Abroad, Maatram's exposure is concentrated: Munfarid Retail Group in Dubai, at ₹2.64 crore a year, is its largest single account, and the Gulf business is why Arabic keeps appearing in sales conversations even though no version of the writer produces it. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is cited in every procurement questionnaire the company receives.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In March 2026 Munfarid asked for generated listing copy in English and Arabic. Maatram said it would look at it. On 14 April a team under Yuthika Gudigar in Bengaluru had a working prototype in nine days, calling a frontier model through the provider's India-region endpoint. The board, on 11 May, asked for a plan by the third quarter.

The pilot ran from 1 to 28 August across eight accounts and 38,400 SKUs, most of them Onam ranges for home and kitchen brands. On 3 September Gudigar presented the economics: ₹4.98 a SKU, built up from logged prompt sizes (Exhibit 1) at the provider's published rupee card (Exhibit 2). A blind editor audit followed from 7 to 18 September (Exhibit 4). On 30 September the platform closed its largest month on record, 6.20 lakh SKUs (Exhibit 3).

Three things have since turned out differently. On 6 October Yagnesh Gatty, reconciling the provider's statement in Pune, found Maatram had been billed, for the pilot window alone, 638.20 million tokens where the model of the pipeline predicted 476.16 million — ₹6.60 a SKU rather than ₹4.98 (Exhibit 5). On 9 October Yudhajit Gurukkal's note from Toronto argued that the audit's headline quality gap was indistinguishable from noise while its attribute-error gap was not. And on 13 October Geevarghese's study of eleven editors reported that what they wanted was not a draft at all.

None of the eight pilot accounts was among the 24 accounts that generate 61 per cent of platform volume and 38 per cent of revenue.

5. The people

Yadunandan Gangadharan, chief product officer, Chennai, owns the recommendation. He has argued for a year that Maatram sells accuracy, not prose. He is not saying that in a corridor in September he told the sales head the writer would be included in the January plans, and that his own objective for the year is feature adoption, which a priced add-on would depress.

Yogalakshmi Gopinathan, co-founder and chief executive, Chennai, wants the writer in the 2027 price sheet and the quarterly EBITDA commitment intact, in that order. She has not told the executive team that a Series C conversation is live and that a revenue line attributable to the feature would matter in it.

Yuthika Gudigar, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru, wants the frontier model shipped through the API within three weeks. Her position is that a weak first release cannot be undone and that running GPUs is not a business Maatram should enter. She has not said that her ₹4.98 came from three days of the pilot that she chose as clean, or that she saw the August invoice total a fortnight before Gatty reconciled it.

Yagnesh Gatty, principal engineer, platform, Pune, found the gap and wants the open-weights model hosted in Mumbai. He is right that the Munfarid contract bars the API today. He is not saying that he spent ₹2.50 lakh of the platform budget on a two-GPU trial without telling product, and that a Mumbai cluster would be the largest thing he has ever owned.

Yojana Geevarghese, design lead for content, Berlin, says the feature is aimed at the wrong unit of work: editors do not want a finished listing, they want the three fields that differ from the last version flagged for approval. Her study covered eleven editors, all from two accounts, both of them in the grammar-covered categories, which she mentions rarely.

Yudhajit Gurukkal, staff data scientist, Toronto, wants an evaluation harness and two months before any price is published. He has not stressed that he assembled the evaluation set from grammar-covered categories, so it under-measures exactly the 32 per cent of SKUs where errors concentrate, and that he has asked twice for two headcount.

Yashpreet Ganiga, head of customer success for Asia and the Gulf, Singapore, reports three accounts worth ₹1.14 crore of annual revenue as at risk without the writer and wants it included free. Two of those three also logged an unrelated service breach in July that is still open, which does not appear in her risk note.

Yograj Gonsalves, senior vice-president of sales for North America and the Gulf, New Jersey, wants it bundled and announced. His largest prospect, Melur Commerce, is an aggregator that would add 2.40 lakh SKUs a month — 39 per cent on top of September's platform volume — for ₹2.40 lakh a month. He has not worked out what that account would cost to serve.

7. Voices

From the 6 October thread, after the reconciliation:

Gatty: Two things explain it, not one. Regenerations give 1.284 and mean-length spec sheets another 1.044. Multiply them on the unrounded figures: 1.341, against the invoice's 1.340.
Gudigar: A regeneration re-runs the English pass, not the translations. That is 1.140, and the bill is still 17.6 per cent above what your 1.140 explains. Two numbers that multiply to the answer are not a diagnosis.

From Gurukkal's note of 9 October:

The difference on no-edit publication is 30 SKUs in 1,200. The models disagreed on 342, so the standard error on that difference is the square root of 342 over 1,200, which is 1.54 points. The gap is 2.5 points: 1.6 standard errors. It is not a finding. The attribute-error difference is 2.75 points with a standard error of 0.57, and that one is real — and it is the one that puts a wrong net quantity on a listing.

From the Sunday call, as minuted:

Gonsalves: Every loss this year cited AI copy. Every single one.
Ganiga: Four of the nine, by the deal-desk notes. Three were price.
Geevarghese: May I ask why the choice in front of us is a model and not a workflow? My editors do not want a listing written. They want to be told which three fields changed.
Gopinathan: The price sheet goes out on the first of December either way.

8. The options as Gangadharan sees them

Option A ships the whole pipeline on the frontier model to every account within three weeks, included in the plan. It is what Gudigar wants, it answers Ganiga's three at-risk accounts, and at September volume it costs ₹30.88 lakh a month, 9.96 per cent of revenue, which turns ₹18.00 lakh of monthly EBITDA into a loss of ₹12.88 lakh.

Option B keeps the frontier model for English and moves the three translations to the small model, at ₹2.30 a SKU. It is the only line in Exhibit 6 that leaves EBITDA positive. It also puts the weaker model on Hindi, Tamil and Telugu, where no adequacy review has yet come back. Gurukkal has pointed out that the attribute block stays with the frontier model in B, so Exhibit 4's error gap is not evidence about what B's translations would do.

Option C sends everything that can wait 24 hours to the batch endpoint at half the rate. The share that can wait was 62 per cent in August; nobody has measured it in a festive month, when a seller's reason for refreshing a listing is that the sale starts on Friday.

Option D hosts an open-weights model in Mumbai. It is the only option Munfarid's contract permits without 45 days' notice, it removes the per-call bill, and at September volume it costs almost exactly what option A costs — while at the twelve-month mean the same reservation costs ₹7.32 a SKU, 47 per cent more than A.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board sits at eleven on Monday 26 October. The 2027 price sheet goes to customers on 1 December, and accounts carrying ₹4.30 crore of annual revenue renew on 1 January. Munfarid's contract requires 45 days' written notice and approval before any new sub-processor touches its data, so a Gulf go-live on 15 January needs notice served by 1 December; Minnal Electricals' procurement has the same clause. The investor letter commits Maatram to positive EBITDA in every quarter from the one ending 31 December 2026; three months of option A would put the March quarter at ₹38.64 lakh negative. Headcount is frozen until the first quarter of 2027-28, so Gurukkal's harness and Gatty's cluster compete for the same two engineers. The provider's rupee card holds until 31 March 2027 and the agreement is month to month on both sides.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Read Exhibit 1. Which parts of a call drive the ₹4.98, and which of them could a product manager change without touching the model?
  2. Exhibit 5 shows a bill one-third larger than the model of the pipeline. What would you measure this week to decide between Gatty's explanation and Gudigar's?
  3. Exhibit 3 offers two volume bases and Exhibit 6 costs the options at both. Which base belongs in a price sheet that will be in force for a year, and why?
  4. Gurukkal calls one quality gap noise and one real. If he is right on both counts, what does that imply for which model goes where in the pipeline?
  5. The 24 largest accounts generate 61 per cent of SKU volume and 38 per cent of revenue. What does that mismatch do to each option in Exhibit 6, and to Gonsalves's Melur Commerce deal?
  6. It is Monday morning. What do you do, what do you tell the board, and what would have to be true for you to be wrong?

Gangadharan closed the deck at half past eleven. The nineteenth slide still said Recommendation. The two numbers he could not reconcile — ₹4.98 and ₹6.60 — were still sitting one above the other in his notebook, where he had drawn a box around both of them.
exp20v2-tech.llm.feature:
Adding an LLM Feature

What it takes to put a language model inside a product, and what each call costs

1. Tuesday, 14 July: a pilot that worked

Aparna Chitnis, head of product at Chitrakoot Home Services Network, had a good problem and a bad spreadsheet. Chitrakoot is a fictional marketplace, modelled loosely on Indian platforms such as Urban Company, connecting households in eleven cities with electricians, plumbers and appliance technicians. Its support desk of 140 agents handles about 1,20,000 tickets a month: a customer in Pune reports that the technician never arrived, or a customer in Lucknow disputes a charge for a part she says was not fitted.

Three weeks earlier, Aparna's team had put a large language model (LLM, a software system trained on enormous amounts of text that produces fluent text in response to text it is given) behind a single button in the agent console. When an agent opened a ticket, the button drafted a reply. Forty agents used it for three weeks. Chirag Apte, who runs support operations, timed them: average handling time fell from 6 minutes to 4.

The decision on the table was whether to roll the button out to all 140 agents, and the review meeting was on 28 July, fourteen days away. The obstacle came from Charulata Bhosale in finance, who had read the first invoice from the model provider and asked a plain question: what will this cost at full volume, and what happens to that number when the product changes? Aparna realised she could not answer it. She knew the feature worked, but not why the invoice had one line for "input tokens" and another, dearer line for "output tokens". If she was wrong by a factor of two, a feature that saved money would quietly cost more than it saved.

2. The idea: a model call is a metered purchase

Adding an LLM feature means sending text to a model over an application programming interface (API, a defined way for one piece of software to ask another to do work) and showing, checking or acting on the text that comes back. The model is usually rented from a provider such as OpenAI, Google or Anthropic, or run on the company's own servers. What the product team builds is everything around the call: what goes in, what is done with what comes out, and what happens when it goes wrong.

Two vocabulary items carry most of the weight. A prompt is the complete text sent to the model on a single call. It is not just the user's question; in a product it is assembled by code from several parts. A token is the unit in which models read and write text: a chunk of characters, roughly three-quarters of an English word. Providers bill by the token, with separate prices for tokens sent in (input) and tokens generated (output).

This pattern, text in and metered text out through an API, became commercially routine only from about 2020, when providers began selling access to large models by the call. It solved a specific problem: building a language-capable system once required a research team, a labelled dataset and months. Renting one reduced the first version of a feature to an afternoon. The cost of building collapsed; the cost of running became a per-use charge that scales with every interaction.

The sentence Aparna could repeat in the meeting without sounding glib was this: every call has a price set by the size of what we send and what we ask for back, so the feature's cost is the number of calls multiplied by the tokens in each, and the product design decides both.

3. How it works, step by step

Figure 1 shows the path of one Chitrakoot call.

First, the code assembles the prompt. The model keeps no memory between calls, so everything it needs to know must be sent every time. At Chitrakoot the prompt has four parts: a fixed system prompt (standing instructions on tone, what the agent may promise, and how to format a reply), excerpts of the refund and cancellation policy retrieved for this ticket, the earlier messages in the ticket thread, and the customer's latest message. The implicit step is retrieval: choosing which policy paragraphs to include is a search problem that sets both quality and prompt size.

Second, the call goes out with settings. A maximum output length caps the output bill. A temperature setting, which controls how much randomness the model uses when choosing each next word, is usually low for support replies.

Third, the model reads the whole prompt and generates the reply one token at a time. The provider returns the text together with a usage record stating how many input and output tokens were charged. That record is the ground truth for cost.

Fourth, the code checks the output before anyone sees it: is it in the expected format, does it quote a refund amount that matches the order, does it include a banned promise? A failed check triggers a retry, which is a second paid call, or a fallback to a blank reply box. Retries are why calls per ticket exceed one. Plan for the occasional unusable answer.

4. A worked example: what one call costs

Avinash Chaudhari, the engineering manager, pulled the pilot logs, and Annelies Claes, a machine-learning engineer in Amsterdam, confirmed the rates. For this page we use illustrative prices, not a real provider's price list: input tokens cost ₹250 per million, output tokens ₹1,000 per million. Output is four times as dear as input because generating is more work than reading. The pilot logs showed an average call sending 3,000 input tokens and returning 350 output tokens.

Prompt componentInput tokensCost at ₹250 per million (₹)
System prompt6000.150
Retrieved policy excerpts9000.225
Ticket history1,1000.275
Customer's latest message4000.100
Total input3,0000.750
Output (draft reply), at ₹1,000 per million3500.350
Total cost of one call3,3501.100

Table 1. Cost of one call. Each cost is tokens x price / 1,000,000; for example 3,000 x 250 / 1,000,000 = ₹0.75.

Input: 3,000 tokens multiplied by ₹250 and divided by a million is ₹0.75. Output: 350 multiplied by ₹1,000 and divided by a million is ₹0.35. One call costs ₹1.10. The logs also showed an average of 1.5 calls per ticket, counting retries and cases where the agent asked for a second draft. So a ticket costs 1.5 x ₹1.10 = ₹1.65, and 1,20,000 tickets a month cost 1,20,000 x ₹1.65 = ₹1,98,000, or ₹1.98 lakh.

Now the benefit side. Chirag's two minutes saved per ticket, at a loaded agent cost of ₹4 a minute, are worth ₹8 a ticket, or ₹9.60 lakh a month across 1,20,000 tickets if every agent uses the draft every time. They will not. At 60 per cent usage the saving is 9.60 x 0.6 = ₹5.76 lakh. Net of model cost: ₹5.76 lakh minus ₹1.98 lakh leaves ₹3.78 lakh a month.

The second pass changes one input. Suppose the model is given the whole conversation, adding 2,000 tokens of history. Input rises to 5,000 tokens: 5,000 x 250 / 1,000,000 = ₹1.25. Output is unchanged at ₹0.35, so a call costs ₹1.60, up from ₹1.10, a rise of about 45 per cent from a 67 per cent increase in input tokens. The monthly bill becomes 1,80,000 x ₹1.60 = ₹2,88,000, or ₹2.88 lakh, an extra ₹90,000 a month. The net at 60 per cent usage falls to ₹5.76 lakh minus ₹2.88 lakh = ₹2.88 lakh. Figure 2 compares the two.

Figure 2 shows where the money goes: most of it is input, because the prompt is long and the answer short. Teams that shorten answers are optimising the smaller bar.

ScenarioCost per call (₹)Monthly model cost (₹ lakh)Net at 60% usage (₹ lakh)
Pilot prompt1.101.983.78
Full history1.602.882.88

Table 2. Both rows use 1,80,000 calls a month and ₹5.76 lakh of agent-time saving.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Tokens are not words, and language matters

A token is about three-quarters of an English word, but text in Hindi, Tamil or Bengali script is split into more, smaller tokens. Suppose a 400-token English message becomes 1,000 tokens in Hindi. Input is then 3,600 tokens, costing ₹0.90, and with ₹0.35 of output a call costs ₹1.25. An English-only cost model understates the bill.

The model does not remember

It does not learn from each ticket; whatever it appears to remember is text your code re-sent. That is why history inflates cost.

Calls per task is the hidden multiplier

Retries, regenerations, a second call to check the first, and chained steps all multiply the bill. A feature that costs ₹1.10 a call but needs 3 calls costs ₹3.30. Measure calls per completed task, not calls per click.

Quality is a separate question from cost

A cheaper model may need longer prompts or more retries to reach the same quality. The unit of comparison is cost per acceptable output, which requires an evaluation set: a collection of real inputs with agreed good answers, run against each option.

What this arithmetic cannot tell you

It cannot tell you whether drafts are accurate, whether a customer was misled, or whether sending ticket text to a third party is permitted. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sharing customer data with a provider is a compliance question.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace, early-stage and large

In a consumer product the call is usually made on behalf of millions of users, most paying nothing. Cost per call then becomes cost per free user per month, and the discipline is capping use, caching common answers and choosing the smallest model that passes the evaluation set. In B2B products the buyer often pays per seat, so the question is whether heavy users, who might make thousands of calls, exhaust the margin earned on their seat.

A marketplace such as Chitrakoot has two sides: text generated for one side is read by the other, so a draft promising a refund the technician disputes creates a conflict. The check step in Figure 1 carries more weight there.

Size changes the economics and the process. An early-stage company, with perhaps 20,000 calls a month, will spend about ₹22,000 a month on a model (20,000 x ₹1.10) and should not waste an engineer's month optimising it; speed of learning matters more. A large company at 20 crore calls a month pays about ₹22 crore at ₹1.10 per call, so a 10 per cent token saving is worth ₹2.2 crore and justifies a dedicated team, negotiated provider contracts and perhaps a self-hosted model.

7. Common mistakes

Costing from the demo

Symptom: the forecast is far below the first month's invoice. Misunderstanding: the demo used short, clean inputs, while production sends long histories and retried calls. Cheapest diagnostic: log the usage record for 200 real calls and compute the average, not the best case.

Counting clicks instead of calls

Symptom: the bill grows faster than usage. Misunderstanding: one click triggers several calls. Diagnostic: divide logged calls by completed tasks for one week.

Optimising output length first

Symptom: engineers trim replies and the invoice barely moves. Misunderstanding: output is the smaller portion of cost when prompts are long. Diagnostic: draw the Figure 2 split for your own feature before choosing a lever.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the same decision looks like this. Before the review, the team has a one-page cost model with both token prices, measured average tokens, calls per ticket, and a Hindi-language sensitivity case. Every call logs its usage record by ticket type. A 300-ticket evaluation set exists, and the output check blocks the three worst failure types. The rollout is staged, with a spending alert at 120 per cent of forecast. Finance sees a range, not a point: ₹1.98 lakh to ₹2.88 lakh a month, with the product decision that moves between the two named.

9. Closing: what Aparna decided

On 28 July Aparna asked for approval for a staged rollout using the pilot prompt, not the full-history version. Her reasoning was arithmetic. Full history raised cost 45 per cent and cut the net benefit from ₹3.78 lakh to ₹2.88 lakh a month at 60 per cent usage (nearly a quarter), and no one had shown it improved replies. She asked Annelies to test it on the evaluation set, and history would be added only where it measurably raised acceptance. Charulata accepted the range, with a monthly review.

To go further, read next how LLMs work, to understand why prompt length and output behave as they do, then AI cost-to-serve and pricing, which turns a per-call cost into a pricing decision.

Two questions to sit with. If your product doubled the tokens in each call and halved the calls per task, would your bill rise, fall or stay the same, and what would you need to know to be sure? And which part of your feature's cost would you most regret not having measured before launch?
case20v1-tech.llm.feature:
Cinnabar Desk: Drafting Replies with a Model

1. Opening

On Monday 19 October 2026, Keshavan Sukumaran, chief product officer of Cinnabar Desk, sat in the company's Kochi office with a one-page note from his engineering lead and a decision due by Friday 23 October. The note proposed a feature customers had requested since the summer: an assistant that reads a support ticket and drafts the agent's reply. The board would meet on 28 October, and the chairman wanted either a launch date within the quarter ending 31 December or a reason for waiting.

Sukumaran did not doubt the feature could be built; a prototype had worked within a fortnight, drafting sensible replies to tickets from a lender and a pharmacy chain. His question was narrower and harder. Which model should sit behind it, and who should pay for each call? Every draft would cost money that no earlier Cinnabar feature had cost, and the cost grew with every ticket a customer received. He had four days to turn a promising demonstration into a number the board could trust.

2. Company background

Cinnabar Desk, founded in Kochi in 2017, sells help-desk software to small and mid-sized Indian businesses: a shared inbox, email and WhatsApp ticketing, and a knowledge base. It had 1,500 paying accounts at an average of ₹14,000 a month, or ₹2.1 crore of monthly revenue. Customers included regional lenders, an online pharmacy chain and a Kerala tea exporter. Together they raised about 9,00,000 tickets a month, 600 per account.

The rivals were bigger. Freshworks and Zoho both marketed AI-assisted replies. Cinnabar competed on price, on support in Malayalam, Tamil and Hindi, and on keeping data in India, a point that mattered more since the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 made customers careful about where personal data travelled. Gross margin was near 70 per cent.

The company had grown without outside capital beyond a Kochi angel round, reaching its 1,500 accounts largely through referrals from accountants and agencies. Its 62 employees worked mainly from Kochi and Bengaluru, with a few specialists abroad, and the product team was small enough that Sukumaran still reviewed every pricing change himself. A feature that moved margins by several points would therefore reach him personally, and the board.

3. The situation

The prototype called a hosted large model through an API. Each call sends a prompt: standing instructions, the customer's thread, and three help-centre articles retrieved to ground the answer. The provider bills per token, a token being roughly three-quarters of a word, and charges four times as much for each output token as for each input token. Exhibit 1 shows what one draft contains and costs on the large model and on a smaller model from the same provider.

Exhibit 1. One draft: tokens and cost
ItemTokensLarge, ₹ per millionLarge, ₹ per draftSmall, ₹ per millionSmall, ₹ per draft
Input (instructions 500 + thread 2,500 + articles 3,000)6,0002501.50250.15
Output (the draft)4001,0000.401000.04
Total6,4001.900.19

Rates are the provider's list prices converted to rupees. Per-draft cost = tokens × rate ÷ 1,000,000.

Kiran Sebastian, the data scientist in Toronto, ran a two-week pilot at six customers, with 40 agents rating 400 drafts from each model (Exhibit 2). The large model was better. Sebastian cautioned that the 6-point gap in acceptance carried a standard error of 2.8 points, so it was real but modest. The wrong-policy rate mattered more to him: a draft that promised a refund the customer's policy did not allow was worse than a clumsy one, because tired agents tend to trust fluent text. The small model made that error twice as often, 18 times against 9, although both counts were small.

The small model also answered in 2.1 seconds against 6.2, which agents in the pilot said felt like the difference between a tool and a wait. Against that, Sebastian had observed that most of the small model's weaker drafts came on the longest threads, where the customer had written several times. He had not yet tested whether trimming the retrieved articles changed either model's accuracy, and said plainly that the pilot could not settle it.

Exhibit 2. Pilot results, 400 drafts per model
MeasureLargeSmall
Drafts sent as-is or lightly edited332 (83.0%)308 (77.0%)
Drafts with a wrong policy claim9 (2.25%)18 (4.5%)
Median time to draft6.2 s2.1 s

Percentages are of the 400 drafts each model produced, judged by agents on different tickets assigned at random.

4. The people

Kripa Shetty, engineering lead in Bengaluru, wanted the large model live at once. The prototype already worked, a weak first impression would be hard to undo, and she had no wish to run servers.

Karthika Salian, customer-success lead in Singapore, wanted the feature in every plan at no charge. Two prospects, a Chennai logistics firm and a Pune training company, would not sign without it, and she argued that a paid add-on would look like a rival's free feature plus a price tag. She reminded Sukumaran that customers compared Cinnabar with Freshworks and Zoho on a single page of a spreadsheet.

Kiran Sebastian wanted a longer test before any commitment. The weekly call ran at 8 a.m. in Toronto and 8 p.m. in Singapore, and he often said so when asked to decide quickly. He also pointed out that every pilot figure came from six customers, none of them among the largest accounts, whose threads ran longer.

5. The options

Exhibit 3 projects a month of running costs for each course, at 80 per cent of tickets receiving a draft. Three courses were open to Sukumaran, and they differed in more than the model: in who paid, in how soon customers saw the feature, and in how much Cinnabar had to learn before committing.

Exhibit 3. Monthly economics by option (₹ lakh unless stated)
LineA. Large, all accountsB. Small, paid add-onC. Self-hosted
Accounts served1,5004501,500
Drafts a month7,20,0002,16,0007,20,000
Model cost13.680.416.00
Add-on revenue0.009.000.00
Revenue less model cost-13.688.59-6.00

A and B: drafts × ₹1.90 and × ₹0.19 respectively. B assumes 30 per cent of accounts (450) adopt at ₹2,000 a month, averaging 600 tickets each. C is rented GPU capacity at a fixed ₹6.00 lakh and excludes engineers' time.

Option A ships the large model to every account. It matches rivals and gives the best drafts, but the ₹13.68 lakh monthly cost equals 6.5 per cent of revenue and would take gross margin to about 63.5 per cent with nothing coming back. It could ship within three weeks and would give Salian her answer for the two prospects.

Option B ships the small model as an add-on at ₹2,000 per account. It is cheap, fast and profitable, but its drafts are less often accepted, and the adoption rate is a guess. Customers who did not buy the add-on would see nothing, and the launch would slip to about four weeks while billing was configured. Sebastian's data gave no way to test what share of accounts would pay.

Option C hosts an open model in India. It answers the data-location worry, yet needs about four months, and at 7,20,000 drafts it costs more than option B's small model would for the same volume. The marginal cost of each draft would fall close to nothing, but the fixed bill would arrive in the first month, whether or not anyone used the feature, and Shetty's team would have to learn to run models in production.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. In Exhibit 1, which part of a draft drives its cost, and which lever would reduce it most? What does your answer imply for which engineers should work on the feature?
  2. Is the gap in Exhibit 2 large enough to matter, and to whom?
  3. Why does Exhibit 3 look so different for option B, and what must hold for 30 per cent adoption?
  4. Which option would you choose by Friday, and what evidence would make you change it?

7. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision as three questions: what goes into a call, what does a call cost, and who bears that cost. Input tokens make up 79 per cent of each large-model draft (₹1.50 of ₹1.90), though each costs a quarter of an output token, so the retrieved articles and the thread are the lever, not the length of the reply. A well-reasoned answer prices the feature per call before debating its quality.

One defensible path is option B with safeguards. The small model's acceptance of 77.0 per cent is lower, but agents review every draft, which reduces but does not remove the wrong-policy risk (4.5% of small-model drafts in the pilot, and Sebastian warns that tired agents trust fluent text). Cut retrieval from three articles to two, which would remove about one-sixth of input tokens, if each article runs near 1,000 tokens, and meter cost per account so heavy users show up early. Charge for the add-on because only then do the costs have revenue behind them.

Set a revisit trigger now and review at 90 days: if, on at least 1,000 drafts, acceptance falls below 70 per cent or wrong policy claims exceed 7 per cent, move long threads to the large model. Reject A because it spends margin without buying revenue, and C because it spends months and fixed cost to solve a problem the contract terms and an India-region endpoint may already solve. Salian's competitive worry is real, so test pricing with her two prospects first. Sebastian's request for evidence is also met, because the 90-day review turns his open questions into measurements taken on real tickets rather than six pilot customers.

A model in the product turns a one-time build cost into a running cost per use, and the first job of a product manager is to make that cost visible, assign it to someone who earns revenue from it, and decide in advance what result would send the team back to the choice of model.
exp20v2-tech.deploy:
Technical Fluency / Delivery & Technology

Deploying a web product

1. A Thursday in October

On Thursday, 8 October 2026, Hiral Parekh, head of product at Ghoomar Learning Labs, opened the planning board in a 14-person office in Pune and counted the days. A mock-test series for Class 10 board-exam candidates was due to open on Monday, 2 November, twenty-five days away. Forty partner schools had enrolled 300 students each, 12,000 in all, and each school was promised a first scheduled test on Sunday, 8 November, at 7 pm. It ran on the laptop of Ikram Sheikh, the lead engineer, but it was not yet on any address that a student in Nashik could type into a phone.

Ikram had put two proposals on the table. The first was to rent three virtual servers from a cloud provider and configure them by hand. The second was to push the code to a managed platform that would configure them on the team’s behalf. Hiral needed to choose which risks the company would carry on 8 November. If the site failed at 7 pm in front of 7,200 teenagers and their teachers, forty school relationships would be damaged in a single evening, and the renewals due in January would be a harder conversation. If the team spent three weeks building infrastructure, the product itself would stand still.

2. The idea

Deployment is the act of taking software that works on its builder’s machine and placing it on computers that stay switched on, connected to the internet and reachable under a stable name, so that strangers can use it. Three terms recur. A server is simply a computer whose job is to answer requests from other computers. A URL is the address a user types, such as mocktests.example. The production environment is the live copy that real users touch, as distinct from staging, a private rehearsal copy built to resemble production.

The problem deployment solves is the gap between “it works for me” and “it works for everyone, all the time.” Early web teams closed it by hand, copying files to a machine and hoping. Two developments changed this. Amazon Web Services began renting virtual servers by the hour in 2006, so that no firm needed to buy hardware. Heroku, founded in 2007, went further and let a developer push code with one command while the platform handled the machines; its engineers later published the “twelve-factor app” guidelines (2011) describing how to write software that such platforms can run. Jez Humble and David Farley’s Continuous Delivery (2010) added the discipline: release often, in small steps, through an automated path.

“Deploying is not copying code; it is choosing who answers the phone when a thousand people call at once, and making that choice repeatable.”

It names the two things a product manager must hold in mind: capacity under load, and repeatability of the release.

3. How it actually works

When a student types the URL, a chain of steps runs in under a second. First, the phone asks the Domain Name System (DNS), the internet’s directory, to translate the name into a numeric address. Paul Mockapetris designed DNS in 1983 so that people would not need to memorise numbers. Second, the phone opens an encrypted connection using HTTPS, which depends on a certificate, a digital document proving that the site owns its name. Free certificates arrived with Let’s Encrypt in 2015. Third, it reaches a load balancer, a traffic director that hands each request to one of several identical application servers. Fourth, the application server runs the product’s code and, where needed, asks the database for the student’s test paper.

Figure 1 shows the path. The dashed spare server illustrates a practice that is often left implicit: capacity is bought for the worst quarter-hour, not the average hour, and one extra machine is kept so that the loss of any single server does not take the product down.

Behind that live path sits a second one, the release pipeline. A developer saves a change in a shared code repository; an automated process builds the product, runs the tests, installs it on staging, and, after a person approves, replaces the production copy. Three further steps are rarely mentioned: configuration (secret passwords and settings are stored outside the code and differ between staging and production), migration (changes to the database’s structure are applied in a controlled order), and rollback (the ability to return to the previous version within minutes).

4. A worked example

Hiral asked Ikram to size the 8 November test. The inputs were these: 12,000 enrolled students; an assumption, taken from a pilot, that 60 per cent would log in during the first 15 minutes; and a measurement that each login produces about 12 requests (the page, its scripts, and several calls for the question paper). Peak traffic is rarely uniform, so Ikram applied a 3-times multiplier to the average. One application server, load-tested on staging, handled 150 requests per second.

StepWorkingResult
Students arriving in 15 minutes12,000 × 60%7,200
Requests generated7,200 × 1286,400
Average rate over 900 seconds86,400 ÷ 90096 per second
Peak rate96 × 3288 per second
Servers needed288 ÷ 150 = 1.92, rounded up2
Servers to buy2 plus 1 spare3

Rounding up matters: 1.92 servers is not purchasable, and a server run at 96 per cent of its limit has no margin. Now change one input. Suppose the schedule allows students to start any time in a two-hour window rather than a 7 pm rush. The same 86,400 requests spread across 7,200 seconds average 12 per second; at the 3-times multiplier that is 36 per second, or 0.24 of one server. One server would suffice, and two (with the spare) would be generous. Alternatively, suppose a live countdown timer polls the server so each login produces 30 requests rather than 12. Then 7,200 × 30 = 216,000 requests, an average of 240 per second, a peak of 720, and 720 ÷ 150 = 4.8, so 5 servers plus 1 spare, which is 6. A design choice made by a designer changed the infrastructure bill by a factor of two.

Monthly running cost (₹)A: servers by handB: managed platform
Application servers3 × 2,400 = 7,2002 × 3,600 + 40 = 7,240
Database3,5004,500
Load balancer1,8000 (included)
Total per month12,50011,740
Engineer setup time40 hours8 hours
Setup cost at ₹1,500 per hour60,00012,000
First three months (3 × monthly + setup)97,50047,220

Prices are illustrative round figures. Three months: A is 3 × 12,500 = 37,500 plus 60,000; B is 3 × 11,740 = 35,220 plus 12,000. The difference is ₹50,280, almost all of it engineer time. The platform runs two instances always and adds the third for the 8 test hours: 8 × ₹5 = ₹40.

In the 30-request design, option A always-on becomes 6 × 2,400 = 14,400, plus 3,500 and 1,800, or ₹19,700 a month, while an always-on B becomes 6 × 3,600 + 4,500 = ₹26,100. Yet if B runs two instances and scales to six only for the four two-hour Sunday tests, with each instance at ₹3,600 ÷ 720 hours = ₹5 per hour, four extra instances for 8 hours add 4 × 8 × 5 = ₹160, and the month costs 7,200 + 160 + 4,500 = ₹11,860. Paying only for the peak is the economic argument for managed platforms.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Deploying is not the same as releasing

Deployment puts code on servers; release exposes it to users. A team can deploy on Tuesday and switch the feature on for 5 per cent of schools on Thursday. Separating them shrinks the damage an error can do.

A server is not a product

Running is not the same as working. A site can answer every request and still return the wrong paper because a setting differs between staging and production.

Hosting types are points on a spectrum

Renting raw servers, using a platform, and using “serverless” functions (code that runs only when called) trade control against labour. More control means more engineering hours.

Load testing predicts only what you simulate

Ikram’s 150 requests per second came from a test that imitated typical students. It cannot reveal what a thousand students refreshing in panic will do.

The database is usually the real constraint

Application servers are easy to multiply, because they are identical. The database holds the only copy of the truth and is much harder to scale. When a figure like 150 per second is quoted, ask whether the database was in the test.

Where data lives is a business question

Student records fall under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. A Mumbai region affects speed, and may affect what a school’s lawyer will sign.

Rollback is a feature, not an afterthought

Ask how long to undo before asking how long to ship.

What deployment cannot tell you

A successful deployment says nothing about whether anyone wants the product. It proves reachability, not value, and it is silent until instrumentation is added.

6. Different products, different shapes

In a consumer product, traffic is spiky and unpredictable; the dominant risk is a sudden surge, so autoscaling and a content delivery network (a worldwide set of copies of static files) matter. In a B2B product, like Ghoomar’s school offering, load is predictable because the customer publishes a timetable, but the cost of failure is concentrated: one outage is felt by a whole institution, and contracts may demand written uptime commitments and data-location promises. A marketplace must keep two sides alive; a buyer-side surge can starve seller tools sharing one database.

Stage matters too. An early-stage company should buy labour with money: the managed platform in option B is correct when engineers are scarce. A large company often has a platform team, formal change approvals and separate environments for dozens of teams; there, the risk is not too little process but a release path so slow that teams batch changes into large, dangerous releases.

7. Common mistakes

Treating the first launch as the finish line

Symptom: the team celebrates, then needs two days to ship a one-line fix. Misunderstanding: deployment is an event rather than a repeatable path. Diagnostic: ask for a stopwatch run of a trivial change from saving to live.

Sizing for the average

Symptom: slow pages or errors in the first ten minutes of every scheduled event, then calm. Misunderstanding: total daily traffic was compared with capacity. Diagnostic: request the requests-per-second figure for the busiest 15 minutes and divide by tested capacity.

Secrets and settings living in people’s heads

Symptom: only one engineer can redeploy, and holidays become risks. Misunderstanding: configuration is treated as knowledge, not as a stored asset. Diagnostic: ask a second engineer to deploy to staging while the first watches silently.

Never testing the backup

Symptom: backups exist, yet nobody has restored one. Misunderstanding: a backup is judged by its creation, not its recovery. Diagnostic: restore last night’s copy into staging and time it.

8. What good looks like

In the best version of Hiral’s decision, the sizing table is written down before any vendor is chosen. A single command sends a change from the repository to staging, a load test replays the 7 pm rush at the 288-per-second peak, and a second engineer, not Ikram, performs the release. The team rehearses a rollback on 31 October and records that it took six minutes.

9. The decision, and what follows

Hiral chose option B, the managed platform, and told Ikram to retest the 150 requests per second after every design change. Her reasoning was arithmetic and honesty about scarcity. The first three months cost ₹47,220 against ₹97,500, and the ₹50,280 gap was nearly 34 hours of engineer time at ₹1,500 an hour, hours the team could spend on question quality instead. She also refused the live countdown poll, which would have taken the peak from 288 to 720 requests per second, and replaced it with a timer that runs on the student’s own phone. The first scheduled test, on 8 November, was to be preceded by a full rehearsal with two schools on 4 November.

Next, read web architecture basics, because the boxes in Figure 1 are the vocabulary of every conversation with engineers. Then study instrumentation with product analytics tools, since a product that cannot be measured is half shipped, along with the build log and testing basics, which decide whether the automated path can be trusted.

Two questions to sit with. First, which single input in your own product, such as a timer, a refresh, or a notification, could double your infrastructure need without anyone in a design review noticing? Second, if your most knowledgeable engineer were unreachable on release day, could someone else deploy and undo it within an hour?
exp40v2-tech.deploy:
Technical Fluency / Delivery & Technology

Deploying a web product

The economics of getting code in front of users, and what the field has not settled.

1. Two rooms, sixty days apart

On Tuesday, 15 September 2026, Purvi Raikar, vice-president of product at Qalam Reading Network in Bengaluru, had a media plan on one screen and a capacity report on the other. Qalam publishes serialised audio fiction in Hindi, Marathi and Tamil: 18,00,000 monthly active users, of whom 2,60,000 of 18,00,000, or 14.4 per cent, pay ₹149 monthly. That is ₹3.874 crore of monthly revenue against a cloud bill of ₹58 lakh, 15.0 per cent of it.

Qalam had sponsored a cricket broadcast on Saturday, 14 November 2026, sixty days away, to launch a new drama; the agency forecast 9,00,000 installs across that 72-hour weekend. Rameez Qadri, the principal engineer, had load-tested the platform on Friday, 3 July 2026 and found a ceiling of 3,600 requests per second. The plan implied a peak of 6,400. The question was not whether to buy capacity but which mechanism — pre-warming, autoscaling, edge caching or deliberate degradation — would absorb a seven-minute surge.

She had inherited a reason to care. On Sunday, 15 March 2026, a schema migration held a table lock for 11 minutes 40 seconds. Against the 43.2 minutes a month implied by a 99.9 per cent target, those 11.67 minutes spent 27.0 per cent of the budget in one evening.

Two days later, on Thursday, 17 September 2026, Pallavi Rathi faced the mirror image in Ahmedabad. Rasad Freight Exchange, where she was director of product, matches cement and steel shippers to truck fleets and reconciles their e-way bills. Eleven enterprise customers produced ₹7.48 crore of annual recurring revenue, an average of ₹68 lakh each. The largest, Rohtas Cement Industries, paid ₹1.4 crore — 18.7 per cent of revenue — and its deputy chief information officer, Rukmini Pendse, had sent a renewal rider: deploy inside Rohtas’s private network; release only on the first Saturday of each month, every change submitted to a change-advisory board ten working days ahead; and commit to 99.95 per cent availability, penalty 5 per cent of the quarterly fee — ₹1.75 lakh — per tenth of a point below. Rasad deployed fourteen times a week into one shared environment. Quresh Sanghvi, its chief technology officer, called this “a request to become a different company.”

2. The idea, and who disputes it

Deployment is the controlled transfer of a named version of software, with its configuration and its data schema, onto infrastructure serving real traffic under a stable name. Three clauses do the work. Named version: you must be able to say what is running. With configuration and schema: the parts that are not code cause most incidents. Controlled: the transfer must be reversible, observable and repeatable by someone other than its author.

Mark Burgess’s CFEngine (1993) introduced convergence: describe the state a machine should be in and let a program drive it there. Amazon’s EC2 (2006) turned a capital decision into an operating one. Humble and Farley’s Continuous Delivery (2010) argued that the release path is itself a product with a cycle time, and Heroku’s twelve-factor guidelines (2011) codified what software must do to be machine-deployable. Docker (2013) and Kubernetes (2014, from Google’s Borg) made the unit of deployment an immutable image, not a mutated server. Google’s Site Reliability Engineering (2016) supplied error budgets: an availability target is a licence to fail by a measured amount, and spending it is how you buy change. Accelerate (2018) found deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and restore time moving together rather than trading off.

“Deployment is not a step at the end of building. It is how a company converts decisions into evidence, and its cycle time is the company’s learning rate.”

Four schools disagree about what follows. The continuous-delivery school will sign that every merge should reach production automatically within the hour; it will not sign that a human approval gate adds safety. The reliability-engineering school will sign that an error budget should govern velocity, so a team that has exhausted its budget stops shipping features; it will not sign that velocity is intrinsically good. The platform school will sign that product teams should never configure infrastructure; it will not sign that every team should own its pipeline. The change-control school, which governs most enterprise deployment, will sign that production changes must be reviewed, scheduled and auditable with a named approver; it will not sign that automation substitutes for accountability.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice begins with a demand model, not a vendor, because capacity is bought for a quarter-hour and that quarter-hour must be named. Qadri took every coefficient from measurement: 48 requests per first session from the August 2026 cohort, the 2.5 peak-to-average ratio from two prior sponsorships, and the 2,400-per-second evening load from four weeks of 9 pm medians.

Two findings follow. The primary is comfortable, so the binding constraint is the tier easiest to add, which turns sizing into timing. And the 55 per cent absorbed at the edge is a product decision in disguise: personalise the launch screen and that share collapses, taking the origin peak towards 6,400 and the instances to 20.

Timing is where the arithmetic turns against autoscaling. Baseline evening traffic of 2,400 per second produces 1,080 at the origin, which four instances (4 × 320 = 1,280) serve with a small margin. Let origin demand rise linearly from 1,080 to 2,880 over the seven-minute ramp: 1,800 extra requests per second across 420 seconds is an increase of 4.286 every second. Capacity is breached at (1,280 − 1,080) ÷ 4.286 = 46.7 seconds. The autoscaler waits for two consecutive 60-second periods above threshold (120 seconds), and a new instance needs 190 seconds to be useful: 95 to pull the image, 60 to warm caches, 35 for health checks. Help arrives at 46.7 + 120 + 190 = 356.7 seconds, when demand is 1,080 + (4.286 × 356.7) = 2,609 per second against 1,280.

Shortening detection invites flapping and the 190-second boot is mostly physics, so capacity must be bought before the event.

Pre-warming is usually presented as paying a premium for safety; here it is cheapest, because autoscaling holds a floor across all 72 hours while pre-warming buys a block against a known window. Elasticity is valuable when demand is unpredictable; when it follows a broadcast schedule, a calendar beats a control loop.

4. The conditions, stated as claims

Four testable claims decide whether the standard continuous-deployment answer applies. One: the cost of a bad release is bounded and recoverable. Largely true for Qalam, whose rollback median is 4 minutes 20 seconds. False for Rasad: a failed release in a Rohtas dispatch window strands trucks at a weighbridge, and no rollback recovers a lorry that left. Two: you control the release calendar. Qalam does; Rasad does not. Three: one production environment serves all customers. True for Qalam by construction; for Rasad it is the question. Four: demand is unpredictable. False for Qalam on 14 November, which is why elasticity is the wrong instrument, and false for Rasad, whose load follows dispatch schedules.

The idea becomes actively misleading when deployment frequency is imported as a goal into a context whose constraint lies elsewhere. Rasad could deploy fifty times a week and Rohtas would still see twelve changes a year; chasing the first number while the second is fixed builds an untested backlog at the gate — the opposite of the small-batch logic that justified frequent deployment.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

The multi-tenant seam is the most expensive, and its precedent price is computable.

Exhibit 4. Rasad’s monthly infrastructure, shared versus single-tenant (₹ per month).

Eleven single-tenant estates would cost 11 × 1,71,000 = ₹18,81,000 a month, which is 18,81,000 ÷ 3,86,000 = 4.87 times the shared figure — ₹14.95 lakh a month more, or ₹1.794 crore a year. Log retention reflects the CERT-In direction of April 2022: 180 days of logs, incidents reported within six hours.

Annualised, the shared estate costs ₹46.32 lakh against ₹748 lakh of revenue, or 6.19 per cent; eleven private estates would cost ₹225.72 lakh of 748, or 30.2 per cent — a different business. Yet for Rohtas alone the number is modest: ₹20.52 lakh a year against a ₹1.4 crore contract, and since Rohtas is about 31 per cent of platform load its allocated share of the shared estate is already ₹14.36 lakh. The premium is ₹6.16 lakh, 4.4 per cent of the contract. The decision is about precedent: can Rasad say yes to Rohtas and no to the other ten, averaging ₹60.8 lakh?

Other seams recur. In two-sided products, a release safe for shippers can starve fleet operators, because both sides share a database and the shipper side generates the writes. In regulated contexts — SEBI’s cloud framework, the Reserve Bank of India’s payment-data storage direction of 2018, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — the deployment region becomes a contractual term, and “we will move to a Mumbai region later” costs a migration. At Rachana Devices Group, whose fuel-flow meters report to a web back end, that back end deploys hourly but the firmware cannot, so every deployment serves two protocol versions. At Qiyas Inference Labs, a 14-gigabyte weight file pushes the 190-second boot in Figure 1 towards fifteen minutes, killing autoscaling as a surge response.

Mature companies handle these seams less tidily than they describe. The stated process is a platform team offering a paved road; the practice is that road for the median service plus a hand-built exception for the two services that earn most, kept alive by one engineer who remembers how.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Deployment frequency is a symptom, not an objective

Frequency correlates with safety because both follow from a short, automated, reversible path; raising it on a path that is none of those raises risk alone. The tell-tale sign is a team told to deploy daily that now batches two days of work into a nightly window.

The scarce resource is lead time, not compute

Compute is purchasable within the hour; the interval between a decision and evidence about it is not. The tell-tale sign is a leader who quotes the cloud bill to the rupee but not how long a one-line copy change takes to reach a user. Lead time reads as an efficiency metric; it is the learning rate’s denominator.

Autoscaling cannot win a race against a marketing calendar

Control loops respond to the past, and a broadcast-driven ramp outruns detection plus boot. The tell-tale sign is a runbook with a scaling policy and no pre-warm step, or a campaign calendar engineering never saw.

The migration is the deployment

Code is immutable and can be swapped back; data has moved and cannot. Qalam’s March incident was a lock held by an ALTER TABLE on a 4,20,00,000-row table, not a code failure. The tell-tale sign is a release plan with a step called “deploy” and none called “migrate”.

Capacity ceilings are usually connection limits, not processors

Qalam’s July rehearsal found that 11 instances holding 40 database connections each want 440 against a primary configured for 300, so the eighth instance (8 × 40 = 320) starts being refused while every processor graph looks calm. The tell-tale sign is a load test quoting utilisation but not connections.

Canary duration must be derived from the defect rate you fear

A twenty-minute canary is a habit, not a measurement. The tell-tale sign is a policy stating a duration without stating what it should detect. As Exhibit 5 shows, the requests you must expose are fixed by the defect rate, so fraction and time trade against each other.

Your customer’s change-control process is part of your architecture

Rathi cannot plan a January launch on her own cadence if Rohtas’s board meets monthly and wants ten working days’ notice. The tell-tale sign is a roadmap assuming the supplier’s rhythm for a customer with a published one. Read as bureaucracy, it is misread: it constrains iteration speed.

“Zero downtime” means zero downtime for the median request

A rolling replacement that drains connections cleanly still abandons long-lived ones, so an audio stream or an upload breaks while the dashboard records a flawless release. The tell-tale sign is availability measured by a prober issuing short requests.

7. Differences by product type and stage

Three differences are real. Consumer products face unpredictable demand and cheap individual failure, so they optimise for reversibility and edge absorption. Enterprise and regulated products face predictable demand and expensive contractual failure, so they optimise for auditability and scheduled windows; Rasad’s constraint is a document, not a load curve. Platforms add backward compatibility: the oldest client in the field sets the pace.

Two claimed differences are not real. Mobile apps supposedly escape deployment concerns, but store review and upgrade lag mean several versions hit one back end at once. And hardware and AI products are called fundamentally different; the difference is quantitative, not conceptual.

Stage changes the binding constraint, not the principles. Below roughly twenty engineers it is attention: buy a managed platform and accept its opinions. Between twenty and two hundred it is coordination, and a platform team earns its cost. Above that it is heterogeneity. Rasad, with nineteen engineers, sits at the first boundary.

8. Three worked examples

The failure. On Sunday, 15 March 2026, Qalam shipped a migration adding a defaulted column to a table of 4,20,00,000 rows; the statement held a table-level lock for 700 seconds. At 2,100 requests per second, 2,100 × 700 = 14,70,000 requests were affected, of which 8,52,600 — 58 per cent — returned an error. No rollback was possible: the deployment could be reversed, the half-applied migration could not.

The cost appeared the next week: 3,400 cancellations against a seven-day baseline of 1,250, an excess of 2,150; at ₹149 each that is ₹3,20,350 of monthly recurring revenue, or ₹38,44,200 annualised at the same rate. The recovery was a different pattern. Re-expressed as expand-and-contract, the change backfilled in batches of 50,000 rows: 4,20,00,000 ÷ 50,000 = 840 batches, each 1.3 seconds of work plus a 0.2-second pause, so 840 × 1.5 = 1,260 seconds, or 21 minutes — and no user-visible errors, because it never held a lock. Elapsed time is the wrong objective function for a migration; held locks are the right one.

The rehearsal. Qalam’s load test of 3 July 2026 found its 3,600-per-second ceiling set by the 300-connection limit, not by processors. Pieter Rooijakkers, Qalam’s reliability engineer in Amsterdam, made the point: the number was an artifact of a configuration file. After a pooler multiplexed 440 client connections onto 120 server connections, a ratio of 3.67 to one, the same hardware passed a retest at 6,400 per second.

The canary. Rasad serves 480 requests per second at its origin, so a 5 per cent canary receives 24 and a 50 per cent canary 240. Pranay Lokhande, its release engineer, worked out what each could detect.

Exhibit 5. Requests that must be exposed to observe ten failures at a given defect rate, and how long that takes.
Defect rateRequests to exposeAt 5 per cent (24/s)At 50 per cent (240/s)
1 in 4004,000167 s17 s
1 in 5,00050,0002,083 s (34.7 min)208 s (3.5 min)
