Requests exposed are identical in the last two columns — 4,000, 50,000 and 4,00,000. Fraction and duration trade against each other; their product does not move.

Rasad’s policy was a 5 per cent canary for 20 minutes, exposing 24 × 1,200 = 28,800 requests. That detects a one-in-400 defect decisively: 28,800 ÷ 400 = 72 observed errors against 28,800 ÷ 5,000 = 5.76 expected at baseline, an elevation of 72 ÷ 5.76 = 12.5 times. It is blind to a one-in-40,000 defect, which yields 0.72 expected errors. Since the reconciliation errors Rasad fears are exactly that rare, the policy was theatre: such defects need shadow-traffic comparison running for days.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Sizing against the average. Early sign: errors confined to the first ten minutes of every scheduled event, then calm. Diagnostic: requests per second in the busiest fifteen minutes, divided by tested capacity. Caught late, the cost falls on the one day the company bought attention for.

An untested rollback. Early sign: the procedure exists in a document and has never been timed. Diagnostic: when was it last run against production, and by whom? Caught late, the team discovers mid-incident that rollback needs a schema reversal nobody wrote.

Configuration drift. Early sign: a defect that reproduces in production but not on staging. Diagnostic: diff the two configurations and ask who can change production’s without review. Caught late, staging stops carrying information.

An error budget spent unnoticed. Early sign: nobody can state the month’s remaining allowance. Diagnostic: minutes of unavailability this month against target — 43.2 at 99.9 per cent, 21.6 at 99.95. Caught late, a penalty arrives before the engineering conversation does.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does a human approval gate add safety? The continuous-delivery position, resting on the DORA research programme, is that approvals by people distant from the change do not reduce failure rates but do lengthen lead time. The change-control reply is that DORA’s evidence is self-reported survey data from volunteers in mostly unregulated firms, and that where failure has legal consequences a named approver is an accountability mechanism, not a safety one. The first is wrong if failure rates fall where gates are strongest, controlling for batch size; the second if approvers approve without reading.

Who should own production? “You build it, you run it” holds that separating authors from operators destroys the feedback that makes software operable. The reliability-engineering reply is that operational expertise is a specialism, that error budgets give a separate team a principled way to refuse an unsafe release, and that nineteen engineers cannot each carry a pager. The first falls if on-call degrades quality beyond the operability it buys; the second if that team becomes a queue.

Is multi-region a resilience gain? One camp treats a second region as the answer to correlated failure. The other observes that failover paths are rarely exercised, that replication introduces consistency bugs, and that several large outages were caused by the failover machinery rather than the thing it guarded. For Rasad, writing against 99.95 per cent, 21.6 minutes a month is close enough to the cost of a failover mistake to leave the question open.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this arrives at a launch review with a demand model rather than a request for more servers, and can name every coefficient’s source. They ask about undo before ship, and have a timed number for it. They read a marketing calendar as an infrastructure document and a customer’s change-control policy as an architectural constraint, and own the release path as a product with a cycle time.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Raikar chose option C: pre-warm to 11 instances and 3 replicas for the six hours around the broadcast, keep the autoscaler as a backstop beyond the window, and hold the edge share at 55 per cent by refusing to personalise the launch screen. She also set a degradation rule in advance — above 3,200 origin requests per second, beyond the 2,880 forecast but inside the 3,520 that 11 instances serve, recommendations would come from cache and the listening-history write be queued — because what to sacrifice is better decided in September than at 9.14 pm on 14 November.

Rathi neither accepted Pendse’s rider nor refused it. She offered Rohtas a single-tenant estate at a disclosed ₹6.16 lakh annual premium, with the monthly window and the advisory-board submission, on two conditions: that Rohtas use the shared staging environment for testing, and that security and regulatory fixes be exempt from the ten-day notice. The premium was affordable and the precedent was not, so the price should sit visibly in the contract.

Three questions. First, Raikar’s pre-warm was cheaper and safer than autoscaling; under what conditions does that inversion hold, and what does it imply where demand is genuinely unpredictable? Second, if the exposure invariant in Exhibit 5 cannot be beaten, what gate replaces the canary for rare defects, and who pays for the days it takes? Third, if six of the eleven customers accept the ₹6.16 lakh premium, Rasad’s infrastructure share of revenue roughly doubles — where should Rathi have refused?

13. Going deeper

AI-assisted building is where the artifact now comes from, which shifts the bottleneck to the pipeline. Web architecture basics for PMs supplies the tiers in Exhibit 2 as vocabulary. Instrumentation with product analytics tools made 48 requests per first session a measurement rather than a guess. The build log is the audit trail an advisory board actually wants, and testing and quality basics decides whether an automated suite can be trusted enough to remove a human gate. How web and mobile apps work explains the multi-version problem store review creates; APIs and integration basics and reading an architecture diagram are prerequisites for backward compatibility. Data modelling for PMs and databases, storage and caching are where expand-and-contract and the 1.6 queries per request come from, and cloud infrastructure basics prices the instance-hours in Exhibit 3.
case20v1-tech.deploy:
Thaal: The Link That Slept

A decision case on deploying a web product

1. Opening

At 9:30 on Monday 19 October 2026, Ekjot Lehal sat in Thaal's Pune office with a laptop open to a web address that had embarrassed him four days earlier. Singapore was on the call at noon, Dubai at eight, and Elvin Lakhanpal in New Jersey at midnight, still awake because the deal was his. Nobody on the call disputed that the product worked. The dispute was about everything around it: the machine it ran on, the address people typed, and who would answer when it failed at lunchtime.

The Dubai facilities group that had agreed to a three-campus pilot of Thaal's lunch pre-ordering product wanted an answer by Friday 23 October: where would the product live, and would it be reachable by employees on Monday 2 November, six days before Diwali? Ekjot, Thaal's head of product, had three ways to get it online and a week in which to defend one of them to a team that disagreed.

2. Company background

Thaal was founded in Pune in 2023 and employs fourteen people. It sells a simple promise to cafeteria operators: employees choose lunch on their phones before 11:30, collect it at a counter and skip the queue. Until this year the service ran on WhatsApp messages and a form, for two Pune cafeterias, and earned about ₹84 lakh in the last financial year.

Swiggy and Zomato already feed office parks through delivery, and meal-card issuers such as Pluxee and Zeta hold the payment relationship. Thaal competes where delivery cannot reach: the campus counter. Payments go through UPI on Razorpay, so Thaal never stores card details. Its customers are cafeteria operators and the facilities groups that hire them, not the employees who eat, which matters here: an operator judges Thaal by whether the counter queue disappears, and a single failed lunch hour is remembered for months. Thaal's seed investors expect the pilot to anchor a funding conversation in the new year.

3. The situation

Over three weeks Ekjot and Eshwin Lidder, the engineering lead, built a web version with AI coding assistants. It works. But it lives on a free preview address that goes to sleep when idle. On Thursday 15 October, fourteen people from the Dubai group opened it together. The page took nine seconds to appear, and two staff gave up. Afterwards Eshwin noticed that the database password was written into the code repository.

The group's IT team then asked two questions Ekjot could not answer: where employee phone numbers are stored, and who can get at them under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. The pilot fee is ₹1.5 lakh a month, conditional on going live on 2 November.

The team sees this from three time zones. Eshwin, in Bengaluru, wants a foundation he will not be woken for at night. Esther Lubana, in Singapore, takes the Dubai group's calls and needs a stable address. Elvin, awake at night in New Jersey, wants the date held and hears every technical caution as delay. Exhibit 1 sizes the load; Exhibit 2 prices the choices; Exhibit 3 sets them against the calendar.

4. The people

Ekjot Lehal, Pune, head of product, owns the decision. He wants a pilot that works on day one and does not become a wasted rebuild. He is not an engineer, and the AI-assisted build has made him confident about features and unsure about everything beneath them.

Eshwin Lidder, Bengaluru, engineering lead, has seven years of experience and would be the only person on call. He prefers a proper cloud setup he controls, and says plainly that a link which works in demonstrations is not a service.

Esther Lubana, Singapore, customer success lead, wants one fixed address, a status page and named support hours, because every outage reaches her first, and because Dubai's afternoon is her evening.

Elvin Lakhanpal, New Jersey, sales head, closed the pilot. A rollout to nine more campuses will be decided in January, and he wants 2 November kept, since a late pilot makes January harder to win.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 turns the pilot into traffic. About 800 orders arrive daily, and 640 of them fall between 10:30 and 11:30, an average of 10.7 a minute. That is modest on average, so raw capacity is not the worry. Reliability is: the hour is short, every user arrives at once, and Thursday's nine-second page, repeated at 11:00, would turn hungry employees back to the old queue. Exhibit 1 also shows why Hinjewadi matters most, carrying 304 of the 640 peak orders.

Exhibit 2 prices the three options in thousands of rupees. Option A costs ₹12,000 a month against ₹9,000 for B, a gap of ₹3,000 on a ₹1.5 lakh fee. B's extra ₹1.08 lakh of setup would take 36 months to recover. The real difference is in days, and in who carries the risk of a failure at lunchtime.

Exhibit 3 places the options on the calendar. Only A is ready before the date; B finishes after it, and C is not close.

6. The options

Option A: a managed platform. Connect the code repository to a hosting service such as Render or Railway, choose its Mumbai-region setup, add a managed database with daily backups, a staging copy, HTTPS and a company domain. Secrets move out of the code. Live three working days after start, with one-click rollback and almost no operations work. A failed release can be reversed in minutes, and the bill is a known monthly number. The cost is platform limits, a slightly higher bill and some lock-in.

Option B: Eshwin builds on AWS Mumbai. One rented server, a database and scripts to publish new versions. It gives control and the lowest monthly bill. But it needs twelve working days of Eshwin's time, finishes after 2 November and leaves him as the only person who can repair it. A server patch, a full disk or an expired certificate would each need him, wherever he is.

Option C: build the full platform first. Containers, automated tests and monitoring, done properly. It is the cleanest end state and the slowest. Dubai would be asked to move the pilot to December, past Diwali. It would also leave Elvin with nothing to show his customer for six weeks.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What must be true for real users to reach Thaal reliably on 2 November, and which of those did Thursday's demo show to be missing?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, what load does the pilot create, and does it strain any option?
  3. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, what does each option cost in rupees and in days, and which cost matters more here?
  4. Which option would you choose, what would make you change it, and what must be true on 2 November whichever you choose?

8. A note for the learner

Deployment is the last step of building. A product running on your laptop or a preview link is not yet reachable. Four questions frame it: where does the code run, how does a new version get there, how do we know it is up, and how do we undo a mistake.

A strong answer is specific about what a live product needs, and it first finds the binding constraint. Here it is time, not money. The monthly gap between A and B is ₹3,000, two per cent of the fee, and recovering B's extra setup would take 36 months. B cannot be ready by 2 November at all, and C abandons the pilot to be tidy.

One defensible path is Option A, with conditions met before go-live: a company domain with HTTPS; separate staging and production; secrets removed from the repository and the database password changed; one test restore from backup; a ₹1 live UPI order through Razorpay; an uptime alert to Eshwin and Esther covering 10:30 to 11:30 IST; and a rehearsed rollback. Ekjot should tell the Dubai group's IT team where the data sits and who has access, in writing, before Friday.

Revisit B only if January's rollout to nine more campuses is signed and the hosting bill passes ₹30,000 a month (a judgement trigger, not derived here), because, if each new campus matches the pilot average, 12 campuses would carry about four times the pilot's load. The decision is a staged one, and the reasoning matters more than the label. A learner who picks B on cost alone, or C on elegance, has answered a different question from the one the calendar asked. Whichever option a class prefers, it should say what evidence would change its mind.
case40v1-tech.deploy:
Vyapti Commerce Technologies: Eight Nights to the Freeze

A Pune platform company has rebuilt the web product 118 brands sell through, and has until the end of October to put it on the live URLs. A 2024 onboarding shortcut may stop it.

1. The night before

At twenty to eleven on the night of Friday 16 October 2026, the garba in the society behind Vyapti Commerce Technologies' Baner office was still going, and Gatik Minhas had shut the window against it. Vyapti's vice-president of product had a steering committee at half past nine on Monday morning and a slide with three columns on it that he did not believe.

Vyapti ran the storefronts 118 Indian consumer brands sold through, and since April had been rebuilding that product. The new stack, V3, was faster, cheaper to run and the only version that could be hosted in the Gulf; 37 tenants were already on it. The remaining 81 included all eleven tenants that paid for most of the company. Vyapti's peak-season change freeze would begin at the midnight opening Saturday 31 October and run to Monday 16 November: eleven possible cutover windows left, and after the blackouts, eight. Vaqar Retail Group in Dubai had a contractual go-live on Monday 2 November, inside the freeze. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November.

That afternoon something had opened rather than closed. The card-on-file token files lodged with the networks on Friday 2 October had completed their fourteen-day processing, so from today 23 tenants could legally take a payment on V3. The other 58 could not. Minhas had spent the evening deciding whether that number was a constraint or a mercy.

2. How Vyapti got here

Gunvir Munjal and two colleagues founded Vyapti in Pune in 2019 on a narrow bet: brands wanted their own storefront on their own domain, not a stall in a marketplace, and wanted it this week. By FY26 the platform carried ₹6,420 crore of gross merchandise value and earned Vyapti ₹142 crore, of which ₹86.0 crore was a platform fee of 1.34 per cent on GMV (Exhibit 1).

The decision that shapes October was taken in April 2024 and was, at the time, obviously correct. Onboarding was losing to Shopify on one step: pointing a brand's domain at Vyapti needed its DNS zone moved to a provider supporting an alias at the apex, which took the agency two weeks. Gomtesh Mokha's team shipped an alternative in nine days: publish one load-balancer address, 203.0.113.17, and tell the brand to set a single A record at the apex. Ten minutes, no migration, no agency. Fifty-one of the 118 tenants came in that way.

What nobody minuted was that an A record is a promise about an address, not about a service. A tenant on an alias can be moved by Vyapti alone, in the time a cache takes to expire; a tenant on an apex A record can only be moved by its own DNS operator. Figure 1 shows the two paths, and the asymmetry is the whole of Vyapti's October problem.

3. The industry

Vyapti sat between two kinds of competitor. Above it were the global platforms — Shopify most of all — which brands reached for when they wanted certainty. Beside it were Zoho Commerce and Unicommerce, and the ONDC network, which was making a brand's own storefront less of a moat and more of a shopfront among many. Below it, demand was being reshaped by Flipkart, Meesho and Reliance Retail at one end and Zepto and Swiggy Instamart at the other: a site taking three and a half seconds to paint was judged against ten-minute delivery.

Regulation bore on the deployment directly, not as background. The Reserve Bank's card-on-file tokenisation rules meant a saved card on V2 did not work on V3 until the networks re-mapped the tokens, on their clock and not Vyapti's. GST e-invoicing required each tenant's GSTIN to be re-whitelisted against the new invoice endpoint, seven days per tenant. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed what could move where, and Vaqar's regulator required Gulf customer records stay in the UAE — which V2, a single Mumbai deployment, could not do at all.

4. What happened, what was believed, and what turned out to be wrong

The V3 programme was funded on Wednesday 1 April 2026 with ₹14.6 crore and a target of every tenant by 30 September. Vaqar's master agreement was signed on Monday 11 May, with go-live on 2 November. The first tenant, a Jaipur home-linen brand, went live on 15 June; by Saturday 1 August there were 19, and the runbook was declared stable.

Three things were believed in that period. The first was that no tenant need act: the edge vendor's documentation offered an alias at the apex, and the plan assumed Vyapti would re-point every zone. On Saturday 12 September the vendor confirmed in writing that the alias works only where it also hosts the zone. Forty-five of the 81 unmigrated tenants sit on an apex A record with the zone hosted elsewhere, which is 56 per cent of them.

The second was that the 37 completed migrations proved the method. Exhibit 2 sets that plan against what was observed. Six of the 37 were apex tenants whose DNS step ran a median of nineteen hours, performed by somebody who did not work for Vyapti.

The third was that V3 paid for itself immediately. Mutreja's North America annexe of Thursday 3 September quotes a p75 largest-contentful-paint of 1.9 seconds, the figure on that week's dashboard. Migrations were paused after the 37th on Monday 14 September; on Tuesday 13 October Mangat circulated Exhibit 4 with a note saying it would not survive a referee. On Wednesday 14 October the database vendor quoted six weeks — no earlier than 25 November — to raise the replication cap. Finance circulated Exhibit 5 on 15 October, and the crawl behind Exhibit 1 the same day.

8. The options as Minhas sees them

Path A — stage what is legal. Cut over the 23 token-ready tenants — two enterprise, neither of them Vanamala, seven growth and fourteen long tail — across the eight open windows, which costs 34 of the 48 slots, and leave 58 on V2 through peak, dual-running both stacks. Eleven of the 23 sit on apex A records. Vaqar misses 2 November unless the freeze is broken for it. Finance puts this at ₹195.6 lakh. It does not attempt the nine remaining enterprise tenants, which is where Munjal's diligence problem lives; Exhibit 5's ₹120 lakh provision is the only place it appears.

Path B — one night. Take all 81 on the morning of Friday 30 October. Exhibit 5 costs this at ₹153.4 lakh, the cheapest column; Exhibit 3 says the night holds six slots.

Path C — defer to January. Freeze V3, run peak on V2, migrate from the second week of January. Exhibit 5 puts it at ₹592.0 lakh against the ₹340 lakh left in the programme, so it is a board decision.

Madaan's margin note on the printed copy reads: "fourth column — stop calling it a migration."

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Time. Eleven windows, eight open, the last on the morning of Friday 30 October; the freeze runs from midnight opening Saturday 31 October to Monday 16 November (Exhibit 6). A window is 02:00 to 05:30 IST — 22:30 the previous evening in Berlin until the 25th and 21:30 after it, and 16:30 the previous afternoon in Newark and Toronto until 1 November.

Money. Of ₹14.6 crore funded on 1 April, ₹11.2 crore was spent to 15 October, leaving ₹3.4 crore, or ₹340 lakh.

People. Six platform engineers, two on duty per window, four available from 27 October.

Regulation. Tokens for 23 tenants cleared today; the next lodgement clears 2 November. Each GSTIN needs seven days of e-invoice re-whitelisting. Vaqar's records must stay in the UAE, which only V3 can do.

Contracts. Vaqar: go-live 2 November, ₹182 lakh of credits. Vanamala Silks, the largest tenant at ₹1,106 crore of FY26 GMV, renews on 30 November under a clause barring platform changes within 21 days of a designated sale event; Diwali on 8 November closes that window from Sunday 18 October.

At ten to midnight Minhas had a message to Munjal written and not sent. The garba had stopped. Behind the draft, the 23 token-ready tenants were listed in green, and 203.0.113.17 was still answering for 42 domains, or 45, that belonged to somebody else.
